sens: Eldest son of the prophet Samuel, judge in Israel during the united monarchy
Levite, father of the singer Heman who served in the temple
H3100G.detail:
1. Joel is the eldest son of the prophet Samuel. He is also called Vashni ("the second"), a name that emphasizes that he is the first of the two sons that Samuel had with his wife. Along with his brother Abijah, he was a judge at Beersheba, responsible for administering justice to the people, according to the customs of the time (1 Samuel 8:2).
2. Joel is also the father of the singer Heman, an important Levite who officiated in the temple worship during the reign of King David. Heman led the music and sacred songs, which shows that Joel belonged to the tribe of Levi and to the priestly family dedicated to the service of God (1 Chronicles 6:33 and 15:17).
H3100G.origine: The name Joel means "Yahweh is God" (from "Yahweh" and "El," which means god). This name expresses a confession of faith: the one who bears it proclaims that the Lord is God. Several men bore this name in ancient Israel, notably the prophet whose book is included in the Bible, but this article specifically concerns the son of Samuel.
H3100G.emploi: Joel, son of Samuel, appears in three biblical references. First in 1 Samuel 8:2, where we learn that he was a judge with his brother Abijah at Beersheba, suggesting that Samuel entrusted an important responsibility to his sons. Then, he appears twice in 1 Chronicles: he is named Vashni in chapter 6:28, and presented as the father of the famous singer Heman in chapters 6:33 and 15:17. These mentions show that Joel was a man of the tribe of Levi and that his descendants played a significant role in Israelite worship.
H3100G.portee: The story of Joel and his brother Abijah illustrates an important reality of spiritual life: the responsibility of parents to pass on faith to their children does not guarantee that all children will live it correctly. Although Samuel was a godly man and a great prophet, his sons did not walk in his ways, which caused a crisis in Israel and led the people to demand a king (1 Samuel 8:3-5). However, Joel's descendants, through his son Heman, magnificently contributed to the worship of the Lord, showing that God can use subsequent generations to restore what was broken.

sens: A chief of the tribe of Simeon during the divided monarchy
H3100H.detail: 1. Joel is a man from the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms (after the death of Solomon). He appears in a genealogy of the chiefs of Simeon in 1 Chronicles 4:35, where he is named among the ancestors of an important family of his tribe.
H3100H.origine: The name Joel means "Yahweh is God": it is formed from two Hebrew elements, Yo (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh) and El (God). It is a very common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several distinct biblical characters. The same name also designates the prophet who authored the book of Joel, although they are different individuals.
H3100H.emploi: This Joel of Simeon is cited only once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 4:35. It is a simple mention in a list of descendants of Simeon, with no details about his life or actions. Unlike other Joels in the Old Testament (notably the prophet), this character plays no narrative role and is known only by this single reference.

sens: A man from the tribe of Reuben during the divided monarchy
H3100I.detail: 1. Joel is a man from the tribe of Reuben, who lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the north and the south. He is the father of Schemaiah, as indicated by the text of 1 Chronicles 5:4 which lists his descendants.
H3100I.origine: The name Joel means "Yahweh is God" in Hebrew. It comes from the combination of two elements: the divine name Yah (or Yahweh) and el (God). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by many individuals in biblical history, including the prophet Joel son of Pethuel, one of the twelve minor prophets.
H3100I.emploi: This particular Joel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:4, where he is mentioned as an ancestor in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben. He belongs to the period of the divided monarchy and is known only by his position in this family genealogy.

sens: A man from the tribe of Reuben during the divided monarchy
H3100J.detail: Joel is an ancestor mentioned only once in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben. He is the father of Shema, from whom Bela descended, who lived in the region of Aroer (1 Chronicles 5:8). This character belongs to the period when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms.
H3100J.origine: The name Joel means "the Lord is God" or "God is eternal." It is formed from two elements: "Yo" (a contraction of the divine name Yahweh) and "El" (God). This theophoric name expresses a statement of faith: the one who bears it confesses that the Lord is the true God. Several people bear this name in the Old Testament, notably the prophet Joel, son of Pethuel, author of the book that bears his name.
H3100J.emploi: This Joel is a man from the tribe of Reuben mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 5:8 in a genealogy. He appears as an ancestor of Bela, a chief or notable of the tribe. The context indicates that he lived during the divided monarchy, a period when the tribes of Israel maintained their distinct territories. His appearance in this genealogical record shows the importance of preserving the memory of significant tribal lines in Israel.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H3100K.detail: 1. Joel is a chief of the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in the historical books of the Bible. He appears in the list of Gadite chiefs at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the northern and southern kingdoms (1 Chronicles 5:12).
H3100K.origine: The name Joel literally means "The Lord is God": it combines the divine name Yah (root of the tetragrammaton) and El ("God"). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several men in the Old Testament, the most famous being the prophet Joel, author of the book that bears his name.
H3100K.emploi: Joel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:12, among the listed chiefs of Gad during the reign of Joash, king of Israel. He is presented as the first in this list of Gadite dignitaries, suggesting his relative importance among the chiefs of his tribe at that time.

sens: Chief of the tribe of Issachar during the divided monarchy
H3100L.detail: 1. Joel is a chief of Issachar mentioned only once in the Bible: he is the son of Izrahiah and the brother of Michael, Obadiah, and Ishiah (1 Chronicles 7:3). His name means "the Lord is God" in Hebrew, expressing the conviction that God alone deserves this divine title.
H3100L.origine: The name Joel comes from the combination of two Hebrew elements: "Yo" (the Lord, abbreviated from the divine name) and "El" (God). This confessing structure is typical of Israelite names, which often proclaim divine identity or power. The name appears for at least thirteen different individuals in the Old Testament, but here it specifically designates a prince of the tribe of Issachar.
H3100L.emploi: This Joel of 1 Chronicles 7:3 appears only once in the provided references. He is presented as one of the five sons of Izrahiah who were chiefs of their house during the time of the divided monarchy (when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah existed separately). His inclusion in this genealogy shows his role in the administration and leadership of his tribe, but no details of his life or actions are conveyed.

sens: Warrior of David's army
H3100M.detail: Joel is a proper name referring to a man who served in King David's army, brother of the warrior Nathan. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:38, among the list of mighty warriors ("the valiant men") who made up the king's personal guard.
H3100M.origine: The name Joel means "The Lord is God" in Hebrew, formed from two elements: "Yo" (the Lord) and "El" (God). It was a name borne by several people in Israel, notably the prophet Joel whose book is included in the biblical canon. This name expresses a statement of faith at the very heart of the name given to the child.
H3100M.emploi: Joel the warrior appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 11:38. He is listed among the "mighty men" (valiant warriors) who joined David. The Bible designates him as the brother of Nathan, also an elite warrior, suggesting a family of renowned soldiers in the service of the king. This enumeration of David's warriors shows how the king gathered around him courageous and faithful men for the defense of the kingdom.

sens: A Levite during the time of King David, chief of the sons of Gershom
H3100N.detail: 1. Joel is a chief Levite mentioned in the organization of worship under King David. He is presented as the chief of the sons of Gershom, one of the three main families of Levites (1 Chronicles 15:7). He also appears alongside other important Levites, Uriel, Asaph, and others, called by David to participate in solemn religious ceremonies (1 Chronicles 15:11). This Joel represents a figure of liturgical responsibility in the temple of Jerusalem during David's time.
H3100N.origine: The name Joel means "the Lord is God" in Hebrew (yô = the Lord, and ël = God). It is a classic theophoric name in the Old Testament, formed from the divine name and an attribute of God. Several people bore this name in the Bible, which reflects its popularity among the Israelites.
H3100N.emploi: This Joel is a Levite who holds a position of responsibility during the time of King David. He appears in the context of the organization of worship and the transport of the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem. The only two mentions designate him as chief of the sons of Gershom (a subdivision of the tribe of Levi) and as a participant in the ceremonies personally orchestrated by King David, alongside other important Levites.
H3100N.portee: This character illustrates the essential role of the Levites in temple worship under the Israelite monarchy. It reminds us that divine service required a hierarchical organization and that men dedicated their lives to this liturgical order established by God.

sens: Levite son of Laadan, brother of Zetham and Jehiieli, keeper of the temple treasury
H3100O.detail: Joel is a Levite of the lineage of Laadan, mentioned in the lists from the time of King David. He was the brother of Zetham and one of the sons of Jehiieli (or Jehiel according to text variants). Along with his brother Zetham, he was responsible for guarding the treasures of the house of the Lord, that is, the wealth accumulated in the temple of Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 26:22). This was an important charge entrusted to the Levites, who served the sanctuary.
H3100O.origine: The name Joel means "the Lord is God" (in Hebrew יְהוָה אֵל, Yéhovah El). It is a theophoric name, formed from the divine name Yah (abbreviation of Yéhovah) and the word El (God). This name expresses the conviction that God alone is the true God. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, notably the prophet Joel son of Pethuel, author of the book of Joel.
H3100O.emploi: Joel, in these two references from Chronicles, is a Levite living during the time of King David. He belonged to the sub-tribe of Levites called Laadan (or Laadan). The two passages where he is named show him alongside his brother Zetham and mention their role as keepers of the temple treasures. This charge was one of the responsibilities assigned to the Levites in the functioning of worship and the life of the sanctuary.

sens: Son of Pedah, chief of the half-tribe of Manasseh during the time of King David
H3100P.detail: 1. Joel is an Israelite tribal chief mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King David organizes the administration of his twelve tribes. He is specifically designated as responsible for the half-tribe of Manasseh established west of the Jordan, and he is identified as the son of Pedah (1 Chronicles 27:20).
H3100P.origine: The name Joel means "Yahweh is God": it combines two Hebrew elements, Yo (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh) and El (God). It is a very common theophoric name in Israel, borne by many people of various ranks in the Old Testament — from the great prophet Joel, son of Pethuel, to tribal chiefs, Levites, and descendants of exiles. This type of name expresses the trust that the people of Israel placed in God as strength and protection.
H3100P.emploi: The Joel mentioned in 1 Chronicles 27:20 is part of an administrative list where David establishes the chiefs responsible for each of the twelve tribes of Israel. This list reveals the organization of the kingdom at the time of its stability and power. Unlike other Joels in the Bible — notably the prophet Joel or Levites — this one is identified only by his tribal function and kinship, with no additional details about his actions or religious role.

sens: Levite, chief of the Kohathites during the reign of Hezekiah
The Lord is God (meaning of the name)
H3100Q.detail:
1. Joel is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:12. He is the son of Azariah and belonged to the group of Kohathites, one of the three major families of Levites. He rose up with other Levites to participate in the religious reforms of King Hezekiah, notably the cleansing and sanctification of the temple of Jerusalem.
2. The name Joel means "The Lord is God," composed of two Hebrew elements: the divine name (Yah) and the word elohim (God). This name expresses a confession of faith in the uniqueness and sovereignty of God.
H3100Q.origine: The name Joel comes from the Hebrew root Yah (short form of the divine name) combined with El (God), forming a theological statement: "The Lord is God." This nominal structure was common in the Old Testament to express a fundamental religious truth. Several biblical characters bore this name, the most famous being the prophet Joel, author of the second book of the twelve minor prophets.
H3100Q.emploi: Joel the Levite appears only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Chronicles 29:12, during the reforms of King Hezekiah (circa 715 B.C.). He is presented as a chief of the Kohathites who rose up to participate in the cleansing and sanctification of the temple. His only mention in the Bible shows him engaged in a holy and collective mission, alongside other Levites and religious leaders, thus demonstrating the importance of the Levites in the worship and religious reforms of Judah.

sens: Man from the time of Exile and Return
H3100R.detail: 1. Joel is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from Exile: he is one of the sons of Nebo who had to send away his foreign wife after marrying outside his people (Ezra 10:43). This passage is part of a list of those who took non-Israelite wives and who repented of this infidelity to the Law.
H3100R.origine: The name Joel means "Yahweh is God" or "God is Yahweh" in Hebrew: it combines the divine name Yahweh (rendered "Lord" in English) and the word "El" which means God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, expressing the confession that God alone is master and sovereign. This name was borne by several important figures in Israel's history, notably the prophet Joel son of Pethuel, author of the book that bears his name.
H3100R.emploi: This particular Joel is known only by his unique mention in Ezra 10:43. He was among those who, upon returning from the Exile in Babylon, violated the covenant by taking foreign wives. Ezra's register lists the men who committed this offense and who acknowledged it, showing the rigor with which the religious leaders sought to preserve the purity of the restored people after captivity. The context suggests an ordinary man rather than a prominent figure.

sens: Benjamite, son of Zichri, leader of the inhabitants of Jerusalem at the time of the Restoration
H3100S.detail: 1. Joel is a man from the tribe of Benjamin, son of Zichri, who lived during the return from exile. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:9, where we learn that he was the leader of the inhabitants of Jerusalem — that is, he was responsible for overseeing and organizing the life of the community in the restored city after the Babylonian captivity.
H3100S.origine: The name Joel means "the Lord is God" or "the Lord is my strength" in Hebrew: it is composed of the divine name Yah (the Lord) and the word el (God, power). It is a common name in Israel that expresses the conviction that God is the only true God. Several characters in the Bible bear this name, including the prophet Joel, son of Pethuel, author of the book that bears his name, but this Joel from Nehemiah 11 is a different person.
H3100S.emploi: This Joel is mentioned only once in Scripture, in Nehemiah 11:9, in the list of leaders and notable figures who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He represents the leaders who helped to rebuild and organize the community life of the city of God. His role was to be the leader (a verb that literally means "to be over") of the inhabitants of Jerusalem — a position of authority and service to the restored people.

sens: The prophet whose book bears his name
Son of Pethuel
H3100T.detail:
1. Joel is the prophet to whom the second book of the twelve minor prophets is attributed. He received the word of the Lord and conveyed it to Judah, probably during the time of King Uzziah. His name means "the Lord is God."
2. He is presented as the son of Pethuel in Joel 1:1, which identifies him precisely among the many bearers of this name in the Old Testament.
H3100T.origine: The name Joel comes from two words: Yah (the Lord) and El (God), forming a name that proclaims "the Lord is God." This type of compound name was common in Israel to express a religious conviction. Several other characters in the Bible bear this same name, but only this one is known as a prophet with a biblical book.
H3100T.emploi: Joel is mentioned only once in the Bible as a prophet: at the beginning of the book that bears his name, where he is designated as the recipient of the word of the Lord. The book of Joel contains his prophecies regarding the judgment of Judah, the coming of the day of the Lord, and the promises of restoration. Tradition places his prophetic ministry during the time of the divided monarchy, probably under the reign of King Uzziah of Judah.
H3100T.portee: The book of Joel calls for repentance in the face of God's judgments and reveals promises of salvation and the gift of the Spirit for all who call on the name of the Lord. The Apostle Peter quotes Joel 2:28-32 at Pentecost to explain the gift of the Holy Spirit, showing how Joel's prophecies are fulfilled in God's plan of salvation.

sens: son of Elkana, Levite during the time of the united monarchy
ancestor in the genealogy of the temple singers
H3100U.detail:
1. Joel is a Levite mentioned in the genealogy of the singers of Israel during the time of David. He is the father of Elkana and the grandson of Uzziah, placing him in a family of musicians and servants of the temple worship (1 Chronicles 6:36). This name appears several times in the chronicles to identify different characters of the people of God.

2. As a Levite, Joel belongs to the tribe called to serve the tabernacle and the temple: he is a man of worship, liturgical song, and the prayer of the people. His place in the genealogies shows how God chose entire lineages dedicated to His service.
H3100U.origine: The name Joel means "Jehovah is God" in Hebrew: it combines the divine name Jehovah and the word Elohim (God), expressing a confession of faith. Joel bears a name that proclaims the identity of the living God — not a god among others, but the only true God.
H3100U.emploi: In the genealogy of the temple singers (1 Chronicles 6), Joel is situated in the lineage of the sons of Levi, a family of musicians and servants of worship. This Levite is the ancestor of Heman, one of the three great singers of the temple during the time of David. His name also appears in other contexts, such as that of Shaul, showing that several men bore this same name in the history of Israel, all linked to the service of the people or the worship of God.

sens: father of Gideon
man of the tribe of Manasseh
defender of the worship of the Lord
H3101G.detail:
1. Joash is the father of Gideon, the famous judge who delivered Israel from the oppression of the Midianites. He is the one who owned the oak of Ophrah where the angel of the Lord appeared to his son (Judges 6:11).
2. Joash belongs to the family of Abiezer, from the tribe of Manasseh. He lived during the time of the judges, before kings ruled Israel, in a context where faith was often weakened and neighboring peoples oppressed the people of God.
3. When Gideon destroyed the altar of Baal in the village, Joash defended his son against the furious inhabitants. He told them that if Baal was really a god, he could defend himself (Judges 6:31), showing a courageous faith in the Lord at a time when it was dangerous.
H3101G.origine: The name Joash means "given by the Lord." It is a theophoric name that carries within it trust in God, as it indicates that the child was a gift received from the divine hand. The name expresses an act of faith and a recognition towards God for the life granted.
H3101G.emploi: Joash is mentioned six times in the book of Judges. He is first presented as the owner of the oak of Ophrah and the father of Gideon (Judges 6:11 and 6:29). He then appears at the heart of the conflict: the men of the city threaten him to force his son to pay for his transgression against Baal (Judges 6:30), but Joash courageously refuses to sacrifice him and defends the honor of the Lord (Judges 6:31). Later, Joash's name is recalled during Gideon's exploits, to show that this deliverer was the son of this man of faith (Judges 7:14 and 8:13).
H3101G.portee: Joash shows us that a father can pass on to his son not only a name that speaks of trust in God but also a living and courageous faith. His refusal to bend to the pressure of idolaters, and his challenge to those who defended a false god, teach that remaining faithful to the Lord requires courage and does not depend on the number of those who support us. It is in this house that Gideon grew up, called to become a deliverer of Israel.

sens: Son of King Ahab, living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
Officer or figure of the royal court of Israel
H3101H.detail:
1. Joash is a character briefly mentioned in the accounts of Israel during the time of the division between the two kingdoms. He is the son of King Ahab, and thus of the same generation as Kings Ahaziah and Joram, his brothers. His name means "given by the Lord" in Hebrew.
2. In the two passages where he appears (1 Kings 22:26 and 2 Chronicles 18:25), he seems to hold a position at the court of the king of Israel, or at least to be well-known enough to be associated with the authorities and the leaders of the city. The context is that of the judgment of the prophet Micaiah, whom King Ahab orders to be brought before Amon, the chief of the city, and Joash, the son of the king — suggesting that he had some authority or responsibility in the city.
H3101H.origine: The name Joash is formed from two Hebrew elements: Yo (a form of the name of God, YHWH) and ash (to give), hence the meaning "given by the Lord." Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament — notably two kings of Judah and Israel — but this one is the son of Ahab, king of the ten northern tribes.
H3101H.emploi: Joash, son of Ahab, is mentioned only twice in the Bible, in two parallel and practically identical passages: 1 Kings 22:26 and 2 Chronicles 18:25. In these two accounts, King Ahab, after hearing the prophecy of the prophet Micaiah announcing his military defeat, orders that he be imprisoned and handed over to Amon and Joash. This brief mention shows him as a figure of authority at court, although his exact functions are not specified. He is one of the sons of Ahab mentioned in the Scriptures.

sens: King of Judah during the divided monarchy, son of Ahaziah
Saved from death at a young age by his aunt Jehosheba
Restorer of the temple in Jerusalem
Assassinated by his servants after a reign of forty years
H3101I.detail:
1. Joash is a king of the tribe of Judah who reigns during the period of the divided monarchy, at a time when Israel and Judah are separated. He is the son of King Ahaziah and Zibiah. His story begins dramatically: while Athaliah, his grandmother, massacres all the royal princes to usurp the throne, Jehosheba, his aunt and wife of the priest Jehoiada, manages to save him from the massacre by hiding him in a chamber of the temple with his nurse (2 Kings 11:2).

2. At the age of seven, Joash is proclaimed king thanks to Jehoiada, who organizes the overthrow of Athaliah. Under the tutelage of this high priest, he follows the righteous ways of the Lord and restores the temple of Jerusalem by dedicating the money collected from the people.

3. However, upon the death of Jehoiada, Joash gradually abandons the commandments of the Lord and listens to the princes of Judah who lead him towards idolatry. The prophet Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, rebukes him in the name of God, but Joash has him stoned to death in the temple courtyard.

4. Weakened by his disobedience, Joash is mortally wounded by the king of Israel in battle, and shortly thereafter, his own servants strike him and kill him in the house of Millo (2 Kings 12:20). Although called king for forty years, his reign ends in tragedy and disgrace.
H3101I.origine: The name Joash means "given by the Lord" in Hebrew (from Jehovah, "the Lord," and from the root meaning "to give"). This prophetic name expresses the idea that a child is a gift from the Lord to his parents. In the Bible, it is borne by several characters: the most well-known is this king of Judah miraculously saved in his youth. The name exists in two forms: Joash and its longer variant Jehoash (יְהוֹאָשׁ).
H3101I.emploi: Joash, king of Judah (son of Ahaziah), is the main character in these references. The Segond refers to him as "Joash" in French. His story unfolds over several chapters of 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles, from his miraculous rescue in childhood to his assassination. The passages first describe his protection from Athaliah's massacre (2 Kings 11:2 and 2 Chronicles 22:11), then his reign under the influence of the priest Jehoiada, his restoration of the temple, and finally his moral decline and violent death at the hands of his own servants (2 Kings 12:20). The chronicles emphasize his progressive unfaithfulness after the death of his advisor and his divine judgment, while 2 Kings serves as a warning about the consequences of abandoning the Law.
H3101I.portee: The story of Joash teaches the Christian reader several profound lessons. First, the sovereignty and protection of God: even when evil reigns and threatens the innocent, the Lord preserves His people and His promises. Next, the crucial importance of surrounding oneself with faithful advisors and remaining attached to the divine Word: as long as Joash listens to Jehoiada, he walks uprightly; as soon as he strays from him, his life and reign degenerate. Finally, his fate reminds us that external prosperity and political power are not sufficient without obedience to the Lord.

sens: king of the northern kingdom of Israel during the divided monarchy
son of King Jehoahaz
father of King Jeroboam II
H3101J.detail: Joash is a king of Israel (the northern kingdom) who reigned after his father Jehoahaz. He is first mentioned in 2 Kings 13:9, where he succeeds his father. Joash fought against the king of Syria, Ben-Hadad, and achieved victories: in 2 Kings 13:25, it is written that he "restored the cities taken from Joahaz, his father, by Ben-Hadad, son of Hazael." He also had a conflict with Amaziah, king of Judah, as reported in 2 Chronicles 25:18: "Joash, king of Israel, sent word to Amaziah, king of Judah: The thistle of Lebanon sent to the cedar of Lebanon..." — a parable to humiliate the king of Judah. Joash is also the father of Jeroboam II, whom the Lord used to save Israel from annihilation (2 Kings 14:27). Upon his death, he was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel (2 Kings 13:13).
H3101J.origine: The name Joash means "given by the Lord." It is also known by the full name Jehoash (יְהוֹאָשׁ), where "Jeho" is a short form of the divine name (YHWH). It is a theophoric name, common in the royal dynasties of Israel, which expresses the belief that children are a gift from God. Several men bore this name: kings of Israel and Judah, and other less significant figures.
H3101J.emploi: The Joash in question here is the 12th king of the northern kingdom, son of Jehoahaz. He reigned during the period when the prophet Elisha was active. Although he is not presented as a great religious reformer, Joash achieved military victories against Syria with divine assistance. He is mentioned in the prophecies of Hosea and Amos, his contemporary prophets. His short reign (13 to 14 years by calculations) falls within the decline of the northern kingdom, but God used him to preserve a remnant, for it is through his son Jeroboam II that Israel would experience a period of relative prosperity.
H3101J.portee: Joash illustrates how God works at the heart of Israel's political and military history, even when the kingdom strays from Him. Although this king was not a model of religious fidelity, the Lord granted him victories to preserve His people from annihilation. His story reminds the reader that God keeps His promises to Israel and governs even through imperfect kings to fulfill His plans of salvation.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in genealogies
Descendant of Shelah, son of Judah
H3101K.detail:
1. Joash is a man of the tribe of Judah living in the time of Egypt and the desert. His name appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:22, amidst a genealogy of the tribe of Judah.

2. According to the provided genealogy, Joash was either a direct son of Shelah or a son of Jokim. He belonged to an ancient lineage of Judah and is mentioned alongside important figures of his tribe such as Jokim and Saraph, who according to the text ruled over Moab.
H3101K.origine: The name Joash (יוֹאָשׁ) literally means "given by the Lord" or "the Lord has given." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of divine gift. This name, borne by several important figures in the history of Israel (notably kings of Judah and Israel), reflects the belief that children are a gift from God to His people.
H3101K.emploi: Joash is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:22. This passage is a detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah that lists the descendants of Shelah, son of Judah. The text places Joash among ancestral figures of Judah, in ancient times, and links him to other men of his family such as Jokim and Saraph, who distinguished themselves by their power over Moab.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin who joined David
H3101L.detail: 1. Joash was a warrior of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Shemaah of Gibeah. He was among the soldiers who rallied to David during his stay at Ziklag, before he became king of Israel (1 Chronicles 12:3). He is one of the many fighters listed in this passage as recognizing the divine anointing on David.
H3101L.origine: The name Joash means "given by the Lord" in Hebrew. It is a compound formed from two elements: "Yo" (abbreviation of the divine name) and "ash" (to give). This name expresses the action of God giving, reflecting the faith of parents in divine providence.
H3101L.emploi: Joash is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:3. He appears in the list of warriors from Benjamin and Judah who came to find David at Ziklag, before he was anointed king. This context shows that he was a trustworthy man, capable of recognizing that God had chosen David to govern Israel. Several other biblical characters bear the same name (kings of Judah and Israel, father of Gideon), but this specific usage concerns only this Benjaminite warrior.

sens: son of Issachar
also called Jashub
H3102.detail:
1. Job is one of the four sons of Issachar mentioned during the descent into Egypt with Jacob. He appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 46:13, in the list of sons that Issachar fathered. He is one of the direct descendants of Jacob who enters Egypt.
2. This same man is also called Jashub (יָשׁוּב), which means "he returns." The two names refer to the same person, as was sometimes the case in biblical genealogies.
H3102.origine: The name Job (יוֹב) comes from the Hebrew root meaning "persecution" or "to be persecuted." It is a distinct name from the well-known Job of the Book of Job, who is a later character and has no genealogical connection to this son of Issachar. The name Jashub, which also refers to this same person, comes from the root "to return" or "to come back."
H3102.emploi: Job is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 46:13, among the sons of Issachar listed when Jacob descends into Egypt at Joseph's request. He is one of the twelve tribes of Israel that were born from this journey. His name also appears in the form Jashub in other genealogical lists, indicating that it is the same person designated by two different names. No other action or particular event concerning Job is reported in the Scriptures.

sens: Son of Joktan, descendant of Shem
King of Edom in ancient times
King of Madon in northern Canaan
H3103G.detail:
1. Jobab is the last of the sons of Joktan mentioned in Genesis 10:29, in the genealogy of the peoples descended from Shem. He represents an ancient people or lineage from the ancient Near East.
2. The Bible also remembers a Jobab who was king of Edom, the neighboring kingdom of Israel to the southeast, before the kings of Israel reigned.
3. Another Jobab is king of Madon, a city in northern Canaan, and he opposed Joshua during the conquest of the promised land before being defeated near the waters of Merom.
H3103G.origine: The name Jobab means "a desert" in Hebrew, evoking the arid lands of the southeastern Mediterranean and the Near East from which these peoples came. Several characters bear this name in biblical antiquity, all rooted in these ancient and distant regions.
H3103G.emploi: Jobab appears twice in the provided usages: first in Genesis 10:29 as the son of Joktan, in the list of peoples descending from Shem and populating the known world after the Flood. He reappears in 1 Chronicles 1:23 in the same genealogy. Other biblical passages mention kings named Jobab, including the one from Madon who opposed Joshua. The name designates both an ancient figure in human genealogy and political leaders of the ancient Levant.

sens: King of Edom, son of Zerah of Bozrah
Successor of Bela in the dynasty of Edomite kings
H3103H.detail:
1. Jobab is a king of Edom mentioned in the genealogical list of Edomite kings. He is the son of Zerah and reigns from the city of Bozrah after the death of Bela (Genesis 36:33). His reign is part of the long dynastic succession of Edomite rulers before the emergence of the Israelite monarchy.
2. After his own reign, Jobab is succeeded by Husham, who is from the land of the Temanites (Genesis 36:34). The repetition of this information in 1 Chronicles 1:44-45 shows the importance that Scripture places on this royal genealogy.
H3103H.origine: The name Jobab means "a desert," likely evoking the arid lands of Edom. It appears four times in the Bible, only in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1, as a dynastic name among the Edomite kings prior to the formation of the people of Israel.
H3103H.emploi: Jobab is mentioned four times in the Bible, all in genealogical lists: twice in Genesis 36:33-34 and twice in 1 Chronicles 1:44-45, which repeat the same content. Each mention places him in the chronology of the kings of Edom, a people descended from Esau. These references show that the Bible documents the Edomite royal succession precisely, even if few historical details are given about each individual reign.

sens: king of Madon in northern Canaan
opponent of Joshua during the conquest
H3103I.detail:
1. Jobab is the king of Madon, a city in northern Canaan (Joshua 11:1). He is a local leader who governs his territory at the time when Joshua is conquering the land.
2. Jobab is one of the Canaanite kings who rise against Joshua: he receives a message from Jabin, king of Hazor, and joins an alliance to resist the Israelite invasion (Joshua 11:1). With his allies, he marches against Israel but is defeated at Meron.
H3103I.origine: The name Jobab means "a desert" in Hebrew, possibly evoking the environment of northern Canaan. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament: a descendant of Shem through Joktan, other kings of Edom, and Benjaminite leaders. Each Jobab was a distinct figure in the history of Israel.
H3103I.emploi: Jobab appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 11:1. He is the king of Madon who, informed by Jabin of Hazor, rallies to a coalition of Canaanite monarchs to confront Joshua during the conquest of the land. He represents the local resistance of established peoples in Canaan against the arrival of the Israelites.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin
H3103J.detail: 1. Jobab is a man belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, whose existence is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of the descendants of Shaharaim (1 Chronicles 8:9). He is one of the many sons listed in this family lineage.
H3103J.origine: The name literally means "a desert" in Hebrew. It could evoke the aridity or isolation characteristic of the Benjaminite territory or a personal condition. This name is borne by several people in biblical history: a descendant of Shem through Joktan, a king of Edom, and a king of Madon who confronted Joshua during the conquest of Canaan.
H3103J.emploi: Jobab is cited only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:9, as one of the sons of Shaharaim and Hodesh, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. He appears in a genealogical list established during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel. This isolated mention suggests that Jobab did not play a major role in the history of Israel, unlike the other Jobabs mentioned in the Bible.

sens: man of the tribe of Benjamin
son of Elpaal
H3103K.detail: Jobab is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:18. He is presented as one of the sons of Elpaal, alongside many brothers including Jishmerai and Jizlia. The context shows that he belongs to a genealogical lineage of Benjaminite family leaders established at the time of the divided monarchy.
H3103K.origine: The name Jobab literally means "a desert" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that denotes aridity or desert space. This name was borne by several characters in the history of Israel: a descendant of Shem, several kings of Edom and Canaan, and this Benjaminite family.
H3103K.emploi: Jobab appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:18, in a detailed genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is presented as the son of Elpaal and brother to ten other men, indicating that he came from a powerful house of Benjamin. These genealogies in the book of Chronicles serve to establish the lineages of Israelite families and their territorial settlement after the conquest of Canaan.

sens: Ram's horn or trumpet made from this horn
The resounding sound of a trumpet
Year of jubilee, holy year when debts are forgiven and properties return to their original owners
H3104.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a ram's horn or a trumpet made from this horn. It is an ancient, robust, and resonant musical instrument. In Exodus 19:13, when the trumpet sounds at Sinai, it signals that the people may approach the mountain.
2. The word is also used for the loud and resounding sound produced by this instrument. In Joshua 6:4, the priests carry seven "resounding" trumpets that will cause the walls of Jericho to collapse: it is not just any noise, but the powerful and sonorous sound of the instrument.
3. By extension, the jubilee is the holy year celebrated every fifty years, marked precisely by the sound of these trumpets. It is a year of grace when slaves regain their freedom (Leviticus 25:10), debts are forgiven, and everyone returns to their family property (Leviticus 25:13). This year proclaims freedom and the restoration of divine order.
H3104.origine: The Hebrew word יוֹבֵל (yobèl) likely comes from a root that evokes a cry, a loud sound. Its original image is that of the ram's horn, which was the quintessential signaling instrument in antiquity. It was by sounding the yobèl that solemn years and important events were proclaimed. The word thus initially designated the object (the horn), then the sound (the loud cry), and finally the event that this sound announced (the holy year).
H3104.emploi: The word appears about 25 times in the Bible, mostly in Leviticus and Joshua. In the laws of Leviticus (chapters 25 and 27), it almost always refers to the year of jubilee: it is the major institution of the Old Testament that guarantees social justice, as every sold property returns to its owner at the jubilee, and no one can be enslaved forever. In the account of Jericho (Joshua 6), the word takes on the meaning of a loud trumpet, the instrument that announces both the jubilee and the victory that God grants. In Exodus 19:13, it is the signal of God's presence at Sinai. The usage of the word thus varies according to the context: sometimes the instrument itself, sometimes its sound, sometimes the event it proclaims.
H3104.portee: The jubilee reveals God's heart for justice and freedom: it guarantees that no one will ever be chained indefinitely, that no property is permanently acquired, and that the created order must be regularly restored. For the believer, this word reminds us that God is the true master of all, and that He desires a society where everyone can start anew. The sound of the jubilee is a cry of freedom and grace, a word from God that proclaims: "Enough; let them breathe."

sens: Flow of water that flows
Watercourse or brook
Source of water supply (figuratively)
H3105.detail:
1. The word refers to the flow or continuous movement of water that flows: it is moving water, lively and flowing, in contrast to stagnant water. In Jeremiah 17:8, the tree "extends its roots toward the stream," evoking those waters that flow constantly and nourish the plants.
2. More broadly, it is a watercourse — a brook or a small river — where water circulates naturally. The biblical image is one of life and fertility: a tree with roots plunged into the stream does not suffer from heat or drought.
3. Figuratively, the stream of water becomes a symbol of what nourishes and sustains: a constant supply of blessings and spiritual strength, as shown in the continuation of the verse where the tree "bears fruit" without interruption.
H3105.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to flow" or "to run." It is related to words that denote flow and current. The image is that of the natural and continuous movement of water — not collected or held water, but flowing, living, and dynamic water. This etymology explains why the Bible uses it to evoke vitality and the ability to survive trials.
H3105.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 17:8. It is found in a famous parable about the man who trusts in God: this man is compared to a tree planted by the waters whose roots extend toward the stream. The context shows that the stream of water is not just one element among others, but the foundation of the tree's prosperity and stability, allowing it to "bear fruit" even in a year of drought.
H3105.portee: This word teaches a profound spiritual truth: whoever roots their life in the "living waters" of God's word and trust in Him will not be dried up by trials. Like the tree by the stream, the believer draws strength from an inexhaustible source. This image invites us to meditate on what truly nourishes our soul and the necessity of being "rooted" not in changing circumstances, but in what flows eternally.

sens: son of Lamech and Ada, brother of Jabal and Tubal-Cain
inventor of stringed and wind musical instruments
H3106.detail:
1. Jubal is a character from Genesis, living before the Flood. He is the son of Lamech and Ada, and he has brothers: Jabal and Tubal-Cain. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:21, which makes him remarkable for his brevity in the biblical narrative.

2. Jubal is known as the father of all who play the harp and the flute. This means he is presented as the inventor or founder of instrumental music. He represents the origin of this human practice: he developed string instruments (like the harp) and wind instruments (like the flute or the reed).
H3106.origine: The name Jubal (יוּבָל in Hebrew) means "stream" or "course of water." This name evokes the image of flow and movement, which corresponds well to one who created the flow of musical sounds. The name belongs to the genealogy of the descendants of Cain, a lineage known for its technical and artistic innovations before the Flood.
H3106.emploi: Jubal appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:21. He is presented in the context of Cain's genealogy, where God gives each descendant special gifts: Jabal becomes a shepherd, Tubal-Cain a blacksmith, and Jubal invents music. This unique mention shows that the Bible recognizes music as an ancient human gift, predating the Flood, and Jubal is its first representative in history.
H3106.portee: Jubal reminds us that music is an original gift, inscribed in human history since its beginnings. It is not a recent or superficial invention, but a creative expression that God allowed from antiquity. For the Christian, this underscores that music, long before being an art or entertainment, is linked to the human capacity to create and express one's relationship to the world and to God.

sens: Servant of King Joash of Judah who participated in his assassination
H3107G.detail: 1. Jozacar is one of the two servants of King Joash who struck him fatally (2 Kings 12:21). He is an officer or close associate of the king, influential enough to have access to the royal person and powerful enough to commit this crime against the sovereign.
H3107G.origine: The name Jozacar means "Jehovah has endowed" or "Jehovah has enriched," composed of the divine name Yahweh and the verb "to endow." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, recognizing God as the source of blessings. The same character is also called Jozabad elsewhere.
H3107G.emploi: Jozacar appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 12:21. He is designated as the son of Shimeath and presented alongside his accomplice Jozabad (son of Shomer) as one of the two servants who assassinated King Joash. This act marks the end of Joash's reign, who had once restored the temple but turned away from God after the death of the priest Jehoiada. His son Amaziah succeeded him.

sens: Warrior in the service of King David
H3107H.detail: Jozabad is one of the valiant warriors who joined David at Ziklag, according to 1 Chronicles 12:4. His name means "Jehovah has endowed" or "Jehovah has granted," reflecting gratitude to God for the gift of a child. He is mentioned in the list of powerful military leaders who rallied to David during the time when he had not yet reigned over all Israel.
H3107H.origine: The name Jozabad is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Jo" (a contraction of Jehovah, the name of God in Israel) and "zabad" (meaning "to endow" or "to grant"). This name reflects a common theology in ancient Israel: recognizing that every child is a gift from God. Several men bore this name in biblical texts, including a Levite from the descendants of Korah during the time of David.
H3107H.emploi: Jozabad appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:4, where he is listed among the mighty warriors of Israel who came to join David at Ziklag. He is described as coming from Gedera and is included in an impressive list of competent military leaders, demonstrating that David had gathered around him courageous and experienced men in battle.

sens: Warrior who joined David
Military leader of the tribe of Manasseh
H3107I.detail:
1. Jozabad is one of the military leaders of Manasseh who joined David during his return to Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:20). He was among the "thousands" — that is, the leaders of contingents — who rallied to David to strengthen his troops.
2. His name means "Jehovah has endowed" or "the Lord has enriched," reflecting his parents' trust in divine blessing. Among the warriors listed, Jozabad represents the loyalty of the military leaders from the north (Manasseh) towards David.
H3107I.origine: The name Jozabad combines Jehovah (Jah) and the verb zaḇad, "to endow, enrich, fulfill." It is a theophoric name — a name that incorporates the divine name — common in Israel to express that the child is a gift from God. Several men bore this name at different times (Levites, warriors, priests), testifying to its popularity.
H3107I.emploi: Jozabad appears only once in the Segond 1910, in 1 Chronicles 12:20, where he is cited as one of the military leaders of Manasseh who came to reinforce David. The context shows that he was a ranking officer, commanding a unit of warriors. This unique mention places him among the strategic supporters of David during the tumultuous period following Saul's death.
H3107I.portee: This character illustrates how, even before David was recognized as king by all Israel, military leaders from the northern tribes saw in him a trustworthy leader and a man blessed by God. His rallying symbolizes the gradual unity of Israel around David, despite the political divisions of the time.

sens: Warrior of David, military leader of Manasseh
H3107J.detail: Jozabad is a military leader who joined David at Ziklag, providing support to the future king during the time he was fleeing from Saul. He commanded units of warriors from the tribe of Manasseh and is among the valiant men who strengthened David's army (1 Chronicles 12:20).
H3107J.origine: The name Jozabad means "the Lord has endowed" or "the Lord has granted": it combines the divine name (Jah) and the verb "to give" or "to enrich." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the belief that God provides for all needs. Several men bore this name in the history of Israel.
H3107J.emploi: Jozabad appears in 1 Chronicles 12:20 as one of the military leaders of Manasseh who joined David at Ziklag. The Bible presents him among the valiant warriors who rallied to David before he became king. This mention highlights his role in gathering the troops that supported David during his struggle for the throne.

sens: Levite in charge of the temple treasury administration during the reign of Hezekiah
H3107K.detail: 1. Jozabad is a Levite who lived during the divided monarchy of Israel and Judah. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 31:13, where he is listed among the officials placed in charge of the reserves and the treasury of the temple in Jerusalem.
H3107K.origine: The name Jozabad means "the Lord has endowed" or "the Lord has granted." It is composed of the divine name Yah (abbreviation of Yahweh) and the verb zabàd which means "to provide" or "to enrich." This name expresses trust in God as the source of all goods and abilities.
H3107K.emploi: Jozabad appears only once in the provided biblical text: 2 Chronicles 31:13. On this occasion, he is named among ten officials (Jehiel, Azariah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Jismachiah, Machath, and Benaiah) who worked under the direction of Conaniah and his brother Shimeah. They acted on the orders of King Hezekiah and Azariah, chief of the house of God. These men oversaw the stocks and wealth of the temple, ensuring their proper management in a context of religious reform.

sens: Levite leader during the reign of King Josiah
H3107L.detail: Jozabad is a chief of the Levites mentioned during the great Passover celebrated under the reign of King Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:9). He is among those who organized and provided the sacrifices for this solemn feast, alongside Conaniah, Shemaiah, and Nethaneel.
H3107L.origine: The name Jozabad literally means "Jehovah has endowed" or "Jehovah has enriched," composed of Jo (a contraction of the divine name) and Zabad (which means "to endow, enrich"). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to God for His gifts. Several people bore this name at different periods in the history of Israel.
H3107L.emploi: Jozabad is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 35:9, during the Passover celebrated by King Josiah. In this passage, he is presented as one of the chief Levites who took the initiative to generously give for the worship: he contributed, along with his colleagues, five thousand lambs and five hundred oxen for this great feast. His action illustrates the central role of the Levites in organizing worship at the temple.

sens: Levite who assisted the priest during the weighing of offerings upon return from exile
H3107M.detail: Jozabad is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:33. He is the son of Joshua and participated in the solemn weighing of the silver, gold, and sacred utensils that the Israelites brought back from Babylon. Alongside the priest Meremoth and the Levite Noadiah, he assisted in this fundamental religious act: verifying and documenting the temple goods before their official handover. This role shows the importance given to the Levites in the reconstruction of worship after the exile.
H3107M.origine: The name Jozabad means "the Lord has provided" or "the Lord has endowed." It is composed of the divine name (Yah) and the verb meaning "to give" or "to provide." It is a typical theophoric name from the Old Testament periods, expressing trust in divine providence.
H3107M.emploi: Jozabad, son of Joshua, appears only once in the current biblical texts: in Ezra 8:33, at the time of the return from exile under Ezra's leadership, around 458 B.C. He is designated as a Levite responsible for administrative and religious duties related to the temple goods. Although the text is brief, it illustrates the essential role of the Levites in managing and preserving the sacred resources of the restored community.
H3107M.portee: This character reminds us that the return from exile was not only a political liberation but a gradual restoration of divine worship. Jozabad embodies the commitment of the Levites to serve faithfully, even in administrative tasks. For the believer, this is a call to faithfulness in the responsibilities entrusted to us, great or small, in the service of the faith community.

sens: man who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return
H3107N.detail: Jozabad is a proper name referring to a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:22. He is listed among the sons of Pasher who agreed to put away their foreign wives during the return from Babylon, at a time when Ezra sought to restore the purity of the restored people. The name means in Hebrew "The Lord has endowed" or "The Lord has granted," expressing that this child was a gift from God to his parents.
H3107N.origine: The name Jozabad is composed of two Hebrew elements: Yo (a short form of the divine Tetragrammaton, the Lord) and Zabad (to give, to endow, to grant). This composition reflects a common belief in Israel that male children were gifts from the Lord. Several men bore this name in the history of Israel, including Levites and warriors during the time of David, but this entry concerns only the one mentioned in Ezra 10:22.
H3107N.emploi: Jozabad appears only once in the biblical texts provided: in Ezra 10:22. He is named among the descendants of Pasher (a priestly name) who had married foreign women and who, at Ezra's exhortation, agreed to put them away. This context reflects one of the major crises of the return from Exile: the risk of religious and cultural mixing. Jozabad thus represents an ordinary man of the people who responded to this call for renewal of the covenant.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi living during the time of the Exile and the Return
H3107O.detail: Jozabad is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:23, among those who had married foreign women and had to put them away during the return from exile to Jerusalem. His name means "The Lord has enriched" or "The Lord has endowed" in Hebrew, expressing a divine blessing.
H3107O.origine: The name Jozabad is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Yo" (Yah, a shortened form of the name of God) and "Zabad" (to endow, to enrich, to grant). It belongs to a family of names that celebrate God's action, like Zechariah (God remembers) or Matthew (gift of God).
H3107O.emploi: Jozabad is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:23. He is among the Levites who had taken wives from the peoples of the land, contrary to the Law of Moses. Upon the return from exile to Jerusalem, the people committed to uphold the Law, and these Levites, including Jozabad, put away their foreign wives to restore the purity of worship and community. His case illustrates the importance of respecting religious separation in Israel after the exile.

sens: Levite of the return from Exile period
He who explained the Law in Jerusalem
H3107P.detail: Jozabad is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, during the solemn reading of the Law in Jerusalem after the return from Exile. He was one of the Levites who stood to explain and make the text of the Law understood to the assembled people (Nehemiah 8:7). His name means "Jehovah has endowed" or "God has enriched," reminding that the Levites were one of the tribes of Israel charged with the service of the Temple and the teaching of the Law.
H3107P.origine: The name Jozabad is composed of two Hebrew elements: Yo (a contraction of the divine name Jehovah) and Zavad (to give, to endow, to provide). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that incorporates the name of God, very common in Israel. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, including Levites and warriors during the time of David.
H3107P.emploi: Jozabad appears only once in the preserved biblical texts: in Nehemiah 8:7. He is among a group of thirteen Levites who, under Ezra's leadership, were tasked with explaining the Law of Moses to the people gathered at the Water Gate during the Feast of Tabernacles. This event marks a crucial moment in Israel's return from Babylonian Exile: the reaffirmation of the covenant with God through the public reading and interpretation of the Law. Jozabad thus represents the spiritual leaders engaged in restoring the religious and communal life of Israel.

sens: A Levite of the Restoration period after the Babylonian Exile
H3107Q.detail: Jozabad is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:16. He was responsible for the external affairs of the house of God (the rebuilt Temple) and was among the leaders of the Levites in Jerusalem after the return from exile. His name means "the Lord has endowed" or "the Lord has enriched," expressing how God had provided him for this important function in the restoration of worship.
H3107Q.origine: The name Jozabad (יוֹזָבָד) is composed of two elements: Yo (a contraction of Yaho, the divine name) and Zabad ("to endow, to enrich"). It is a theophoric name characteristic of the Jewish period, where it was confessed that it is God who gives abilities and wealth. The same name can refer to several other characters in ancient traditions (notably a son of Korah during the time of David), but the Jozabad of Nehemiah 11:16 is a distinct figure from the time of the return from exile.
H3107Q.emploi: Jozabad appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:16. He is presented as a Levite in charge of the external affairs of the Temple in Jerusalem (probably the administration and management of the sanctuary's properties) and as a leader among the Levites. Alongside his colleague Shabbethai, he represents the religious and administrative leadership of the Temple during the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the return from captivity.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin
Son of Beriah
H3109G.detail: Jocha is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible. He was the son of Beriah and the brother of Arad, Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Eder, Michael, and Ishpah (1 Chronicles 8:16). Nothing else is known about him.
H3109G.origine: The name Jocha literally means "the Lord gives life." It is composed of two elements: a form of the divine name (Yaho or Yo) and a verb meaning "to live" or "to give life." It is a typical theophoric name of the Old Testament, expressing trust in God as the source of life.
H3109G.emploi: Jocha appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:16, in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. He is listed among the sons of Beriah, with no other biographical detail or reported event concerning him. His mention is part of the genealogical lists that reconstruct the Israelite families after the exile.

sens: Elite warrior in the service of King David
H3109H.detail: Jocha is one of the renowned warriors of King David, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the brother of Jediah and belongs to the family of Shimri. According to 1 Chronicles 11:45, he is designated as "the Tizite," which likely indicates his geographical origin or tribe.
H3109H.origine: The Hebrew name יוֹחָא literally means "God gives life." It is composed of the divine name Yahweh ("Jehovah") and a verb evoking the action of giving or making live, reflecting the faith of the parents who sought to honor God by naming their son. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, a common practice in Israel.
H3109H.emploi: Jocha is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:45, where the list of David's most valiant warriors is presented. He is described as the brother of Jediah and as part of those elite men who constituted the king's personal guard or army. This mention attests to his honor and recognition in the kingdom of Israel during the divided monarchy period.

sens: Jewish military leader after the fall of Jerusalem
Son of Kareach
Trusted man of the governor Gedaliah
Opponent of Ishmael
H3110G.detail: 1. Jochanan is primarily a leader of Jewish troops who emerged after the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon in 586 B.C. He represents the resistance and authority of the Jews who remained, alongside the governor appointed by the king of Babylon. 2. He is the son of Kareach, a powerful man, and is regularly referred to by this lineage (“Jochanan, son of Kareach”) throughout the narrative of Jeremiah, highlighting the importance of his family in the political context of the time. 3. He shows loyalty to the governor Gedaliah, son of Ahikam, warning him of the betrayal plotted by Ishmael, son of Nethaniah. He is a man who seeks to preserve peace and political stability despite tensions (Jeremiah 40:16). 4. When Ishmael assassinates Gedaliah and massacres his men, Jochanan pursues him, catches him, and defeats him, then rallies all the saved people to himself (Jeremiah 41:13-15). He then becomes the gatherer of the small Jewish remnant. 5. Following these events, Jochanan and the leaders of the troops lead the people to consult the prophet Jeremiah to know whether they should stay or go to Egypt (Jeremiah 42:1-8).
H3110G.origine: The name Jochanan means “Jehovah has shown favor” or “God has granted grace.” It is formed from “Yah” (an abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh) and “Hanan” (grace, favor). This theophoric name expresses the belief that the child is a gift of divine grace. It is a common name among Jews of this time, borne by several individuals in the Old Testament, but this Jochanan is the most prominent due to his political and military role.
H3110G.emploi: Jochanan appears 15 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the accounts of Jeremiah (chapters 40-43), at a critical moment in the history of Judah after 586 B.C. He is first introduced in 2 Kings 25:23 as one of the military leaders who come to the governor Gedaliah. In Jeremiah chapters 40-41, he plays a crucial role: he attempts to warn Gedaliah of Ishmael's plot, then avenges the governor's assassination by defeating Ishmael and saving the people. He then leads the survivors to Jeremiah to seek divine will. His character is nuanced: both a military man and one seeking prophetic guidance, he embodies the fragility of the small Jewish remnant in exile. The references show a respected figure (“all the leaders of the troops”) but also one subjected to events beyond his control.
H3110G.portee: Jochanan exemplifies the faithfulness of Jewish leaders in the darkest moments of the people's history: despite the ruin of Jerusalem, exile, and the temptation of despair, he acts to preserve what remains. His endeavor to consult the prophet Jeremiah shows that a wise leader seeks the word of God before deciding the future. His ultimate failure to fully listen to Jeremiah (he takes the people to Egypt despite the prophetic warning) reminds us that human will, even benevolent, can stray from divine will if it lacks true courage of faith.

sens: eldest son of King Josiah
name meaning the action of divine grace
H3110H.detail:
1. Jochanan is the eldest son of King Josiah, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 3:15. He is the firstborn among the sons listed in the text, before Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, and Shallum. He is a prince of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy.
2. His name, Jochanan, literally means “Jehovah has granted grace” or “Jehovah has bestowed favor.” This name expresses the belief that God has granted an act of grace, likely by giving this child to the royal family.
H3110H.origine: The name Jochanan comes from the Hebrew root chan (חנן), which means “to grant grace” or “to show favor.” It is composed of the divine name Yah (Jehovah) and this root, literally forming “Jehovah has granted grace.” Similar names appear in the Bible, such as Hanan (grace) or Hananiah (Jehovah is favorable). This name expresses the belief that God was blessing the one who bore it.
H3110H.emploi: Jochanan is mentioned only once in the Hebrew Bible: in 1 Chronicles 3:15, where he is listed as the firstborn of King Josiah. The text of Chronicles enumerates the sons of Josiah in order of their birth, and Jochanan appears in the first position. It is possible that he is the same character as Jehoahaz, another name given to one of Josiah's sons who became king after his father's death. His exact role in the history of the kingdom of Judah remains poorly documented in the preserved biblical sources.
H3110H.portee: This name reminds the reader that even the princes and kings of Judah bore theophoric names expressing dependence on divine grace. It testifies to the faith of the people of Judah in God's mercy, inscribed from the birth of its children. This invites the believer to recognize that all life, even that of the great of this world, remains under God's grace.

sens: A man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
Son of Elioenai and brother of several other figures mentioned in 1 Chronicles
H3110I.detail:
1. Jochanan is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Judah, contemporary of the period when the kingdom was divided between Israel and Judah. He appears in the genealogy of Judah recorded in 1 Chronicles 3:24, where he is listed among the descendants of David.
2. He is specifically identified as the son of Elioenai (also called Eljoenaï) and had six brothers: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Delaiah, and Anani. These seven sons are presented together in the royal genealogical lineage.
H3110I.origine: The name Jochanan comes from Hebrew and means “God has granted grace” or “Jehovah has grace.” It is composed of two elements: “Yo” (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah) and “chanan” (which means to grant grace, show kindness). This name expresses gratitude to God for His benevolence. Several other men bore this name in biblical history, including a priest who returned with Zerubbabel after the exile and a Jewish military leader.
H3110I.emploi: Jochanan is mentioned only once in the Bible at 1 Chronicles 3:24, in the context of a detailed genealogy of the descendants of Judah. He is among the sons of Elioenai, who himself was a direct descendant of the royal house of David. This genealogical mention is important for establishing the continuity of the Davidic line in the history of Israel and for documenting the families of the tribe of Judah during the period of the divided monarchy.

sens: Priest of the Levitical lineage during the divided monarchy
Son of Azariah and father of another Azariah during the time of Solomon
H3110J.detail:
1. Jochanan was a priest from the tribe of Levi, living during the period known as the divided monarchy (after the separation of the kingdom of Israel and Judah). He appears in the priestly genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6:9.
2. In this same genealogy, it is learned that Jochanan was the son of an Azariah and the father of another Azariah. His son Azariah served as a priest (that is, the high priest) in the temple that Solomon built in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 6:10). This succession of three generations shows the importance of Jochanan in the official priestly lineage of God's people.
H3110J.origine: The name means “the Lord has granted grace” in Hebrew, composed of “Jehovah” (the Lord) and the verb “hanan” (to grant grace, show compassion). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God and expresses a divine blessing. This type of name reflected the faith of the Hebrews in the Lord's benevolence toward His family.
H3110J.emploi: Jochanan is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 6, in the genealogy of the Levitical priests. He appears in the list of ancestors of the high priest Azariah, who served during the time of Solomon. These two verses suffice to place him historically: he lived during the divided monarchy and descended from a major priestly line. His discreet appearance in the genealogy shows that his primary value was to ensure the continuity of divine service in the temple.

sens: Head of a family among the exiles who returned from Babylon
H3110K.detail: 1. Jochanan is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, as a head of a family during the return from exile: he leads one hundred ten men from his house, the house of Azgad, during the journey back from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:12). He represents those leaders who organized the return of God's people after captivity.
H3110K.origine: The name Jochanan comes from Hebrew and means "Yahweh has shown grace" or "Yahweh is gracious": it is composed of "Yah" (the name of God) and "hanan" (to show grace, to be merciful). This name expresses trust in divine goodness, which is particularly significant for a man living at the time of the return from exile, when the people were experiencing God's forgiveness and restoration.
H3110K.emploi: Jochanan appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 8:12, where he is presented as one of the sons of Azgad, one of the heads of families returning from exile with the scribe Ezra. He brings with him one hundred ten men of his kin. Although simple in appearance, this verse shows that Jochanan was a man of responsibility and authority, capable of mobilizing and leading his large family on this perilous journey back to the promised land, a testimony of how God was restoring His people.
H3110K.portee: This character reminds the reader that behind the great biblical events of restoration after exile, there were ordinary yet faithful men who obeyed God's call. The very name Jochanan — "Yahweh has shown grace" — emphasizes that the return from exile was primarily an act of divine mercy towards His rebellious people. It is an invitation to recognize that God fulfills His promises through men who trust in His goodness.

sens: A priest during the Exile and Return, son of Joiada, brother of the high priest and father of Jaddua.
H3110L.detail: Jochanan is a Levite and priest mentioned twice in the book of Nehemiah at the time when Israel is rebuilding after the Babylonian exile. He belongs to the lineage of the high priests: he is the son of Joiada and the father of Jaddua. In Nehemiah 12:22, he is seen among the chief Levites who were officially registered under the reign of the Persian king Darius. In Nehemiah 12:23, it is reported that the genealogies of the heads of Levite families were recorded "until the time of Jochanan, son of Eliashib," marking an important stage in this reconstruction. He embodied the continuity of the worship of the Lord after captivity.
H3110L.origine: The name Jochanan comes from Hebrew and means "Jehovah has shown grace." It is composed of two elements: Yo (an abbreviated form of the divine name YHWH, "the Lord") and Chanan ("to show grace, to show kindness"). It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, expressing God's gracious action towards His people. The name Jonathan (Yonatan) is a variant of the same name.
H3110L.emploi: Jochanan is mentioned only in the book of Nehemiah, which recounts Israel's return from exile and the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the Temple. The two passages (Nehemiah 12:22-23) place Jochanan among the high-ranking Levites, priests, and heads of families, whose names have been carefully preserved in official records. He represents a pivotal generation: the one that ensured the transition between exile and the restoration of Levitical worship in the Promised Land. His role was to maintain the order and holiness of the rebuilt Temple.

sens: Son of Paseach, one of the rebuilders of Jerusalem after the exile
H3111G.detail: 1. Jojada is a man who lived at the time of the return of the Jews from exile (around 445 B.C.). He is the son of Paseach and appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:6, where he is mentioned among those who participated in the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem. Along with Meshullam, son of Besodia, he repaired the old gate of Jerusalem, covering it and setting up its doors, locks, and bars — a work of masonry and carpentry in the collective project launched by Nehemiah.
H3111G.origine: The name Jojada means "Jehovah knows" or "the Lord knows." It comes from the Hebrew root "Yah" (Jehovah) combined with "yada" (to know). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the confidence that God knows and watches over the one who bears it. Several biblical characters have borne this name or a similar form (Jehoiada), including the high priest Jehoiada during the reign of Joash.
H3111G.emploi: Jojada appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:6. He is part of the list of restorers of the walls and gates of Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. This enumeration in Nehemiah 3 shows how, under the leadership of Nehemiah and with the approval of the Persian king Artaxerxes, the returning Jews mobilized to rebuild their capital, each taking charge of a section of the fortifications. Jojada and Meshullam are responsible for the old gate, a major entrance to the city.

sens: High priest during the time of Nehemiah and the reconstruction of the Temple
H3111H.detail: Jojada is a proper name referring to a character from the time of the return from exile. He is the son of the high priest Eliashib and the father of Jonathan. The text of Nehemiah 12:10-11 establishes him in the genealogical line of the high priests: "Eliashib fathered Jojada, Jojada fathered Jonathan." He lived under the reign of Darius the Persian, around the 5th century B.C., and belonged to the tribe of Levi. The Bible mentions him notably as an actor in the religious and administrative life of the restored Temple.
H3111H.origine: The name Jojada (also written Joiada or Jehoiada in some passages like Nehemiah 13:28) literally means "Yahweh knows" or "God knows." It is composed of the divine name (Yah) and the verb "to know." This type of theophoric name was common in Israel to express trust in divine knowledge and providence.
H3111H.emploi: Jojada appears four times in the book of Nehemiah, all in chapters 12 and 13. Listed in Nehemiah 12:10-11 as a link in the genealogical chain of the high priests, son of Eliashib, he holds an important role in the religious life of the people returned from exile. In Nehemiah 12:22, he is mentioned alongside Eliashib, Jochanan, and Jaddua as a witness to the registration of the heads of Levite families under Darius. The reference in Nehemiah 13:28 designates him as the father of a son-in-law of Sanballat, which also reveals the political tensions of the time.

sens: King of Judah, son of Jehoiakim
King who reigned only three months before his capture by Nebuchadnezzar
Babylonian prisoner released after 36 years of captivity
H3112.detail:
1. Jehoiachin is a king of the tribe of Judah who reigned at a time when the kingdom was divided between Israel and Judah. He was the son of King Jehoiakim and succeeded his father on the throne of Judah.

2. His reign was extremely short: only three months and ten days. The king of Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar, besieged him in Jerusalem and took him prisoner, ending his reign before he could truly govern.

3. After his capture, Jehoiachin was taken to Babylon and imprisoned for thirty-six years. The Bible notably mentions him in Ezekiel 1:2, dating the prophet's visions in relation to his captivity: "the fifth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin." This shows that even in exile, his name remained a reference for the Judeans.
H3112.origine: The name Jehoiachin (or Jehoiakim in the Vulgate) means "Jehovah establishes." It is a shortened form of the more complete name Jehoiakim. This short form was commonly used, just as the prophet Jeremiah calls him by other names: Coniah (Jeremiah 22:24) or Shallum (Jeremiah 22:11). The name reflects a theology of God who establishes kings, even though Jehoiachin's fate contrasts sharply with this assertion.
H3112.emploi: Jehoiachin appears in biblical texts as a king of Judah mentioned notably during the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The biblical chronicles place him as the penultimate king of Judah before the Babylonian captivity. He is referenced in Ezekiel 1:2, where the prophet dates his visions in years of Jehoiachin's captivity, highlighting the significance of this event for the exiles. The biblical account emphasizes that despite his capture and long imprisonment, he was ultimately released, which is a significant act of divine providence even in calamity.
H3112.portee: The story of Jehoiachin illustrates the humiliation of Judah and the fulfillment of God's judgments pronounced by the prophets. However, his release after 36 years of imprisonment offers a glimmer of hope: it shows that even in exile, God does not completely abandon His people and that restoration remains possible. For the Christian, this account reminds us that the consequences of sin are real and serious, but that God's grace never entirely disappears.

sens: Jewish high priest, son of Joshua, living during the time of the Exile and the return
Spiritual leader of the people during the reconstruction of the Temple and the walls of Jerusalem
H3113.detail: 1. Jehoiakim is a high priest of the tribe of Levi who lived during the period of the Babylonian exile and the return of the Jews to Jerusalem. He is the son of Joshua (the high priest who returns from captivity) and the father of Eliashib, another high priest.
