His name means "the Lord raises up" or "the Lord establishes," expressing the hope of the people's restoration. 2. Jehoiakim exercised his priestly ministry at the crucial time of the reconstruction of the Temple and the walls of Jerusalem. The book of Nehemiah mentions him as the head of the priestly families of his time, leading the priests who offer sacrifices and ensure the worship of the Lord in the rebuilt Temple (Nehemiah 12:12).
H3113.origine: The name יוֹיָקִים (Jehoiakim) is composed of two elements: יוֹ (Jo), a shortened form of the divine name יהוה (the Lord), and יָקִים (yakim), from the verb קום (qum) meaning "to rise, to raise up, to establish." Together, the name means "the Lord raises up" or "the Lord establishes." It is a characteristic name of the return from exile, carrying a message of hope: God raises His people and restores their worship.
H3113.emploi: Jehoiakim is mentioned three times in the book of Nehemiah, all in chapter 12. He first appears as the son of Joshua and the father of Eliashib in the genealogy of the high priests (Nehemiah 12:10), establishing his place in the priestly succession. He is then named as the head of the priestly families during the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:12), showing his role as a spiritual leader. Finally, he is mentioned in verse 26 as a major chronological marker for situating other events: "in the time of Jehoiakim" (Nehemiah 12:26). These references highlight the importance of this figure in the religious organization of the return from exile.
H3113.portee: Jehoiakim embodies the spiritual renewal after captivity. His very name - "the Lord raises up" - expresses a profound truth for all Christians: God does not reject His people; He raises them up and restores them. The presence of Jehoiakim in the reconstruction of the Temple reminds us that restoration is the work of God, not just of men, and that the continuity of worship and community depends on the faithfulness of the priestly service.

sens: Chief of a priestly family in Jerusalem
Priest during the time of Nehemiah
H3114G.detail:
1. Jehoiarib is the name of a family of priests descended from Levi. This name appears in the lists of those who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. It designates an important priestly lineage in the restored community.
2. At the time of Nehemiah, Jehoiarib represents one of the families of priests who perform worship at the temple. He is mentioned alongside other priests like Jedaiah in the organization of the religious service of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 11:10; 12:6).
H3114G.origine: The name Jehoiarib means in Hebrew "the Lord contends" or "God pleads." It is also written as Jojarib, with the same meaning. It is a classic theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God (Yah in Hebrew). This type of name expresses trust in divine intervention.
H3114G.emploi: Jehoiarib appears three times in the Bible, all in the book of Nehemiah (11:10; 12:6 and 12:19). Each time, it refers to a priestly family. According to 1 Chronicles 9:10, Jehoiarib was also the chief of the first of the twenty-four classes of priests established by King David to ensure the continuous service of the temple. At the time of Nehemiah (around the fifth century B.C.), his family was among the priestly families living in Jerusalem and participating in the religious reconstruction of the city after the exile.

sens: Chief of the priests and teacher during the time of Ezra
H3114H.detail: Jehoiarib is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the context of the return from exile. In Ezra 8:16, Ezra summons him among the leaders and teachers to help organize the return of the Israelites from Babylon to Jerusalem. His name means "the Lord contends" or "the Lord pleads," expressing the idea that God defends His people. Although few details are given about his personal life, his presence alongside Ezra suggests that he was a respected and knowledgeable figure among the priests and teachers of the Law at this crucial time of restoration for God's people after the exile.
H3114H.origine: The name Jehoiarib is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Yo" (Jah, the name of God) and "jarib" (to contend, to plead). This type of theophoric name, which contains the name of God, was common among the Hebrews and expressed a spiritual conviction or a prayer from the parents at the time of birth. The name reflects the assurance that God fights for His people and defends their cause.
H3114H.emploi: Jehoiarib appears only once in the canonical Bible, in Ezra 8:16. He is cited among the leaders that Ezra gathers to organize the return from exile and the restoration of worship in Jerusalem. He is identified both as a leader and as a teacher, indicating that he possessed dual authority: that of his priestly position and that of his knowledge of the Law. His inclusion in this group shows the importance attributed to him during this pivotal period in Israel's history.
H3114H.portee: Jehoiarib embodies the role of spiritual leaders and teachers of the Law in the restoration of God's people after the trial of exile. His presence reminds the reader that reconstruction did not occur solely through arms or politics, but also through spiritual leadership and instruction in God's Word. For today's Christian, this passage emphasizes the importance of faithful leaders and teachers who guide God's people during times of renewal and transformation.

sens: Man of Judah during the time of Exile and Return
Son of Zechariah and father of Adajah
H3114I.detail: Jojarib is a man of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:5, where he appears in a genealogy. He is identified as the son of Zechariah and the father of Adajah, placing him in the period of the return from exile to Jerusalem. His name means "The Lord contends" or "The Lord disputes," evoking the idea of an action of God. He represents one of the families that resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity.
H3114I.origine: The name Jojarib is composed of the divine name "Yô" (the Lord) and the verb "rîb" (to contend, to dispute). It is a common theophoric name in Hebrew, where the name of God marks a connection between the person and their Creator. This type of name reflects the faith of the parents and expresses trust in God's protective action. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament at different times (Davidic period, time of Ezra, time of Nehemiah), but they refer to distinct individuals.
H3114I.emploi: Jojarib appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:5. He is listed in a genealogy of those who resettled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. This genealogy places Jojarib in a specific family line: he is the son of Zechariah and the father of Adajah, thus integrating his family among the recognized inhabitants of restored Jerusalem. His inclusion in this official record underscores the importance of preserving the memory of families and lineages in the post-exilic community.

sens: Woman of the tribe of Levi, mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam
H3115.detail: Jokébed is a woman of the tribe of Levi who lived in Egypt during the time of slavery and the Exodus. She is the wife of Amram and the mother of three children who play a decisive role in the history of Israel: Moses, the liberator and lawgiver; Aaron, the first high priest; and Miriam, the prophetess who leads the people. She appears twice in the Bible, first in Exodus 6:20 where her marriage to Amram is mentioned, and then in Numbers 26:59 which summarizes her descendants. Her name means "Jehovah is glory," expressing that the greatness of her children comes from God.
H3115.origine: The name Jokébed is composed of two elements: "Yo" or "Jah," the abbreviated name of God, and "kebed," which means glory or weight. It thus expresses that glory belongs to God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name, a common practice in pious families of Israel.
H3115.emploi: Jokébed appears only twice in the Bible, both in genealogical lists of the Exodus and the wilderness. In Exodus 6:20, she is presented as the wife of Amram and mother of Aaron and Moses. In Numbers 26:59, the text specifies that she is the daughter of Levi, and bore to Amram three children: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. These two passages establish her genealogy and her central place in the family that leads Israel out of Egypt and toward the promised land. Although mentioned briefly, her role as the mother of the three greatest spiritual leaders of Israel makes her fundamental to the history of salvation.
H3115.portee: Jokébed reminds the reader that behind great liberators and servants of God often stand faithful and pious parents. Her life shows that the faith of parents has eternal consequences for their children and for the people of God. She also embodies the divine promise: God can use ordinary women, in difficult circumstances, to accomplish His wonderful plans.

sens: Servant of King Zedekiah sent to the prophet Jeremiah
H3116.detail: Jucal is an officer of the royal palace of Jerusalem, serving King Zedekiah at the time of the city's fall in 586 B.C. He is among the princes who heard Jeremiah prophesy against the people and who wanted to have him killed (Jeremiah 38:1).
H3116.origine: The name Jucal (יוּכַל) means "The Lord is powerful" or "The Lord can." It is a shortened variant of the name Jehucal (יְהוּכַל, H3081). It is a very common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in divine power.
H3116.emploi: Jucal appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 38:1, where he is presented as the son of Shelemiah and one of the four princes of Jerusalem who heard Jeremiah's words announcing the city's capture by the Chaldeans. These princes denounced him to the king and demanded his death, showing Jucal's role in opposing the prophetic message.

sens: The period of light between sunrise and sunset, opposed to night
The duration of a complete day, from evening to morning, or from morning to evening
A moment or a particular time in history, which can last a long time
The entire life of a person, their existence on earth
A historical period or an anticipated future event
A present or immediate moment
H3117G.detail:
1. The day is primarily light: what illuminates the sky and allows us to see, as opposed to the darkness of night (Genesis 1:5: "God called the light day, and the darkness He called night"). This is the simplest and most concrete experience of the word.

2. A day is also a complete unit of time: a rotation of the earth, from evening to morning or from morning to evening. Genesis 1:8 shows this — "there was evening and there was morning: it was the second day" — marking the natural limits of a 24-hour day.

3. The word also designates an indeterminate moment or period: "the day when" can mean a specific instant (Genesis 2:17: "in the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die") or an era (Leviticus 26:34: "the time it will be desolate"). The idea is one of an occasion or circumstance in history.

4. Our "days" in the plural refer to our entire life: the number of days granted to a person measures their existence (Psalms 90:9: "All our days pass away"). It is the duration of life on earth.

5. The day can also refer to a great future event — "the day of the Lord" or "the day that is coming" (Jeremiah 47:4: "the day is coming when all the Philistines will be destroyed"), the moment when God acts.
H3117G.origine: The Hebrew word yom comes from an ancient root meaning that which divides, that which separates: it naturally evokes the division between light and darkness. In the Bible, it is used over 1600 times, in all books, making it the most fundamental word for speaking about time. It is a universally understood word: wherever it appears, the context determines whether it refers to daylight, a day, a broader period, or a life.
H3117G.emploi: The word day appears 1662 times in the Bible. At the beginning of Genesis, it structures the entire creation narrative: each day of the seven days is marked by the formula "there was evening and there was morning." Then, day counts the ages of the patriarchs (Genesis 5 gives the days of each one's life). It also measures timeframes: "the fifth day," "three days and three nights." In the historical books, it names the chronicles of the kings (2 Kings 21:25: "the book of the Chronicles"). In the Psalms and the prophets, it takes on an eschatological hue: "the day when" announces judgment or God's intervention. The context changes everything: a day can be an instant or a reign, a period of work or an entire life.
H3117G.portee: Understanding that the word "day" means much more than a simple 24-hour unit helps the reader grasp the depth of biblical promises. When God says "in the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die," He speaks of a defining moment, not a clock. When the Bible speaks of "the day of the Lord," it designates the solemn moment when God acts according to His plan. It is a word that reminds us that time is never neutral: each day belongs to God, and every moment of our life is counted.

sens: twenty-four hour period
daylight period
duration of a life or existence
moment, time or era
year
H3117H.detail:
1. The day in its strict sense is the twenty-four hour period that forms a unit of time. It is the basic unit for measuring time in the Bible, marked by the alternation of evening and morning as indicated in the creation narrative in Genesis.
2. The day can also refer to the duration of light, the time when the sun shines, in contrast to night. This is the most immediate usage, encountered when simply speaking of "day" and "night."
3. In the plural, "the days" signifies the entire lifespan of a person. In Jeremiah 6:11, the text speaks of "one who is laden with days," meaning an elderly person, rich in long life experience. In Job 15:10, "richer in days than your father" means "older," having lived longer.
4. The word can also signify a specific moment or an indefinite period. In Job 32:4, it is written that Elihu waited "until that moment," a punctual instant in the passage of time.
5. Rarely, the word designates a year, that is, a complete annual period.
H3117H.origine: The Hebrew word yom (יוֹם) is one of the oldest roots in Semitic languages to express the idea of time passing. Its primary image is that of the natural cycle of light and darkness, the day that rises and the day that ends. It belongs to a family of words that also includes expressions of time, season, and epoch. This word appears thousands of times in the Old Testament, demonstrating its fundamental importance for understanding time in Hebrew thought.
H3117H.emploi: The word yom appears five times in the provided usages, all extracted from wisdom literature (Job and Jeremiah). In these passages, it never simply designates "the day" in the sense of an ordinary day, but takes on a figurative or poetic meaning: it speaks of old age in terms of "accumulated days." In Job 12:12 and 15:10, the "days" represent the experience and wisdom gained over a long life. In Job 30:1 and Jeremiah 6:11, the expression "laden with days" describes an aged person. In Job 32:4, the word takes on the meaning of "moment" or "instant." This polysemy shows that yom transcends the simple objective measurement of time to express the lived experience of time passing.
H3117H.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that time is a creation of God and is measured both objectively and subjectively. The "accumulated days" of a life are not merely a mechanical succession of moments: they become wisdom, experience, and the presence of the Lord. The Bible invites us to see in the length of days a possible spiritual richness, especially when this longevity is accompanied by the fear of God and faithfulness. At the same time, the emphasis on the "days" of existence reminds us that life is limited and must be lived in the light of eternity.

sens: Period of light between sunrise and sunset, opposed to night
Interval of twenty-four hours, from evening to morning
Division of time, measurable duration
Era, moment, circumstances
Year, annual cycle
Life, existence, days of a person
H3117I.detail: 1. The day in the sense of daylight, the time when the sun shines on the earth and allows for seeing and acting — in contrast to night (Genesis 1 defines the day as evening and morning). 2. A complete period of twenty-four hours, from sunset to the next sunset: it is the basic unit of time (1 Samuel 27:7 speaks of the time David stayed with the Philistines as "a year and four months"). 3. A duration of work or travel, a significant moment in the succession of events (Job 10:5: "Are your days like the days of a mortal man?"). 4. An era, a historical period, the circumstances of a given moment ("in this day," "in these days"). 5. The year, the complete cycle of seasons (Exodus 13:10: "You shall observe this ordinance at the appointed time year by year"; 1 Samuel 1:21: "the annual sacrifice"). 6. The days of a life, the duration of an existence: Joshua was "advanced in age," Abraham and Sarah were "old, advanced in age" (Genesis 18:11; Joshua 23:1).
H3117I.origine: This Hebrew word is one of the oldest divisions of time in the language. It primarily designates the day as an observable fact — the passage of the sun across the sky — before meaning any measurable unit of time. The same root is used to form words for "today," "yesterday," "tomorrow," all of which situate a moment in relation to the present day. In the Greek Bible, it is translated as "héméra" (ἡμέρα).
H3117I.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, as it is used to date and count time in almost all historical and poetic books. It is first used in the physical sense of the clarity of day, then to measure durations — a day of travel, a day's work, a twenty-four hour period. Very quickly, it takes on the meaning of an entire year (Exodus 13:10; 1 Samuel 1:21), where a year is a complete cycle. Finally, "days" or "age" designates the entirety of a person's life: Genesis 18:11, Joshua 23:1, Genesis 24:1, and Job 32:6 all speak of a person "advanced in days" or "in age." The usages show that this word naturally shifts in meaning according to context, but always within the framework of measuring time.
H3117I.portee: The word "day" establishes the awareness of time for the biblical reader. It is through this word that the Bible recounts creation in ordered days, measures a life, and recognizes God's work in history. Understanding that life is counted in days — in years — invites the believer to consider their own existence as limited, entrusted, and thus to orient it towards God who alone transcends time. It is also through "days" that the Bible speaks of God's promises that gradually come to fruition in history.

sens: the period of light between sunrise and sunset, opposed to night
a period of twenty-four hours, from evening to the following morning
a particular day, marked by an event or quality
a more or less long period of time, an era
the duration of a life, earthly existence
the daily habit or regular repetition
H3117J.detail:
1. The day as a period of clarity: it is primarily the light of day, the time when one can see and work, as opposed to night. In Genesis 6:5, the thoughts of the heart turn "every day" toward evil: the day is referred to as the moment of conscious activity.
2. The day as a unit of twenty-four hours: it is the fundamental division of time, from evening to the following morning. In Genesis 1, the days create the rhythm of creation. This also includes the night that precedes it.
3. A marked or specific day: in Numbers 7:11, the princes present their offerings "on different days," each on his day, which becomes memorable by the offering presented on it.
4. A period of time, an era: "every day" in Isaiah 58:2 means "constantly, without interruption." It is an indeterminate but real duration.
5. The entire life of a person: in 1 Samuel 18:29, Saul remains David's enemy "all his life," literally "all his days." It is existence itself.
6. Regularity, the habit of each day: in 2 Chronicles 24:11, the Levites empty the chest "daily," that is, every day repeatedly. It is the regular rhythm of daily life.
H3117J.origine: The Hebrew word yom is very ancient and denotes the most fundamental reality of time: what everyone sees upon waking. It is related to roots that express warmth and light, hence the idea of the day as a lit period. The word carries broad meanings: it can qualify an indeterminate period of time, an era, or even existence itself. It is a word that grows in meaning as one reads the Bible.
H3117J.emploi: The word yom appears 44 times in the provided usages and is used in all contexts of daily and cultic life. First, its primary and concrete meaning: a day of twenty-four hours or the clarity of day. Then, repeated and regular meaning: the sacrifices offered "every day" (Exodus 29:38, Numbers 28:3), the Levites serving "day after day" (2 Chronicles 8:14), or the chest emptied "daily" (2 Chronicles 24:11). Then, an expanded meaning: "every day" means "unceasingly" (Isaiah 58:2, Psalms 68:20). Finally, an existential meaning: an entire life designated by "his days" or "his life" (1 Samuel 18:29, Psalms 61:9). Thus, the same word runs from the concrete (a dawn) to the symbolic (an era, an existence).
H3117J.portee: For the Christian reading these usages, the word "day" invites one to live today with awareness. Each day is distinct, carrying its grace and responsibility: it is the present day that determines our faithfulness. The daily repetition reminds us that spiritual life is built through regular habit, not through exceptional moments. And the final day that approaches places every present moment under the light of eternity.

sens: Period of light between sunrise and sunset, opposed to night
Interval of twenty-four hours, a complete day
Limited duration: a workday, a day of travel
Indefinite span of time, era or any period
Continuity without interruption: always, incessantly, throughout life
H3117K.detail: 1. The day in the strict sense is the period of clarity, from dawn to sunset. It is the day as God separates it from the night in the creation of Genesis. 2. But yom also refers to the complete twenty-four hours: a full rotation of the earth, a measured unit of time. 3. A day can also be a workday or the distance traveled in a day's journey — a concrete and finite duration. 4. The word expands to encompass any span of time: an era, a moment in history, any period ("the time you will live in the land"). 5. Finally, when repeated or used in the plural ("the days"), it expresses the entire life, the continuity of time: "every day" means "always," without interruption — which is why yom is translated as "always" or "unceasingly." This is the sense of the psalmist who asks to dwell "always" in the house of the Lord.
H3117K.origine: Yom comes from an ancient root that expresses the idea of warmth and light — hence the sunny day. In Hebrew, related words retain this notion of clarity and expanse. It is a very ancient word, very common in all Semitic languages. Greek translates it by various words depending on the context: hèmera (day, daytime) or even kairos and chronos when the meaning leans toward "era" or "period." The repetition of the word ("day after day") has shifted the meaning toward the idea of continuity and indefinite duration.
H3117K.emploi: Yom is extremely frequent in the Hebrew Bible — the most common word for "day." It is encountered from creation (Genesis 1) where God separates day from night and where each day of creation bears this name. In the laws and narratives of Deuteronomy and the historical books, yom first denotes the literal day (day of travel, workday) but also the entire life: "all the days that you live" often recurs to signify "throughout your life." In the psalms and prophecy, "your days," "my days" are used for the whole life, and "every day" means "without end, always." Translations vary according to this shift: "day" if the meaning remains punctual, "time" if it is a period, "always" if it is the continuity of life or faithfulness ("the Lord will bless you all your days").
H3117K.portee: Understanding yom is to grasp how the Bible speaks of time: first as concrete successions of days (week, year), but also as continuity of life before God. When the Lord promises David "a lamp every day," He does not promise only limited days, but a faithful presence that lasts: this is the meaning of biblical eternity — not the absence of time, but time filled with divine presence. For the Christian, each new day is a gift, and this promise of a perpetual lamp is fulfilled in Christ, who is "the Alpha and the Omega," the master of time.

sens: Period of daylight, opposed to night
Interval of 24 hours, from evening to morning
Workday or activity day
Specific moment, present instant
Historical moment, significant era
Today, the present day
H3117L.detail: 1. The day in the strict sense is the bright period of the day, when the sun shines, as opposed to the dark night (Genesis 1 speaks of it this way). 2. A day can also refer to a complete period of 24 hours, counted from evening to morning, as seen from the creation of the world: "There was evening, and there was morning; the first day." 3. In everyday life, a day can mean a day of labor, a journey completed in one day, or the time needed to accomplish a task (1 Samuel 25:33 speaks of a "day" of avoided violence). 4. The word also designates a moment, an instant: "that day" marks a specific event in time. 5. More broadly, a day can represent a historical era, a moment in history when something is fulfilled or manifested (Deuteronomy 27:9: "Today you have become the people of the Lord"). 6. "Today" means the present day, the moment when one speaks or acts: it is the instant that matters for the one who receives a word from God (1 Kings 8:61: "as it is today").
H3117L.origine: The Hebrew word yom comes from a root that expresses the idea of light and warmth. It primarily designates the light of the solar day, then it has broadened to refer to any division of time. In Hebrew, expressions like "three days" for a span of time, or "the day of God" for an important event can be found. This word is very common in the Old Testament and holds particular theological significance: the expression "the day of the Lord" speaks of the moment of judgment or divine intervention.
H3117L.emploi: The word day appears 192 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is one of the most frequent words, as it structures the biblical narrative: generations are counted in days, events are situated in relation to a particular day, and God's commands often address Israel "today." In historical accounts (Samuel, Kings), it marks decisive moments: "that day," one wins a victory, makes a covenant, becomes the people of God. In the laws of Deuteronomy, "today" calls Israel to obey without delay (Deuteronomy 27:9). Geographical names are formed with this word to perpetuate the memory of an event: "Towns of Jair to this day" (Judges 10:4). The meaning varies slightly depending on the context: a workday, an event-day, the present day, or an entire era.
H3117L.portee: The word day invites the reader to grasp how God acts in concrete time. "Today" creates a spiritual urgency: the Lord's commands are not abstract principles, but calls that require immediate obedience. This word also reminds us that each day counts in the history of salvation: creation, covenants, miracles, the coming of the Messiah are all inscribed in a history of days that have eternal significance. For the believer, "today" is the moment when one can say yes to God and where His grace acts.

sens: Period of twenty-four hours
Daylight, the moment when the sun shines
Era, historical or future period
Occasion, opportune moment
Time of life, duration of existence
H3118.detail:
1. When the text speaks of "thirty days" or "day by day," it refers to a period of twenty-four hours, a complete cycle (Daniel 6:7: "within thirty days"). This is the most concrete and frequent meaning.
2. The word can also evoke daylight clarity as opposed to night, the moment of the day when light prevails.
3. Used without a specific number or modified by an adjective, "day" broadens to the meaning of time, era: "in the course of time" (Daniel 2:28). It then designates a more or less long historical period, an era.
4. In some contexts, "day" refers to a critical moment, a decisive occasion — the day of judgment, the day of victory.
5. The word can also mean life, the duration of a person's existence, as when one says "the days of a life."
H3118.origine: The Hebrew word yom comes from a very ancient root that evokes the clarity and warmth of the sun. Its basic image is that of daylight, from which the meaning of daytime period developed, then of a full day (twenty-four hours), and then more broadly of time and era. In biblical Hebrew, it is one of the most fundamental words for measuring and expressing duration.
H3118.emploi: The word yom appears very frequently in the Hebrew Bible to express duration and time. In the provided passages (Ezra and Daniel), it primarily carries two meanings: a concrete sense of a twenty-four hour period ("day by day" in Ezra 6:9, "thirty days" in Daniel 6:7 and 6:12), and a broader sense of time, era, or historical period ("the ancient times" in Ezra 4:15, "the course of time" in Daniel 2:28, "the appointed time" in Daniel 4:34). The context determines whether to understand a specific day or a more vague period. In Daniel's visions, the word also takes on a prophetic coloring: it refers to future days, events that will occur.
H3118.portee: Understanding the word "day" in all its richness helps the reader grasp how the Bible speaks of time: sometimes as a succession of concrete and countable moments (the thirty days of prohibition in Daniel 6), sometimes as a great period of God's plan that extends over centuries ("the course of time"). For the believer, it is a reminder that God masters time, from the ordinary day to the great day of His judgment. It also invites one to live each day as a gift from God, while awaiting the promised day of His return and eternal reign (Daniel 7:13-14).

sens: during the hours of light, during the time when it is day
moment of a day, daytime period
action or event that occurs during the day
state of alertness or activity, in contrast to night
H3119.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the moment of day when the sun shines, the light time in contrast to night. In Exodus 13:21, the pillar of cloud guides Israel "day" and night, marking continuous protection; in Isaiah 4:6, it protects against the heat of the "day." 2. It is also the active period of a day when one attends to their tasks. Joshua 1:8 invites meditation on the Law "day" and night, intertwining the meditation of God with every moment of life. 3. Sometimes it describes a circumstance or specific action occurring during the day: in Ezekiel 12:3-7, the prophet must visibly carry out his baggage "day," in contrast to a nighttime escape. 4. The word can also express the state of being awake and active: Deuteronomy 28:66 speaks of trembling "day and night," depicting a restless anxiety.
H3119.origine: The word יוֹמָם (yomam) is an adverb derived from יוֹם (yom), which means "day." It takes the adverbial form by adding a specific suffix that makes it a time adverb. The root יוֹם is very ancient and fundamental in Hebrew; it designates both the day as a unit of time and light itself. Yomam enriches yom by situating it precisely in the temporal domain: it means "in the daytime," "in a diurnal manner."
H3119.emploi: The word appears 49 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Psalms, the Prophets, and the Pentateuch. It often describes a continuity or alternation: "day and night" is the preferred formula, emphasizing incessance or totality (Nehemiah 1:6, Psalms 32:4, Jeremiah 16:13). The Law and the Word of God are meditated "day and night" (Psalms 1:2, Joshua 1:8), signaling a permanent devotion. In contexts of protection or miracles, the cloud or fire guides Israel "day and night" (Exodus 13:21-22), showing divine vigilance. In passages of distress or fear, trembling "day and night" (Deuteronomy 28:66) conveys a continual unease. The word can also isolate the daytime action from a nighttime action (Ezekiel 12:3-7), marking public visibility in contrast to clandestineness.
H3119.portee: This word reminds the believer that the day has its own quality: it is the time of divine light, of manifest action, and of vigilance. The alternation of "day and night" invites consideration of God's presence throughout all time, not just during hours of clarity. For one who meditates on the Word "day and night," it is a call to allow the Word to transform their entire existence, in visible moments as well as in intimacy. The word also reinforces the idea that nothing escapes God's gaze: He sees both day and night.

sens: Son of Japheth and grandson of Noah
Greece, Ionia, or the Ionians in general
Region and peoples of the eastern Mediterranean basin
H3120G.detail:
1. Javan is a man living in the time of the Patriarchs, first mentioned in Genesis 10, where he is listed among the seven sons of Japheth. He is known only through his genealogy: his brothers are Gomer, Magog, Madai, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras, and his sons are Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim (Genesis 10:2, 4).

2. The name Javan also designates Greece or the region of Ionia, as well as the Greek peoples who inhabited it. This geographical meaning reflects the fact that the descendants of Javan according to the Bible settled in the ancient Greek world. That is why the sacred text uses the name of the patriarch interchangeably to refer to the region and its inhabitants.
H3120G.origine: The name Javan comes from a Semitic root meaning "Ionia" or "Greece." In Genesis, it is part of the table of nations that enumerates the descendants of Noah and locates the peoples in the ancient world. The term has a dual usage: personal (the patriarch himself) and geographical (the region and its peoples), which is characteristic of biblical genealogies, where an ancestor gives his name to his descendants and territory.
H3120G.emploi: Javan appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:2-4, where he is presented as the son of Japheth and father of four sons, and in 1 Chronicles 1:5-7, which repeats exactly the same genealogies. These two passages constitute the complete biblical description of Javan as a patriarch. His importance lies primarily in the structuring of the table of nations, which establishes the origins of the peoples known in the ancient world from a biblical perspective. The text also designates him by the term "Greek" (Joel 3:6), showing that the Bible clearly identifies the descendants of Javan with the historical Greeks.
H3120G.portee: Javan reminds us that the Bible situates the origins of peoples within the universal history stemming from Noah. His presence in the genealogy shows that God knows and organizes the destiny of all nations, including Greece, which will be central in the history of salvation at the time of the New Testament. This genealogical link confers dignity to Greek culture within the divine plan.

sens: historical region of the eastern Mediterranean corresponding to Greece and Ionia
Greek and Ionian people inhabiting this region
Greek political and military power in prophetic visions
H3120H.detail:
1. Javan geographically designates ancient Greece and more specifically Ionia, a coastal region of Asia Minor populated by Greeks. It is a distant and unknown land to the people of Israel, mentioned alongside other far-off lands: Isaiah 66:19 speaks of sending the glory of God "to Javan, to the distant islands, who have never heard of me."
2. Javan also refers to the Greek people themselves, the Ionians who trade and traffic. Ezekiel 27:13-19 describes Javan as an important trading partner, exchanging slaves, bronze utensils, wrought iron, and spices.
3. In the prophecies of Daniel, Javan represents a major political and military power: the goat of Daniel 8:21 symbolizes "the king of Javan," who opposes the Persian kingdom and whom the angel announces to Daniel in Daniel 10:20 and 11:2 as a key player in future events.
H3120H.origine: Javan comes from Yavan in Hebrew, which historically designates the Ionians, Greeks of Asia Minor. The name derives from the coastal Greek populations. In biblical tradition, it is associated with Javan, son of Japheth (Genesis 10:2), the legendary ancestor of the Greek peoples according to the genealogy of nations. The prophets of the Old Testament use it to refer to the Greek world in its commercial and political dimensions.
H3120H.emploi: Javan appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in a context of commerce or political prophecy. In Isaiah, it is a distant land where divine glory is to spread. In Ezekiel, Javan is a trading partner of prosperous Tyre, exchanging valuable goods. In the book of Daniel, Javan changes roles: it is no longer just a trading partner, but a major military power, symbolized by the goat with the great horn, which will oppose Persia and play a central role in the eschatological events announced in chapters 8, 10, and 11.
H3120H.portee: For the biblical reader, Javan reminds us that divine Providence extends to the most distant and foreign peoples to Israel, including the Greek world. In the prophecies of Daniel, it shows that God controls the history of empires and announces in advance the role of human powers, reassuring the believer that the future remains in God's hands despite great political upheavals.

sens: Soft and wet material formed by soaked earth
State of one who sinks, who is overwhelmed, who loses footing
Situation of spiritual or moral distress
H3121.detail:
1. Mud is earth mixed with water, becoming slippery and sticky: it is a substance in which one sinks and from which one cannot easily escape. In Psalms 40:3, the psalmist says he was taken "out of the miry clay," a concrete image of a difficult extraction.
2. The word also evokes gradual sinking, the impossibility of standing: in Psalms 69:3, the psalmist cries, "I sink in the mire, where there is no standing," like someone who is bogged down and finds no foothold.
3. Spiritually, mud represents distress, suffering, or sin in which the soul sinks; this is why being pulled from the mud becomes a powerful image of salvation and divine help.
H3121.origine: The Hebrew word יָוֵן comes from the root that evokes the idea of sinking, becoming soft and slippery. It is a concrete word, derived from direct observation of the rural world: anyone who has walked on soaked ground understands the image immediately. The biblical context uses it almost always in passages of distress or penitence, which quickly gives it a spiritual charge.
H3121.emploi: The word appears twice in the Psalms, both in cries of distress. In Psalms 40:3, the psalmist gives thanks for being taken from this mud, marking a transition from misfortune to salvation. In Psalms 69:3, he describes his sinking into the mud as a symbol of his present trial, where he finds neither rest nor help. In both cases, mud is the image of a situation from which one cannot escape alone.
H3121.portee: This word helps the reader understand how the Bible speaks of suffering and sin, not as abstract states, but as concrete realities in which one sinks. It shows that crying out to God in distress is like calling for help when one is bogged down. It is also a promise: God can pull from the mud, set on the rock, and firm the steps of the one who cries out.

sens: Counselor of King David, son of Shimeah and nephew of David
A sharp and cunning man, capable of discerning events
H3122G.detail:
1. Jonadab is a historical figure from the time of the united kingdom of Israel, living at the court of King David. He is the son of Shimeah, David's brother, making him the king's nephew. He appears in 2 Samuel 13:3 as a companion of Amnon, David's firstborn son.
2. He is distinguished by his skill (2 Samuel 13:3 specifies that he was "a very shrewd man") and his ability to understand complex situations. In 2 Samuel 13:32-35, he shows his acuity by discerning what actually happened during the murder of Amnon by Absalom, and he reassures the king by explaining the true circumstances of the event.
H3122G.origine: The name Jonadab means "the Lord is willing" or "the Lord is gracious," formed from Yah (the Lord) and nadab (to be willing, to consent). The character in 2 Samuel 13 is distinct from Jonadab son of Rechab, leader of the Rechabites mentioned during the time of Jehu, although the Bible knows of other Jonadabs bearing the same name.
H3122G.emploi: Jonadab appears three times in the biblical text, exclusively in 2 Samuel 13, during the tragic family crisis of King David. In 2 Samuel 13:3, he is presented as Amnon's close friend and as someone perceptive. In verses 32 and 35, after Amnon's murder, Jonadab intervenes with the king to comfort him and provide accurate information about what happened, thus showing his role as a confidant and advisor to the monarch. His sharp mind allows him to understand Absalom's vengeance when others remain uncertain.
H3122G.portee: Jonadab embodies the role of the faithful friend and wise counselor in service to the king, even in times of great family distress. His example shows how a perceptive and loyal person can bring comfort and clarity in crises, speaking the truth without hesitation but with compassion for the one who suffers.

sens: Son of Rechab, founder of the Rechabite movement
Religious leader whose descendants faithfully keep the teachings
H3122H.detail:
1. Jonadab is a man who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Rechab and the founder of a group called the Rechabites, a family devoted to a particular lifestyle, radical and faithful to strict rules (Jeremiah 35:6).
2. Jonadab is best known as the spiritual leader whose descendants scrupulously respect his orders, generation after generation. The Rechabites refuse wine, live in tents, and follow his prescriptions, to the point that their fidelity to this man becomes a model of devotion in the eyes of God himself (Jeremiah 35:10, 35:19).
H3122H.origine: The name Jonadab means "Yah (God) is willing" or "Yah is generous." It is composed of the divine name Yah and the verb "to be willing" or "to consent." This name expresses that God is the one who gives willingly and generously. Jonadab also appears in the form Jehonadab in other passages.
H3122H.emploi: Jonadab is mentioned three times in the Bible, all in the book of Jeremiah in chapter 35. He is presented as the founding father of the Rechabites, whose descendants at the time of the prophet Jeremiah (more than a century after Jonadab himself) continue to respect his orders: not to drink wine, not to live in houses. God notices this superhuman fidelity and praises it, declaring that Jonadab's lineage will never lack descendants who stand before Him. His influence endures long beyond his own life, symbolizing a transmission of spiritual values.
H3122H.portee: The life of Jonadab and the faithfulness of his descendants teach the importance of lasting obedience and the transmission of spiritual values from one generation to the next. In the face of Israel's unfaithfulness, God highlights the example of the Rechabites to show that it is possible to remain faithful to one's commitments. For the Christian, it is a call to cultivate constant fidelity in one's own faith and to pass on one's convictions.

sens: White or gray bird with graceful flight, symbolizing purity and peace
Offering animal in the worship of Israel, especially for the poor
Term of affection or tenderness in love
Figured innocence, gentleness, candor
Sign of return to life and hope
H3123.detail:
1. The dove is a bird recognizable by its delicate plumage and elegant silhouette, capable of traveling far and finding its way back (Genesis 8:11: the ark sends out a dove that returns with an olive branch). It embodies peace and purity by its very nature.
2. In Israelite worship, the dove (or pigeon) is the animal sacrificed by the poor who cannot offer a larger beast (Leviticus 5:7, 12:8: "two turtledoves or two young pigeons"). It is a sacrifice accessible to all, showing God's mercy.
3. In the love poetry of the Song of Solomon, the beloved is called "dove" as a term of admiration and tenderness (5:2: "my dove, my perfect one"), referencing her sweet beauty and innocence.
4. The dove symbolizes innocence in the face of danger: Jesus sends his disciples "as doves among wolves" (Matthew 10:16), an image of vulnerable purity.
5. In times of misfortune and loss, the voice of the mourning dove evokes both suffering and the desire for peace (Isaiah 38:14, 59:11: mourning cries of a dove).
6. The depicted bird that flies seeks rest and safety (Psalms 55:7: "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest").
H3123.origine: The Hebrew word יוֹנָה comes from a root that evokes the cooing or cooing sound, the characteristic cry of the dove. The word has retained its concrete meaning of bird throughout biblical history. In the Greek texts of the Old Testament, the equivalent Greek word is used to designate the same animal, which the Hebrew Bible calls dove or pigeon depending on the context.
H3123.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Hebrew Bible, first in the account of the Flood (Genesis 8) where Noah sends a dove to check for the end of the waters. It appears very often in the texts of the Law (Leviticus, Numbers) to describe offerings accessible to the poor: it is a humble animal but accepted before God. Biblical poetry exploits the dove figuratively: the Song of Songs uses it as a term of affection (1:15, 5:2), the psalms take it as an image of gentleness and flight (55:7, 68:14), and the prophets use it to evoke the groaning of the oppressed (Isaiah 38:14, 59:11) or the regained multitude (Hosea 11:11: the sons return "like doves").
H3123.portee: The dove speaks to the heart of the believer on at least three levels. First, it reminds us that God accepts the gift of the poor as much as that of the rich: a simple dove offered with a sincere heart is valuable before Him (Leviticus 12:8). Next, it teaches confident innocence: Jesus asks His disciples to live "innocent as doves" in the face of the dangers of the world. Finally, the dove from the Flood becomes the image of hope that soars toward new peace: the suffering heart can find its rest in God, just as the dove returns to its nest.

sens: Prophet of the Northern Kingdom sent by God to Nineveh
Son of Amittai, from Gath-Hepher
H3124.detail:
1. Jonah is a prophet who lived during the time of the divided monarchy, under the reign of King Jeroboam II. The Lord calls him to proclaim His message of judgment to Nineveh, the great capital of Assyria. His story is famous because he initially refused this mission: he fled to Tarshish by boat, but God stopped him with a terrifying storm. Thrown into the sea, Jonah was swallowed by a great fish and remained three days and three nights in its belly before being cast onto the shore; he then obeyed and delivered the message to Nineveh.
2. Jonah was the son of the prophet Amittai and came from Gath-Hepher, a small town in the Northern Kingdom. His name means "dove," which evokes gentleness, but his story shows a man reluctant, full of resistance to God's mercy for Nineveh.
H3124.origine: The name Jonah comes from the Hebrew יוֹנָה (yonah), which literally means "dove." This name evokes the pure and gentle bird, a symbol of peace in the Bible. It is a nickname or poetic image, as nothing in the narrative suggests that he is truly gentle: on the contrary, he is a wrathful and disobedient prophet, which makes the name even more striking by contrast.
H3124.emploi: Jonah appears 17 times in the New Testament and in the Old Testament: first mentioned in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet during the time of Jeroboam II, he is best known by the book that bears his name. The account of Jonah shows his attempt to flee, his miraculous capture, his preaching to Nineveh, and his final anger at the city's repentance. The entire book of Jonah revolves around the question of God's mercy toward the pagans and the prophet's reluctance to accept it.
H3124.portee: The story of Jonah challenges every believer regarding their own disobedience and lack of mercy toward others. It reveals that God does not merely judge, but continually offers repentance and forgiveness, even to Israel's worst enemies. Jonah's resurrection from the belly of the fish also foreshadows, for the disciples, the resurrection of Jesus. It is a lesson on God's love and grace that surpass our prejudices and limitations.

sens: Person from Greece or its coastal regions
People or trade associated with ancient Greece
H3125.detail: 1. Javan designates a legendary ancestor and his people: according to Genesis 10, Javan is a son of Japheth and a brother of Magog, Meshech, and other peoples. The name Javan in Hebrew (יָוָן / Yavan) refers to the Greeks and the peoples of the eastern Mediterranean coast. 2. In the provided usage (Joel 3:6), "children of Javan" refers to the Greeks or the peoples commercially linked to them. The prophet Joel denounces the nations that sold the children of Judah and Jerusalem to the Javans, evoking the slave trade practiced by these maritime and merchant peoples.
H3125.origine: The Hebrew word יָוָן (Yavan) comes from an ancient root designating the peoples of the Ionian and Aegean coasts. It is likely related to the word "Ionian" in Greek, as the Greeks who first had contact with the Levant were the Ionians. In the Old Testament, this term identifies both a mythical ancestor (Javan, son of Japheth, in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10) and the entire Greek world in its commercial and political relations with Israel.
H3125.emploi: The word appears primarily in Joel 3:6, where it designates the Greek peoples as commercial partners and slave traders. This passage shows that the Greek nations, known for their maritime power and trading networks, are involved in the trafficking of the children of Israel. The prophetic context of Joel emphasizes divine judgment on this exploitation. In the Table of Nations (Genesis 10), Javan appears as a genealogical landmark to situate the western peoples in the post-flood dispersion.
H3125.portee: This text reminds the reader that God's people cannot be sold, exploited, or enslaved with impunity: God defends His own and judges the nations that oppress them. The mention of the Javans (Greeks) also shows that the prophetic word addresses the known world, not just Israel.

sens: Young shoot or sprout emerging from the soil
Fragile and vulnerable plant at the start of its growth
New plant life arising from barren or sterile ground
Figuratively: that which begins small and without promising appearance
H3126.detail: 1. The word literally designates a young plant, a small shoot that comes out of the ground — something tender and new. In Isaiah 53:2, the Messiah is compared to a "weak plant" that rises: a simple young shoot that grows before God. 2. This plant is fragile because it has just germinated; it does not yet have the strength or solidity of a mature tree. The image emphasizes the vulnerability of the beginning. 3. The text specifies that it comes from a "dry ground" — an arid soil, without natural resources. This reinforces the idea of growth against all odds, like a life emerging from nothing. 4. Figuratively, the word evokes everything that begins humbly, without apparent beauty or visible advantages, but which contains a promise of life and future development.
H3126.origine: The Hebrew word יוֹנֵק comes from a root that means "to be tender, young, succulent" — the idea of what is fresh and full of sap. It describes young and growing realities: children who are breastfed (the "nurslings"), tender branches, or seedlings. The underlying image is that of new life, fragile but vital.
H3126.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 53:2. It is part of the description of the servant of the Lord — the one who grows under the gaze of God without human beauty or splendor. The prophetic context of this passage makes it a key image of humility and the mysterious growth of the Messiah: a divine life that begins with such an ordinary beginning that it could be despised.
H3126.portee: This image teaches us that spiritual greatness often begins with humility and invisibility in human eyes. Like a fragile young plant, the life of Jesus, and more broadly growth in faith, does not first impose itself through its power or beauty, but through faithfulness and hidden life in God. It invites us not to judge by appearances nor to underestimate what begins small.

sens: New shoot of a tree or plant after cutting
Branch or twig of a tree
Figuratively, offspring or descendants of a dynasty
H3127.detail:
1. The shoot is the young sprout that comes from the trunk or root of a tree that has been cut down. It is a sign that the tree can be reborn: "When it is cut down, it will sprout again, it produces more shoots" (Job 14:7). This image evokes life that persists despite destruction.
2. By extension, the word designates the branches or twigs of the living tree. When the Israelite vine prospers, "It sent out its branches to the sea, and its shoots to the river" (Psalms 80:12). Each shoot is a part of the tree that grows toward the sky and bears fruit.
3. In figurative language, the shoot represents the descendants of a royal family or dynasty. God promises to uproot "a tender shoot" from the cedar and plant it on a mountain (Ezekiel 17:22), announcing a king from the royal line who will flourish again.
H3127.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to suck" or "to nurse," related to the idea of nourishing or breastfeeding. A shoot is literally what is nourished and grows. The family of this word includes other terms related to growth and youth. The underlying image is that of life bursting forth, the new emerging from the old.
H3127.emploi: This word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books and the prophets. In the Book of Job, it illustrates the resilience of nature: a cut tree sprouts again thanks to its shoots (Job 14:7), but the wicked will see their shoots consumed by the flame (Job 15:30). In Psalms and Hosea, it describes the prosperity of Israel or the faithful people: the vine extends through its shoots (Psalms 80:12, Hosea 14:6). In Ezekiel, the shoot becomes a messianic promise: a tender shoot from the cedar of David symbolizes the coming Messiah.
H3127.portee: The shoot reminds the believer that life triumphs over destruction. Even when cut, a plant sprouts again: likewise, God's promise persists despite trials and defeats. The image of the tender shoot planted on the mountain (Ezekiel 17:22) conveys hope: God will bring back a faithful royal lineage, announcing the Messiah. This word invites us to see beyond present ruin a future restoration.

sens: Title or musical indication of a psalm
Possibly the name of a well-known melody in David's time
H3128.detail:
1. This Hebrew expression appears only in the title of Psalm 56. It likely designates a melody or musical tune that musicians were to recognize and use to sing this psalm. The full title is "Dove of the distant terebinths" — a poetic formula that evokes either a popular song or an established sacred melody.
2. The exact meaning remains uncertain, but the poetic image suggests something distant, hidden, silent: a dove that has fled to distant trees. This could reflect the context of Psalm 56, written when David was fleeing from the Philistines at Gath (1 Samuel 21) — a situation of isolation and danger where only a distant refuge offered safety.
H3128.origine: The expression combines three Hebrew words: "jonath" (dove), "elem" (silence or terebinths), and "rechoquim" (distant). It is a poetic title, not an ordinary word. Its exact meaning has been lost over time: the musicians of the time understood it as a musical indication, but we only have the written text. Some see in "dove" innocence or vulnerability; others simply see it as the name of an ancient musical tune.
H3128.emploi: This expression appears only once in the Bible, at the head of Psalm 56 ("To the chief musician. On Dove of the distant terebinths"). It is among other musical titles of psalms (like "On the Hind of the Dawn" or "On Mut-labben") that instructed musicians to adapt the lyrics to an existing and known melody. The context of Psalm 56 — David fleeing at Gath — suggests that this title could evoke the feeling of exile or refuge.
H3128.portee: This expression reminds us that the psalms were meant to be sung in the Israelite community, with melodies transmitted orally. It also shows how biblical poetry used imagery (the dove, the distant, the silence) to express the emotion of a prayer. The Christian reading Psalm 56 can meditate on how even our songs and cries are known to God, even when we feel far and abandoned.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
Son of Jada and brother of Shammah
Father of Peleth and Zaza
H3129G.detail: 1. Jonathan is a man of the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of the divided monarchy (when the northern and southern kingdoms were separated). He belongs to the genealogy of Jerachmeel, an important lineage of Judah. 2. He is the son of Jada and the brother of Shammah, who himself died without children (1 Chronicles 2:32). 3. Jonathan is the father of Peleth and Zaza, who continue the lineage of Jerachmeel (1 Chronicles 2:33). These genealogies show how God preserves families through generations.
H3129G.origine: The name Jonathan comes from Hebrew and means "God has given" or "Jehovah has given" (from the root "to give"). It is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, notably the son of King Saul and friend of David, but this one refers to an ancestor of the tribe of Judah mentioned only in 1 Chronicles.
H3129G.emploi: This Jonathan appears only in the genealogy of Jerachmeel in 1 Chronicles 2. Unlike the illustrious Jonathan son of Saul, whose story occupies several chapters of 1 Samuel, this one is known only by his place in the family tree: son of Jada, brother of Shammah, father of two sons. These genealogical lists were essential for the Israelites, as they established the identity of families and their right to the promised land.

sens: Man living during the time of exile and return
Father of Ebbed
H3129H.detail: Jonathan is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile under Ezra. He is the father of Ebbed, who is among the family leaders who accompanied Ezra to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:6). He is a simple Judean in the community that is rebuilding after the Babylonian captivity.
H3129H.origine: The name Jonathan means "Jehovah has given" in Hebrew: it is formed from two elements, "JHVH" (the divine name) and "natan" (to give). It is a popular name in Israel, borne by several important figures in biblical history, including the son of King Saul and friend of David.
H3129H.emploi: This Jonathan appears only once in Scripture, in Ezra 8:6, where he is named as the father of Ebbed, one of the family leaders of the tribe of Adin who returned from exile with Ezra. He represents one of the many Judean families that are reconstituting Jerusalem and the community of God's people after the Babylonian deportation.

sens: A man during the time of exile and return
Son of Asahel
H3129I.detail: 1. Jonathan is a character from the return from exile, mentioned only once in the Bible that has come down to us — in Ezra 10:15. He is the son of Asahel and opposed the repudiation of the foreign wives that the people had married during the Babylonian exile.
H3129I.origine: The name Jonathan means "Jehovah has given" or "the Eternal has given" — a combination of the divine name Jehovah and a verb that evokes giving. It is not a unique name: several important figures in the Old Testament bear this name, including the son of King Saul, friend of David. But this entry concerns only Jonathan son of Asahel mentioned in Ezra 10:15.
H3129I.emploi: Jonathan is mentioned only once in the current biblical texts, at the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in the context of the measures taken by Ezra to purify the people: as many Jews returned from captivity had married foreign women, the assembly decided to repudiate them. Jonathan, son of Asahel, was one of the few who publicly opposed this decision, alongside Jahaziah and supported by two other men. His moral courage to support an unpopular position distinguishes him in this crucial moment of the restoration of the Jewish people.

sens: Priest from the family of Melchijah during the time of Nehemiah
H3129J.detail: Jonathan is a priest belonging to the family of Melchijah, mentioned in the context of the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah. He appears in the list of priests and Levites who participated in the ceremonies of consecration of the rebuilt wall after the return from the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 12:14).
H3129J.origine: The name Jonathan means "the Eternal has given" in Hebrew, composed of Yah (abbreviation of the divine name) and natan (to give). It is a common theophoric name in the Bible, borne by several important figures at different times in the history of Israel.
H3129J.emploi: In the biblical text we have, Jonathan refers to a priest during the time of Nehemiah, belonging to the family of Melchijah. He is cited only once in Nehemiah 12:14, in the official list of priests and Levites who took part in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, after the return from exile. This mention places him in the religious community of restored Jerusalem, among those who ensured the worship of the Lord in the Second Temple.

sens: Levite during the time of Nehemiah, son of Shemaiah
Father of Zechariah, priest who sounded the trumpet at the dedication of the wall
H3129K.detail: 1. Yonathan is a Levite living at the time of the restoration of the temple and Jerusalem, after the return from exile. The text mentions him as the ancestor of a lineage of temple musicians — his son Zechariah is one of the priests who play the trumpet during the solemn dedication ceremony of the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:35). 2. He belongs to the large musical family of Asaph, one of the main dynasties of singers and musicians of the temple since the time of David. Genealogically, he occupies the place of a father of a priest, passing on the temple service to his descendants.
H3129K.origine: The name Yonathan (in Hebrew יוֹנָתָן) literally means "the Eternal has given." It comes from two roots: "Yah" or "Yehowah" (the Lord) and "natan" (to give). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude for the child as a gift from God. The name appears in various forms in the Bible (Jonathan, Yonathan, Jehonathan).
H3129K.emploi: Yonathan is mentioned only once in the Bible: in Nehemiah 12:35. He appears in a long genealogy of priests and Levites who participated in the dedication ceremony of the wall, after the reconstruction of Jerusalem at the return from exile (circa 445 B.C.). His son Zechariah is named among the official musicians. This unique mention places Yonathan in the context of the religious and communal restoration of the Jewish people.
H3129K.portee: This Yonathan reminds us that the temple worship and service to the Lord were passed down from father to son, from generation to generation, even during and after the exile. His name, which means "the Eternal has given," testifies that the Israelite believers recognized in their children gifts from God and dedicated them to His service.

sens: Son of Kareah, Judean military leader after the fall of Jerusalem
H3129L.detail: Jonathan is a Judean captain who lived after the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. He is the brother of Johanan and the son of Kareah. Along with other military leaders like Ishmael and Johanan, he rallies to Gedaliah, the governor appointed by the Babylonians at Mizpah (Jeremiah 40:8). These men represent the last military leaders of the kingdom of Judah, who seek to survive and maintain order in the ruins of the land after the exile.
H3129L.origine: The name Jonathan means "Jehovah has given" in Hebrew. It comes from the combination of Yah (the divine name) and natan (to give). It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, borne by several important figures: the son of King Saul, the son of the priest Abiathar, and others. For this specific Jonathan, he is a minor figure in the biblical text, a simple soldier during the time of the Babylonian captivity.
H3129L.emploi: This Jonathan appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 40:8. He is mentioned among the Judean captains who present themselves to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. His name is listed alongside his brother Johanan and other surviving military officers. This unique mention shows that he is a historical figure of the captivity period, without a major role in the biblical narrative.

sens: Son of the high priest Jehoiada
Successor to the position of high priest
Name meaning 'The Eternal has given'
H3129M.detail:
1. Jonathan is the son of the high priest Jehoiada, mentioned in the genealogical record of the priests during the time of Nehemiah (Nehemiah 12:11). He belongs to the lineage of high priests who served after the return from exile.
2. He succeeds his father Jehoiada in the position of high priest, thus continuing the priestly service in the restored Temple. His son Jaddua succeeds him in turn, marking the continuity of the Levitical priesthood.
3. His Hebrew name means "The Eternal has given," expressing the faith that the people placed in divine Providence for their children and sacred responsibilities.
H3129M.origine: The name Jonathan (יוֹנָתָן) consists of two elements: "Yo" (abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah, the Eternal) and "natan" (to give). It is a classic theophoric name in Hebrew, where the name of God is associated with a verb expressing a blessing. This name has been borne by several important figures in the history of Israel, including the son of King Saul and friend of David, whose prestige led to this name being adopted in other generations and families.
H3129M.emploi: This Jonathan is a priest from the lineage of Jehoiada, living at the time of the return from exile and the reconstruction of the Temple under Nehemiah (around the 5th century B.C.). He appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogical record of the high priests in Nehemiah 12:11, where his place in the priestly succession is clearly established: his father Jehoiada begot Jonathan, and Jonathan begot Jaddua. This mention underscores the importance of the continuity of the priesthood after the Babylonian exile.

sens: Son of King Saul and prince of Israel during the time of the united monarchy
Courageous warrior and military leader known for his bravery
Faithful friend of David despite the rivalry between their fathers
Figure of loyalty to God and wisdom in trials
H3129N.detail:
1. Jonathan is the son of King Saul, prince of Israel, living during the time when the kingdom was united. His name means "The Lord has given." He is the brother of Abinadab, Malchi-shua, and Michal, and he has half-brothers including Ish-Bosheth. His life first appears in the account of the war against the Philistines (1 Samuel 13).
2. Jonathan stands out as a warrior of remarkable bravery. With only his armor-bearer, he assaults the fortified post of the Philistines and routs them: "Jonathan climbed up using his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer followed him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan" (1 Samuel 14:13). The people recognize in him the one who accomplished this "great deliverance in Israel."
3. Despite his father Saul's murderous intentions toward David, Jonathan becomes David's sincere friend and seeks to protect him. His friendship transcends political and royal stakes: he chooses loyalty to the person over power ambitions.
4. Jonathan also appears as a man of conscience before God. Ignoring the people's oath, he eats honey and regains his strength, but he also acknowledges the judgments of the Lord. The verses show a man committed to divine will and honor, who accepts his fate without bitterness.
H3129N.origine: The name Jonathan (יוֹנָתָן) literally means "The Lord has given" (from יְהוָה, the Lord, and נָתַן, to give). There is a longer form, Jehonathan (יְהוֹנָתָן), which is simply a variant of the same name, with the divine prefix more explicit. This name expresses a blessing or gratitude to God for the gift of a son. Several other Jonathans appear in the Old Testament under this name or its variants.
H3129N.emploi: Jonathan, son of Saul, is the major character bearing this name in the provided texts. He appears mainly in 1 Samuel 13-14 and in 1 Chronicles 10, where he dies alongside his father at the battle of Gilboa. The 24 biblical occurrences of the term show Jonathan first as a young warrior prince (1 Samuel 13-14), then as David's friend, whose friendship contrasts with Saul's jealousy. The text depicts him as a man of action, strategic and courageous in the face of the Philistines, but also as a man of religious conscience who respects divine decisions. Although other Jonathans bear this name in biblical history (notably a son of Abiathar the priest, and leaders in post-exilic times), the provided occurrences concern exclusively the son of Saul.
H3129N.portee: Jonathan embodies authentic loyalty and courage in the service of the common good. His friendship with David, despite royal rivalries, shows how a moral conscience can overcome political and familial interests. His death alongside his father also illustrates the complexity of human life: a man of value can be caught in tragedies that surpass him. For the Christian, Jonathan represents the example of sincere friendship, selfless bravery, and submission to divine will, even in the face of adversity.

sens: Son of the priest Abiathar
Messenger announcing the coming of Solomon
H3129O.detail:
1. Jonathan is the son of the high priest Abiathar, who served at the court of King David. He is a member of the priestly family, heir to a lineage of priests dedicated to the service of the temple.
2. He appears in the story as the messenger who brings the news of King Solomon's ascension. Adonijah, who had declared himself king, receives him and recognizes him as a "valiant man" bearing good news (1 Kings 1:42-43). His arrival thus marked a decisive moment in the royal succession in Israel.
H3129O.origine: The name Jonathan, or Yonatan in Hebrew, means "Jehovah has given." It comes from the Hebrew root "Yah" (the name of God) and the verb "natan" (to give). This name therefore expresses the belief that the child is a gift from the Lord. There is a longer form, Yehonatan (Jehonathan), but both are equivalent.
H3129O.emploi: Jonathan, son of Abiathar, appears only twice in the Old Testament, both in the account of chapter 1 of the first book of Kings. During the royal succession at the time of David's death, Jonathan, as a member of the well-favored priestly family, is chosen to inform Adonijah of King David's decision: Solomon will be anointed king. His brief but significant intervention shows the influence of Abiathar's family at that time, although it is in decline (Abiathar will soon be exiled by Solomon).

sens: Warrior of David, son of Shagee
H3129P.detail: Jonathan is one of the valiant men who served King David. He is the son of Shagee and comes from Harar. The Bible mentions him in the list of David's renowned warriors, showing that he was a fighter of value (1 Chronicles 11:34).
H3129P.origine: The name Jonathan (or Jehonathan) means "the Lord has given." It is a theophoric name that expresses a blessing or recognition that God has granted a gift — in this case, this child. The name is composed of two elements: Jehovah (the name of God) and "given." Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, each distinct.
H3129P.emploi: Jonathan, son of Shagee, appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:34. He is listed among the "valiant men" or "mighty warriors" of David — the elite soldiers who accompanied and served him faithfully. This context tells us that he was an experienced and valuable fighter, worthy of being remembered among the heroes of King David.

sens: Eldest son of Jacob and Rachel, one of the patriarchs of Israel
Central figure in the family history of Israel's origins, sold into slavery and then raised in Egypt
H3130G.detail: 1. Joseph is the eldest son that Rachel longed for from God; his name means "may the Lord add" (Genesis 30:24), expressing his mother's gratitude. He becomes the major figure in the narrative of the Book of Genesis: first tenderly loved by his father Jacob, then sold by his jealous brothers into Egypt (Genesis 37:28), where he endures slavery and imprisonment before being elevated to power by Pharaoh, who entrusts him with the administration of the land (Genesis 41:41-42). 2. Joseph embodies faithfulness to God amid trials: falsely accused by Potiphar's wife, he remains upright in prison; he interprets Pharaoh's dreams with divine wisdom and saves Egypt and his family from famine. His story shows how God can elevate those who remain faithful to Him, even when all seems lost.
H3130G.origine: The name Joseph comes from the Hebrew Yosèph, composed of yo ("may Yah") and seph ("add"), literally "may the Lord add." This name expresses maternal desire and divine blessing. Joseph is also called Tsaphnath-Panéach, the Egyptian name given to him by Pharaoh upon his elevation to power (Genesis 41:45).
H3130G.emploi: Joseph appears 188 times in the biblical texts in French (notably as a proper name in the Segond). His story dominates about 14 chapters of Genesis (chapters 30-50), from his birth to his death. The main phases show: first the favored child (Genesis 37:2-3), then the dreamer whose dreams offend his brothers (Genesis 37:5), next the slave and prisoner in Egypt (Genesis 39-40), and finally the powerful administrator who saves the people from famine and reunites his divided family (Genesis 41-45). The Bible shows his spiritual growth: he forgives his brothers and recognizes that God has guided his life (Genesis 50:20).
H3130G.portee: The story of Joseph teaches that God never abandons His children, even in injustice and suffering. It shows how trust in God and moral integrity — notably the refusal of sin even under pressure — lead to exaltation and blessing. The forgiveness that Joseph offers to his brothers reveals how God transforms evil into good to fulfill His plan. It is an invitation to see God's hand in the trials of life.

sens: Father of Igal, sent as a spy for the tribe of Issachar
H3130H.detail: Joseph is the father of Igal, who was chosen among the twelve men sent by Moses to explore the land of Canaan before Israel's entry. Igal represented the tribe of Issachar in this reconnaissance mission (Numbers 13:7).
H3130H.origine: The name Joseph means "the Lord has added" in Hebrew. It comes from the root יסף (yasaph), which means "to add" or "to increase." This name expresses the idea that God adds or grants, often related to the blessing of offspring or new abundance.
H3130H.emploi: Joseph appears only once in the Bible with this passage from Numbers 13:7. He is mentioned only as the father of Igal, with no description of his own life or actions. His role in the text remains limited to this genealogical identification, serving to establish who Igal was among the twelve spies.

sens: Son of the Levite Asaph, musician of the temple during the divided monarchy
H3130I.detail: 1. Joseph is a Levite musician, son of Asaph, who served in the temple during the reigns of the kings of Israel and Judah. His name appears among the descendants of Asaph tasked with leading the songs and musical instruments in worship (1 Chronicles 25:2). He is mentioned as the first of Asaph's sons to whom a lot was drawn for his liturgical function (1 Chronicles 25:9).
H3130I.origine: The name Joseph means "the Lord has added" in Hebrew: it expresses the blessing of a birth granted by God. It is a name borne by several important figures in biblical history, but this one is a Levite musician from the time of the divided kingdom.
H3130I.emploi: This Joseph is mentioned twice in 1 Chronicles 25, in the chapter dedicated to the organization of the temple musicians. Unlike Joseph, the son of Jacob, famous in Genesis, or other Josephs in the Gospels, this one is known only through these two verses that place him among the temple singers under the direction of his father Asaph. He represents the ordinary servants of worship whose memory the Bible preserves without recounting their personal stories.

sens: man who lived during the time of exile and return
who had married a foreign woman
H3130J.detail:
1. Joseph is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the people return from exile in Babylon. He appears in the list of men who had married non-Israelite women and who must repudiate their wives to uphold God's law (Ezra 10:42). He is a simple citizen of God's people upon their return, with no known particular function.
2. His name means "God has added" in Hebrew, but for this man of the time of Ezra, the name is primarily a family heritage. His action—having taken a foreign wife—places him among those who compromised the separation of the chosen people, an infidelity that required restitution.
H3130J.origine: The name Joseph comes from the Hebrew yo.seph, formed from Yah (God) and saphah (to add). The name evokes the idea that God adds a child to his family, as in the case of the famous Joseph, son of Jacob. It was a common name among the Israelites, borne by several men throughout biblical history. Here, it designates a man from the time of Ezra, distinct from the other Josephs mentioned in the Scriptures.
H3130J.emploi: Joseph appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:42. This passage lists the names of the men of Israel who had taken foreign wives during the exile and return. This context shows that Joseph, like the others named, had compromised the purity of the people by uniting with a non-Israelite. His inclusion in this list reveals a critical moment of the people's restoration: the call to faithfulness to God's covenant. No other details about his life, family, or role are provided.

sens: Man of the time of exile and return, priest from the family of Shebaniah
H3130K.detail: This Joseph is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile to Jerusalem. He belongs to the priestly family of Shebaniah and is listed among the priests who returned with Nehemiah to rebuild the temple and restore worship.
H3130K.origine: The name Joseph means in Hebrew "God has added" (from the verb "to add" and the divine name). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the confidence that God grants offspring and blessing. Several men bear this name in the Bible, including the famous son of Jacob, but this one is an ordinary man from the time of the temple reconstruction.
H3130K.emploi: This Joseph appears only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 12:14. He is listed among the priests who returned from Babylonian captivity.
