The mention of his name alongside other priests and priestly families shows his role in the restoration of worship in Jerusalem after the exile. His precise identity eludes us beyond this simple historical record.

sens: Man of the time of exile and return to Jerusalem
H3131.detail: Josiphia is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile in Babylon. He is the father of Shelomith, who led one hundred sixty men of his family back to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:10).
H3131.origine: The name Josiphia means "The Lord adds" or "Jehovah adds." It is composed of the divine name "Jah" and the verb "to add," expressing blessing and divine multiplication. It is a typical theophoric name from the time of exile, carrying hope in God.
H3131.emploi: Josiphia appears only once in the Scriptures, in Ezra 8:10, where he is named as the father of Shelomith. This context is that of the return of the exiles from Babylon under Ezra's leadership in the sixth century B.C. He represents one of the families that were restored and participated in the renewal of God's people after captivity.

sens: warrior of Israel under David
H3132.detail: Joéla is a man's name mentioned only once in the Bible. He was one of the valiant warriors who joined David, probably while he was hiding from King Saul. He was the son of Jeroham, from Gedor, and had a brother named Zebadiah.
H3132.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "may he be useful" or "may he serve." It expresses the idea that God gives usefulness and ability to the one who bears it. It is a compound name with the verb that means "to help" or "to benefit."
H3132.emploi: Joéla appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:7, where he is presented as one of the brave men who joined David at Gedor. The Bible mentions him alongside his brother Zebadiah, both sons of Jeroham. This list of David's warriors is set in the context of the gathering of people around David before he became king over all Israel. These men represent the support that David received even before his accession to the throne.

sens: A man of the tribe of Benjamin, living at the time of the return from exile
Son of Pedaiah and father of Meshullam
H3133.detail: Joëd is a Benjamite mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogical list of the inhabitants of Jerusalem after the return from exile (Nehemiah 11:7). He belongs to a well-established lineage: he is the son of Pedaiah and the father of Meshullam, recorded in the order of generations that rebuilt Jerusalem.
H3133.origine: The name Joëd means "Jehovah is witness" or "the Lord testifies." It comes from the combination of the divine name YHWH (Jehovah/the Lord) and the Hebrew verb that evokes the action of bearing witness, serving as a witness. It is a typical theophoric name of the Old Testament, reminding us that God watches over and attests to the actions of men.
H3133.emploi: Joëd appears only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 11:7, in the genealogy of the Benjamites who returned to settle in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. This list shows how families reorganized and resettled in the city. Although briefly mentioned, Joëd is part of the genealogical chain that illustrates the restoration of God's people and the reconstitution of their families after exile.

sens: Warrior of Korah who joined David at Ziklag
H3134.detail: Joézer is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the enumeration of David's mighty warriors. He belonged to the clan of the Korahites, Levites descended from Korah, and he was one of those who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:6). His name means "Jehovah is help" or "God helps," reflecting trust in divine intervention.
H3134.origine: His Hebrew name יוֹעֶזֶר (Joézer) is composed of two elements: יְהוָה (Yehowah, "Jehovah") and עָזַר (azar, "to help"). This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel to express dependence on God and His protection. Other names from the same family include Eleazar ("God helps").
H3134.emploi: Joézer appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 12:6. He is mentioned among the Korahites who came to support David when he was pursued by Saul and had taken refuge at Ziklag. This passage lists the mighty warriors and courageous men who joined the future king. The Korahites formed an important lineage of Levites, guardians of the tabernacle and musicians, which gives Joézer an honorable place among the faithful of Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Beker
H3135G.detail: Joasch is a Benjamite, one of the sons of Beker, mentioned in the genealogy of the sons of Israel at the time of the Exodus from Egypt and the sojourn in the wilderness. He appears in the family list in 1 Chronicles 7:8, alongside his brothers Zemira, Eliezer, Eljoenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth.
H3135G.origine: The name Joasch means "the Lord hastens" or "the Lord accelerates." It is composed of the divine name Jaho (the Lord) and a root expressing speed or acceleration. This name expresses trust in God's swift help.
H3135G.emploi: Joasch is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:8, in the context of the genealogies of the tribes of Israel. There is no detailed account of his life or actions; his name simply appears in the genealogical record of the tribe of Benjamin, testifying to his place in the history of the chosen people.

sens: Man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel
H3135H.detail: Joash is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:28. He was one of the officers of King David's court, responsible for administrative functions within the royal government.
H3135H.origine: The name Joash means "the Lord hastens" or "the Lord accelerates," composed of "Yo" (the Lord) and "ash" (to hasten). It is a theophoric name, expressing trust in God's swift intervention. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, but they are distinct.
H3135H.emploi: Joash appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 27:28. He is presented as one of the twelve officers appointed by King David to administer the various regions and resources of the kingdom. His specific role entrusted him with the charge of the royal provisions. Although briefly mentioned, he illustrates the sophisticated administrative organization of David's court.

sens: High priest of Jerusalem during the Exile in Babylon
Father of the high priest Joshua who led the reconstruction of the Temple
H3136A.detail:
1. Jotsadak is a man of the tribe of Levi who lived during the Exile in Babylon. He was the son of the high priest Seraiah and the father of the high priest Joshua (Ezra 3:2). Although he descended from a lineage of high priests, Jotsadak himself could never exercise this office as he was taken captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar.
2. Jotsadak is best known as the father of the high priest Joshua, who upon returning from Exile led the reconstruction of the Temple alongside Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:8). This is why he is mentioned in the accounts of the return and the restoration of worship in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 12:26).
H3136A.origine: His name means "Jehovah is righteous" or "Jehovah has justified." It is an abbreviated form of the full name "Jehozadak." Jotsadak belongs to the great Levitical lineage of high priests of Jerusalem, descending from Hilkiah and tracing back to Aaron himself. His name expresses the confidence that God, despite the Exile, remains just in His judgments.
H3136A.emploi: Jotsadak is mentioned three times in the Bible, always in the accounts of the return from Exile (Ezra and Nehemiah). He first appears through his son Joshua, who in 536 B.C. led the reconstruction of the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem (Ezra 3:2). He is then cited during the implementation of the restoration work of the Temple (Ezra 3:8). Finally, he is mentioned as an ancestor in the genealogy of the high priests during Nehemiah's time (Nehemiah 12:26). Although captive in Babylon, Jotsadak remains an important figure in the continuity of the Israelite priesthood through the return.
H3136A.portee: Jotsadak embodies God's promise not to abandon His people, even in exile. Although himself a captive, God allowed his son to lead the restoration of worship: this is a sign that God maintained His covenants and restored what had been destroyed. For the believer, Jotsadak shows that even in dark periods when promises seem blocked, God prepares for return and redemption.

sens: Father of the high priest Joshua at the time of the return from exile
Levite of the lineage of high priests, son of Seraiah
Man taken captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar
H3136B.detail:
1. Jotsadak is the father of the high priest Joshua (also called Jeshua), who leads the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. Although from the family of high priests, Jotsadak himself never held this office (Ezra 5:2).
2. He descends from a long lineage of high priests: he is the son of Seraiah, high priest at the time of the capture of Jerusalem, and the grandson of high priest Hilkiah. Thus, although a prisoner in exile, his family represents the heart of Jewish worship.
3. Jotsadak was deported to Babylon by King Nebuchadnezzar during the fall of Jerusalem, but his name remains associated with the return and restoration of the temple.
H3136B.origine: The name "Jotsadak" comes from Hebrew and means "God (Yahweh) is just." There is also a more complete Aramaic form, "Jehozadak," used in the Aramaic texts of the book of Ezra. The form "Jotsadak" is the one retained in the Hebrew passages and the Segond translation.
H3136B.emploi: Jotsadak appears only once in the Segond, in Ezra 5:2, where he is presented as the father of Joshua during the resumption of the construction of the temple. His name embodies the link between ancient Jerusalem (his family of high priests before the exile) and the renewal under Persian rule. Although mentioned briefly in the text, he symbolizes the continuity of the Jewish priesthood through captivity and exile.
H3136B.portee: Jotsadak reminds us that even in captivity and exile, God preserves those who serve Him. As the father of a restoring high priest, he embodies the secret hope of the faithful people during the years of desolation, and his descendants will play a key role in the spiritual reconstruction of Jerusalem.

sens: Man of the priestly tribe, living during the time of exile and return to Jerusalem
H3136G.detail: Jotsadak is a priest, grandson of the high priest Hilkiah, son of the high priest Seriah, and father of the high priest Joshua (also called Jeshua). His name means "Yahweh is righteous." Captured by Nebuchadnezzar during the deportation to Babylon, he never became high priest himself, unlike his father and son. He is mentioned in Ezra 10:18 as the father of Joshua, whose descendants had married foreign women in Jerusalem after the return from exile.
H3136G.origine: The name Jotsadak comes from Hebrew and literally means "Yahweh is righteous" (from Yahweh, the name of God, and saddaq, "to be righteous"). He belongs to the great Levitical priestly family. His father Seriah was high priest before the exile; his son Joshua was high priest during the reconstruction of the Temple after the return from Babylon.
H3136G.emploi: Jotsadak is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:18. He is designated as the father of Joshua and as a transitional figure between the exile and the return: his father experienced the Temple before its destruction, and his son participated in its reconstruction. Although of eminent priestly rank, he never himself exercised the function of high priest, probably due to his captivity in Babylon.
H3136G.portee: The fate of Jotsadak reminds us that even the descendants of great priestly families suffered from exile and lost privileges, but that God's grace also extended to them in the return. His son Joshua will embody spiritual renewal and the reconstruction of the Temple, showing that God does not abandon His people.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah
son of Shelah
brother of Er, Laada, Joash, and Saraph
H3137.detail: Jokim is a man belonging to the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in Scripture. He is the son of Shelah and the brother of Er, Laada, Joash, and Saraph (1 Chronicles 4:22). He lived during the time of Egypt and the desert, an ancient period according to the text itself. His name means "The Lord raises up" or "The Lord lifts up," expressing confidence in divine intervention.
H3137.origine: The name Jokim comes from the Hebrew root "qum" which means "to rise" or "to lift up." The prefix "Yo" is a short form of the divine name the Lord (Yahweh). Thus, Jokim literally means "The Lord raises up" or "The Lord lifts up." It is a typical theophoric name in Jewish tradition, expressing trust in God's benevolent action.
H3137.emploi: Jokim is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 4:22. He appears in the genealogy of Judah, alongside his brothers Joash and Saraph, who would have ruled over Moab. The text emphasizes that "these things are ancient," indicating that they are distant memories of a bygone era. No additional details are provided about his life or personal deeds.

sens: Rain that falls in Palestine from October to December
Early rain that prepares the land before sowing
H3138.detail: 1. In Palestine, after the long summer drought, this is a rain that arrives from October to December: it soaks the hardened earth so that farmers can sow wheat and other crops. It is essential for agricultural life (Deuteronomy 11:14). 2. This autumn rain is called "first" or "early" because it precedes the latter rains, the more abundant rains of winter and spring. It is the beginning of the agricultural cycle that God alone controls (Jeremiah 5:24).
H3138.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to draw, to throw" or "to teach" — the image of water falling from the sky as if projected. It is a rain specific to the Mediterranean climate, distinct from winter rain (the latter rain) and spring rain.
H3138.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe this autumn rain essential to Palestinian agriculture. In Deuteronomy 11:14, it is promised as a blessing: "I will give your land the rain at the right time." In Jeremiah 5:24, it is recalled as God's work, proof of His power and providence that Israel should recognize with fear. Both passages link this rain to God's agricultural plan and Israel's obedience.
H3138.portee: This word reminds the reader that the life of God's people depends on His hand: neither agriculture nor survival is solely in human hands. The rain that falls at the right time is an act of God towards those who fear and obey Him. It is an invitation to see God's invisible governance in the most everyday realities of earth and sky.

sens: Father or ancestor of a family of Jews who returned from exile in Babylon with Ezra
H3139.detail: Jora is a man who appears at the time of the return from exile, mentioned as the head of a family or ancestor of a clan of Jews who returned from Babylon. During the counting of the repatriates with Ezra, his descendants number one hundred twelve men (Ezra 2:18). He is an example of those household heads or patriarchs whose names mark the identity and continuity of the Israelite families restored in the promised land after captivity.
H3139.origine: The name Jora literally means "he instructs" or "he teaches" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a role of guide or teacher within his family or community. He is also known by the alternative name Hariph, which shows that ancient texts identify him by two different names, a practice not uncommon among household heads in the Old Testament.
H3139.emploi: Jora appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 2:18, at the time of the great return of the Jews from exile in Babylon. He is listed among the heads of families and their descendants who accompanied Ezra on this journey of restoration. The fact that his family is specifically numbered — with one hundred twelve members — underscores his importance as a recognized leader and founder of a lineage that participated in the reconstruction of the people of Israel.
H3139.portee: Jora embodies the faithfulness of Jewish families who maintained their identity and unity during captivity and chose to return to settle in the Holy Land. His name reminds the reader that the restoration of Israel after exile did not occur in a formless mass, but through concrete families, led by named leaders, bearers of the heritage of God's people.

sens: Man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H3140.detail: Joraï is a Gadite, that is, a member of the tribe of Gad, who lived in Gilead in Bashan during the time of King Jotham of Judah. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13, where he appears among his brothers in the genealogy of the family heads of Gad.
H3140.origine: The name Joraï means "The Lord has taught me" or "The Lord instructs me." It is composed of the divine name Yah (Jehovah) and a root that expresses teaching or instruction, reflecting the belief that God guides and instructs His people.
H3140.emploi: Joraï appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13, in the detailed genealogy of the leaders of the tribe of Gad. He is presented as the son of Abihail and brother of six other men: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jaekan, Zia, and Eber. This genealogical context shows that he was a recognized family leader among the Gadites established in Gilead in Bashan during the reign of King Jotham.

sens: son of Toi, king of Hamath
H3141G.detail: Joram is the son of King Toi of Hamath. He is sent by his father to greet King David and congratulate him on his victory over Hadadezer, a common enemy. On this occasion, Joram brings David valuable gifts: vessels of silver, gold, and bronze (2 Samuel 8:10).
H3141G.origine: The name Joram means "the Lord is exalted." It combines the divine name "Yah" (God) and the verb "ram" (to be raised, exalted). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several important figures in the Old Testament, all marked by a strong religious significance.
H3141G.emploi: Joram, son of Toi, appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 8:10. He is mentioned in the context of diplomacy between Hamath and Israel during the reign of David. Although few details are given about his personal life, his diplomatic mission shows the importance of international relations at the time of the united kingdom of Israel.

sens: King of Israel, son of Ahab and Jezebel, who reigned twelve years during the divided monarchy
King of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat, who reigned eight years and led his kingdom back to idolatry
H3141H.detail:
1. Joram is primarily the name of the king of the northern kingdom, Israel, son of Ahab and Jezebel. He reigned twelve years and fought against the Syrians: wounded at Ramoth in Gilead, he withdrew to Jezreel to heal (2 Kings 8:28-29). He was assassinated by Jehu, who killed him on the field that his father Ahab had once stolen from Naboth, thus fulfilling Elijah's prophecy (2 Kings 9:14-16).

2. Joram also refers to the king of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat. He reigned eight years, but his wife Athaliah, who was probably a daughter or sister of Ahab, led him into idolatry by bringing Judah back to the worship of Baal (2 Kings 8:16-18). He is sometimes called Jehoram in biblical texts.
H3141H.origine: The name means "Jehovah is exalted" (from Jehovah and the verb to exalt). It can appear in the form "Jehoram" (יְהוֹרָם), which is more developed. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name, like many royal names in Israel and Judah.
H3141H.emploi: Joram mainly appears in the accounts of the kings of the North and South during the divided monarchy. The nine biblical occurrences primarily designate him as king of Israel (son of Ahab) in his battles against Syria and his death at the hands of Jehu, as well as king of Judah (son of Jehoshaphat) and his family ties with the king of the North. The context involves wars between kingdoms, royal illness, and prophetic interventions against idolatry.
H3141H.portee: The story of Joram of Israel reminds us that political power does not protect against divine judgment: despite his military efforts, he is killed according to an ancient prophecy. The story of Joram of Judah shows the decisive influence of a wicked wife in a king's choices and in a nation's destiny. These two stories invite the believer to meditate on the fragility of human power and the importance of remaining faithful to God rather than being seduced by idolatry.

sens: Levite from the period of the divided monarchy
Ancestor of Shelomith
H3141I.detail:
1. Joram is a man from the tribe of Levi who lived during the divided monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:25, as the son of Isshiah and father of Zicri, in the genealogy of the descendants of Eleazar.
2. Through his lineage, Joram is part of the genealogical line that will lead to Shelomith, a significant figure among the people of God. His name means "the Eternal is exalted," reflecting the faith of the people in God's power and dignity.
H3141I.origine: The name Joram means "the Eternal is exalted" or "God is elevated." It comes from the divine name Yô (the Eternal) combined with ram (elevated, exalted), a common biblical image to express God's greatness and sovereignty. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, including kings of Judah and Israel, but this Joram is simply an ordinary Levite whose name carries the same theological significance.
H3141I.emploi: This Joram is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:25, as a member of the tribe of Levi living under the divided monarchy. He appears in a genealogy descending from Eleazar and leading up to Shelomith, who was in charge of the treasures dedicated to the Lord (1 Chronicles 26:26-28). Although his historical existence is brief in the biblical text, his place in this genealogy shows that the genealogical records of the post-exilic period preserved the memory of priestly and Levitical families.

sens: King of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat
Son of Ahab, king of northern Israel
Levite during the time of David
Son of Toi, king of Hamath
H3141J.detail:
1. Joram is a king of Judah who reigned eight years and succeeded his father Jehoshaphat. He is best known for his wars, particularly against the Edomites reported in 2 Kings 8:21, where he took the lead of his chariots to fight the enemies surrounding him. He is also the father of Ahaziah and Jehosheba, who saved the young prince Joash from death.
2. Another Joram reigns over the northern kingdom, Israel, for twelve years as the son of King Ahab. According to the source, he was assassinated by Jehu on the field of Naboth, thus fulfilling Elijah's prophecy.
3. Joram also refers to a Levite during the time of David, an ancestor of Shelomith according to historical tradition.
4. A fourth Joram is the son of Toi, king of Hamath, mentioned in ancient genealogies.
H3141J.origine: The name Joram means "The Eternal is exalted" in Hebrew, composed of the divine root (YHWH, the Eternal) and a form evoking elevation or exaltation. This name was borne by several important figures in Israel's history. There is a related form, Jehoram (יְהוֹרָם), which is a variant or a full name of the same royal character.
H3141J.emploi: The name Joram appears five times in the Segond 1910, concentrated on the king of Judah of the 9th century BC. The first three occurrences (2 Kings 8:21, 8:23, 8:24) describe the last years of his reign: his military campaigns, his acts recorded in the royal annals, and his death and burial in the City of David according to royal protocol. A fourth mention (2 Kings 11:2) designates him as the father of Jehosheba and likely the father of Ahaziah, situating the account in a dynastic context. The fifth occurrence (1 Chronicles 3:11) places Joram in the complete genealogy of the kings of Judah, confirming his central dynastic position. The predominant context is that of the political and military history of the southern kingdom during the divided monarchy.

sens: Son of Zerubbabel
Man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H3142.detail: Juschab-Hésed is a proper name designating a man from the tribe of Judah who lived during the divided monarchy in Israel. He was one of the sons of Zerubbabel, an important figure in the return from Babylonian exile during the time of Nehemiah and Ezra. The only place he is mentioned in the Bible is 1 Chronicles 3:20, where he is listed among the brothers Meshullam, Hananiah, Shelomith, Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Abiud.
H3142.origine: The name Juschab-Hésed literally means "whose love returns" or "whose goodness returns." It combines two Hebrew words: "yoshav" (to return, to come back) and "hésed" (goodness, faithfulness, covenant love). This name carries the idea of God's response or the return of His favor upon this son of Zerubbabel.
H3142.emploi: Juschab-Hésed appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:20. He is mentioned in the royal genealogy of the house of Judah and David, as one of the nine children of Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel was the governor of Judah upon the return from the Babylonian exile around 520 BC. The enumeration of his sons in Chronicles emphasizes the continuity of the Davidic line after the exile.
H3142.portee: This name illustrates how God preserves and blesses the families of the people of Judah even after the Babylonian exile. The meaning of the name — love or goodness that returns — reminds us that God's faithfulness to His people has not ceased, despite the judgment of exile.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible
H3143.detail: Joschibia is a man belonging to the tribe of Simeon, living during the divided monarchy. He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:35, where he is presented as the father of Jehu and the son of Seriah, in a Simeonite genealogy.
H3143.origine: The name Joschibia comes from Hebrew and literally means "Jehovah causes to dwell" or "God establishes." It is composed of the divine name Jah and a verb expressing the idea of establishment or dwelling.
H3143.emploi: Joschibia appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 4:35. He is listed in a genealogical record of the tribe of Simeon and is identified as the father of Jehu and the son of Seriah. This brief mention, although it gives us little detail about his life or actions, places him in the succession of Simeonite generations and confirms his place in the history of Israel.

sens: A leader of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy
H3144.detail: Joscha is a prince of the house of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:34, where he is presented as the son of Amatzia. He appears in a genealogical list of the leaders of Simeon, alongside Meschobab and Jamlech, during the period of the divided monarchy (after the schism between the Northern and Southern kingdoms). His exact role in the history of Israel is not detailed.
H3144.origine: The name Joscha means "Jehovah makes equal" or "Jehovah equalizes," formed from the divine element Yah (Jehovah) and a root evoking equality or balance. Like many Hebrew names, it carries an affirmation of divine power applied to the bearer.
H3144.emploi: Joscha appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 4:34, in the genealogy of the children of Simeon. He is designated as the son of Amatzia and figures among the recognized leaders of his tribe. This unique mention in a purely genealogical context indicates that he was a figure of some local importance in Judah or in the territory of Simeon, but the details of his life and actions have not been preserved in the biblical narrative.

sens: warrior in the service of King David
H3145.detail: Joschavia is a man who lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is the son of Elnaam and the brother of Jeribaï. He appears in the list of David's mighty warriors (1 Chronicles 11:46), indicating that he had a trusted military role with the king.
H3145.origine: The Hebrew name means "the Eternal equalizes" or "the Eternal makes equal." Like many Hebrew names, it is constructed with the divine name (Yah) and a verb that expresses God's action.
H3145.emploi: Joschavia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:46. He appears in the context of a list compiled by the historian of Chronicles, that of the valiant warriors who served King David. This list celebrates the men who formed the guard and elite troops of the kingdom.

sens: Warrior of David
H3146G.detail: Josaphat is one of the renowned warriors of King David, mentioned only once in the Bible (1 Chronicles 11:43). His name appears in the list of the "Gibbor" — the war heroes who served the king with faithfulness and valor. The details of his exploits are unknown, but his presence in this honorable role indicates that he distinguished himself in battle.
H3146G.origine: The name Josaphat means "The Eternal judges": it comes from two Hebrew terms, yo ("Eternal") and shaphat ("to judge"). This type of theophoric name — where a person's name incorporates the name or a divine quality — was common in Israel, thus expressing God's action or character in the life of the name bearer.
H3146G.emploi: Josaphat appears only once in the Bible: in 1 Chronicles 11:43, where he is cited among the thirty-two heroes who supported David. He is designated as "Josaphat of Mithni" — probably an indication of geographical or familial origin. This catalog of warriors testifies to the military power and loyalty that surrounded David during his reign and helped him establish his kingdom.

sens: Priest and trumpeter during the time of David
H3146H.detail: Josaphat is a priest who served during the reign of King David. He is mentioned during a great ceremony when the ark of the covenant is transported to Jerusalem: along with other priests, he sounds the trumpet before the ark to accompany this solemn moment (1 Chronicles 15:24). His name means "Jehovah judges" in Hebrew.
H3146H.origine: The name Josaphat is composed of two elements: Yah (abbreviation of the divine name) and Shaphat ("to judge"). It is a confession of faith, expressing that God is the one who exercises judgment. This is the same name borne by a much more famous king of Judah, but this Josaphat is just a humble servant during the time of David.
H3146H.emploi: Josaphat is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in chapter 15 of 1 Chronicles. He appears in a list of priests and musicians that David established to celebrate the solemn transfer of the ark of God. This moment carries great religious significance: it marks the beginning of well-organized worship within the unified kingdom of Israel.
H3146H.portee: This obscure character reminds us that many faithful servants of God have acted in the shadows, never receiving lasting honors. Josaphat fulfilled his sacred function with dedication, contributing to the worship of the true God, even though he never became famous. It is a lesson in humility: our worth before God does not depend on our renown.

sens: Youngest son of Gideon, the only survivor of the massacre of his brothers
He who pronounced a prophetic curse against Shechem
H3147G.detail: 1. Jotham is the youngest son of Gideon (also called Jerubbaal). When Abimelech, one of his brothers, kills the seventy other sons of Gideon to establish his power in Shechem, only Jotham escapes the massacre by hiding (Judges 9:5). 2. From his hiding place on Mount Gerizim, Jotham cries out to the inhabitants of Shechem a curse: he reproaches them for supporting Abimelech, and he announces that evil will fall upon their heads (Judges 9:7, 9:57). This curse is indeed fulfilled, as God brings judgment upon Shechem for the crime it committed.
H3147G.origine: The name Jotham means "Yahweh is perfect." It historically designates the son of Gideon during the time of the Judges, before the Israelite monarchy. He is a child who becomes a witness to a fratricidal crime and the bearer of a word of divine judgment.
H3147G.emploi: Jotham appears four times in the book of Judges, exclusively in chapter 9, which recounts the affair of Abimelech. He is first presented as the sole survivor of the massacre perpetrated by Abimelech (Judges 9:5). He then climbs Mount Gerizim and cries a curse against Shechem (Judges 9:7), and then he flees to Beer to escape his brother's vengeance (Judges 9:21). Finally, the Bible notes that the curse he pronounced was fulfilled: God brought evil upon the Shechemites (Judges 9:57).
H3147G.portee: The story of Jotham shows that even in the midst of violence and injustice, one who speaks in the name of God calls for His justice. His curse is not a personal vengeance, but a call to God: "May God hear you!" The fulfillment of this curse reminds us that God does not leave serious crimes unpunished, and that a faithful word spoken in His favor has a significance that transcends the moment.

sens: king of Judah in the 8th century B.C.
son of King Uzziah and father of Ahaz
administrator of the kingdom during his father's leprosy
H3147H.detail:
1. Jotham is a king from the tribe of Judah, who reigned for about sixteen years during the period of the Divided Monarchy. His story unfolds mainly in 2 Kings 15-16 and 2 Chronicles 26-27, where he appears as a transitional figure between his father Uzziah and his son Ahaz.

2. He is first presented as the son of King Uzziah (also called Azariah) and Jerusha. When his father becomes leprous and must withdraw from public life, Jotham "was in charge of the palace and governed the people of the land" (2 Kings 15:5), thus exercising royal authority in his absence.

3. During his own reign, Jotham "became powerful because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God" (2 Chronicles 27:6). He is contemporary with the great prophets Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah, as indicated by the subscriptions of their prophetic books.
H3147H.origine: The name Jotham means "God is perfect" or "The Lord is perfect" in Hebrew. It reflects his parents' faith in the perfection of the Lord. Jotham belongs to the royal lineage of Judah, descending from David and an ancestor of the dynasty that would later include King Hezekiah, a figure of religious restoration.
H3147H.emploi: Jotham appears 19 times in Scripture, primarily in 2 Kings 15-16 and 2 Chronicles 26-27, where his political and religious history is recounted. He reigned for about sixteen years (circa 750-735 B.C.). The references first show his role as regent during his leprous father's reign, then his own reign marked by stability and religious strength. He is also mentioned in the subscriptions of the prophetic books of Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah as one of the kings under whom these prophets exercised their ministry. His son Ahaz, in contrast, will take a less faithful path, highlighting Jotham's spiritual significance in the history of Judah.
H3147H.portee: Jotham embodies the virtue of establishing his ways before God, which leads to power and stability in his reign. His example reminds us that personal faithfulness to the Lord is the foundation of true authority. Unlike many kings, there are no recorded acts contrary to God's law during his reign, providing a model of a ruler who "did what was right in the eyes of the Lord."

sens: Son of Jahdai, from the tribe of Judah
H3147I.detail: Jotham is a man from the tribe of Judah, son of Jahdai and grandson of Caleb. He is mentioned only once in Scripture genealogically, during the enumeration of Caleb's descendants in 1 Chronicles 2:47. His name means "The Lord is perfect" in Hebrew. Although few details are given about his life, his inclusion in the genealogy of Israel shows his belonging to an important lineage of God's people.
H3147I.origine: The name Jotham comes from Hebrew and literally means "Jah (the Lord) is perfect." It is composed of two elements: "Yo" or "Jah," an abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh, and "tam" which means "perfect" or "upright." Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, which was a common practice in Israel to give children theophoric names, that is, names containing the name of God, to express the family's faith and hopes.
H3147I.emploi: Jotham is mentioned only once in Scripture in 1 Chronicles 2:47, in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants. He is presented as one of the six sons of Jahdai: "The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph." He does not appear anywhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Unlike other bearers of the name Jotham (notably the son of King Uzziah and the son of Gideon, who are not mentioned in these references), this Jotham is known only by this simple genealogical inscription, without a detailed account of his life or actions.

sens: What exceeds, what remains of a whole after taking a part
What provides a benefit, a profit, or a superiority
What is in excess, superfluous, or unnecessary
As a particle: "more" or "furthermore"
As a conjunction: "in addition" or "moreover"
H3148.detail: 1. The primary meaning is that of what remains or exceeds: the remainder of the flocks after the sacrifice in 1 Samuel 15:15 ("the rest, we have devoted"); the excess that is set aside. It conveys the idea of a remaining or additional part. 2. The word also refers to the advantage or benefit derived from something: in Ecclesiastes 6:8, the wise man asks what "advantage" he has over the fool — that is, what real profit or concrete superiority. 3. By extension, it refers to anything superfluous or unnecessary, an abundance that does not benefit: in Ecclesiastes 6:11, "many vanities" do not give any "advantage" to man. 4. Used as a particle or adverb, the word means "more" or "further" in a comparison: in Ecclesiastes 2:15, the Preacher states that he has been "wiser" than the fool. 5. As a conjunction, it means "in addition" or "moreover" to add a thought: in Ecclesiastes 7:11, wisdom is as valuable as an inheritance, and "even more" (or "in addition") for those who see the sun.
H3148.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of exceeding, surpassing, or going beyond. It can function as a noun ("the advantage," "the remainder"), as an adverb ("more," "further"), or as a conjunction ("in addition"). This versatility is typical of biblical Hebrew, where the same root can take multiple forms depending on its grammatical context.
H3148.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the historical and wisdom books. In 1 Samuel 15:15, it literally refers to the remainder of the spoils. In Ecclesiastes (6:8, 6:11, 7:11), its use becomes much more philosophical: Qoheleth uses it to question the real utility of wisdom, wealth, or instruction in light of the vanity of human condition. The word oscillates between a concrete sense ("what remains") and an abstract sense ("the interest derived from it"). It also serves to express a comparison or a logical addition in discourse.
H3148.portee: This word reminds us of a fundamental question of faith: what truly has value and utility in life? Ecclesiastes, which uses it repeatedly, urges us not to seek benefit and advantage solely in wisdom, possessions, or human accomplishments, but to recognize that without God, all of this remains empty and superfluous. It is an invitation to seek our true profit in the fear of the Lord rather than in this world.

sens: Benjamite from the time of the divided monarchy
valiant warrior of David
son of Azmaveth
brother of Pelet
H3149.detail: Jeziel is a Benjamite warrior, son of Azmaveth and brother of Pelet, who joined David at Ziklag. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, among the list of brave warriors who rallied to the king: "The chief Ahiezer and Joash, the son of Shemaah, of Gibeah; Jeziel, and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Berachah; Jehu, of Anathoth" (1 Chronicles 12:3). His name appears at the heart of this enumeration of valiant warriors who chose to follow David during the troubled period of the divided monarchy.
H3149.origine: The name Jeziel means "the assembly of God" in Hebrew, composed of the Hebrew "iezah" (assembly) and "El" (God). It belongs to the family of theophoric names among the Benjamites, that is, names that incorporate the divine name, a common practice in families of ancient Israel to signify divine blessing upon the child.
H3149.emploi: Jeziel is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:3, in the context of the gathering of warriors who joined David at Ziklag after he fled from King Saul. This passage lists the chief and valiant warriors from various tribes who recognized David as their king. Jeziel is noted as a warrior of value, alongside his brother Pelet, both sons of Azmaveth, a renowned Benjamite.

sens: Man living during the time of exile and return to Judea
H3150.detail: Jizzija is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile under Ezra. He belongs to the descendants of Pareosch and is among those who married a foreign woman — which the religious leaders of the return considered as unfaithfulness to God's covenant (Ezra 10:25).
H3150.origine: The Hebrew name יִזִּיָּה (Yizziyah) literally means "God sprinkles" or "Jehovah sprinkles": it combines the Hebrew verb "to sprinkle" (the image of worship and purification) and the name of God. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name.
H3150.emploi: Jizzija appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:25. He is listed among the descendants of Pareosch who had taken foreign wives during the exile or upon returning to Jerusalem. Ezra and the elders of Israel demanded the separation of these unions, which were considered contrary to the holiness of the restored people.

sens: Official in King David's administration
H3151.detail: Jaziz is a man from the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. His name means "He who makes prominent" or "He who stands out." He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:31, where he is presented as a Hagarite (a member of the people of the Hagarites, desert nomads) responsible for King David's sheep. He is part of the royal stewards tasked with managing the king's various goods and resources.
H3151.origine: The name Jaziz comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of distinguishing oneself, becoming visible, or becoming prominent. This root reflects the image of one who stands out among others. Jaziz is a personal name, likely held by a person of high rank within the royal administration.
H3151.emploi: Jaziz appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:31. This verse places him in the context of the administrative organization established by King David. During his reign, David had set up a system of officials and stewards to manage his possessions: palaces, fields, vineyards, olive groves, flocks, etc. Jaziz, although a foreigner (Hagarite), had gained the king's trust to the point of being entrusted with one of the major elements of his wealth: the sheep. This brief mention shows that David recruited talented men regardless of their origin.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H3152.detail: Jizlia is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:18. He is the son of Elpaal and the brother of several other Benjamites, including Jischmeraï and Jobab. His name appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin, a record that lists the family heads of this tribe at a time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the north and the south.
H3152.origine: The name Jizlia means "he whom God will preserve" or "whom God will keep." It is formed from Hebrew roots that express the idea of divine guarding and protection. Like many Hebrew proper names, it reflects a prayer or blessing from the parents towards their son, expressing their trust in God's protection.
H3152.emploi: Jizlia appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 8:18. He is listed in a genealogical record of the sons of Elpaal, a family head from Benjamin. This mention is part of the register of the descendants of Benjamin compiled after the exile, which allowed the returning families to root themselves in their tribal heritage. His name, without any particular anecdote attached, simply attests to his existence and his place in the genealogy of the tribe.

sens: Judean military officer at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem
H3153.detail: Jezania is a military leader who survived the fall of Jerusalem before the Babylonians. He appears alongside Johanan, son of Kareah, among the leaders of the troops who turn to the prophet Jeremiah to seek God's will after the destruction of the kingdom (Jeremiah 42:1). His name means "The Lord has listened," reflecting the hope of the afflicted people.
H3153.origine: The name Jezania comes from the Hebrew root זנה (zan) associated with "Yah" (an abbreviation of the divine name יהוה). It literally means "The Lord has listened" or "Yah has listened." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, formed in the pattern of names that express God's benevolent action. Jezania is also referred to as Jaazaniah or Azariah in other passages, indicating that several variants of his name were known.
H3153.emploi: Jezania, son of Hoshaiah the Maachathite, is mentioned only once in the Segond (Jeremiah 42:1) as one of the leaders of the troops who escaped the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem. He comes to find the prophet Jeremiah with Johanan and the entire people to ask him what the Lord's will is. He is a historical figure representing the remnant of the nation after the deportation, engaged in the quest for divine direction during a crucial period of the decline of the Kingdom of Judah.

sens: Liquid that flows from the skin due to heat or effort
Symptom of hard work or fatigue
Sign of guilt or anxiety
H3154.detail:
1. Sweat is the liquid that the body secretes through the pores of the skin, especially when it is hot or when one exerts physical effort. In Ezekiel 44:18, it specifically refers to this physiological phenomenon: the priests must not dress in a way that causes sweating, as it would render them impure for temple service.
2. In the Bible, sweat also evokes hard work and labor. This is why God tells Adam, after the sin: "You will eat your bread by the sweat of your brow" (Genesis 3:19) — it symbolizes the effort necessary to live.
3. Sweat can also signify intense anxiety or fear, as seen in Jesus at Gethsemane, where his sweat becomes "like drops of blood" (Luke 22:44), an image of his spiritual agony.
H3154.origine: The Hebrew word יֶזַע comes from a root that expresses the idea of sweating or perspiring. It literally designates the liquid that flows from the body under heat or effort. It is a simple and direct word, without any connection to a sophisticated metaphorical image: it names the physical phenomenon that everyone knows.
H3154.emploi: This word appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible. In Ezekiel 44:18, it occurs in the priestly prescriptions: the priests serving in the temple must not wear fabric that would prevent air circulation and cause sweating, as their bodies must remain pure for the office. It is a practical and religious detail: sweat, a natural product of the body, was considered a source of impurity in Levitical worship. The word is used in its literal and concrete sense, without particular nuance.
H3154.portee: This verse reminds us that worship requires careful attention to detail and physical purity. For Christians, it invites reflection on holiness not as an abstraction, but as something that touches our entire body. Sweat, a sign of our carnal nature, was carefully regulated in the Old Testament; in Jesus, it is through his incarnation — including his body sweating from anguish — that God draws near to us.

sens: Descendant de Zérah, fils de Juda
H3155.detail: 1. A Jizrachite is someone who belongs to the lineage of Zerah, the son of Judah and Tamar. This term designates an important family line within the tribe of Judah, tracing back to the early days of Israel. In 1 Chronicles 27:8, Schamehuth is presented as a leader of this clan, commanding a division of twenty-four thousand men.
H3155.origine: The word comes from the name Zerah (זֶרַח), which literally means "rising of the sun" or "brightness." Zerah is the son of Judah mentioned for the first time in Genesis 38:30, born from the union of Judah and Tamar. The suffix "-ite" (or "-ite" in Hebrew) marks belonging to a clan or family descending from an ancestor. The descendants of Zerah thus formed a distinct branch in the tribe of Judah, with their own leaders and responsibilities.
H3155.emploi: The term Jizrachite appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:8, where it is used to identify Schamehuth as a military leader. This passage lists the commanders appointed by the king to oversee the different months of the year. The fifth month was entrusted to a Jizrachite, which shows that the family of Zerah enjoyed a position of authority and prestige in the kingdom of Judah.

sens: chef de chœur à Jérusalem
chantre et dirigeant des musiciens
H3156H.detail: Jizrachja is a man who lived during the time of the return from exile. His name means "the Lord shines" or "God rises like the sun." He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 12:42, where he is listed among the leaders of the dedication ceremony of the walls of Jerusalem, rebuilt after the exile to Babylon. He is a Levite, meaning a member of the priestly tribe of Israel, and he was responsible for leading the singers (the musicians and singers) during this important celebration. His role was to guide the voices and instruments in the praises offered to God for the accomplished reconstruction.
H3156H.origine: The name Jizrachja is composed of two Hebrew elements: "God" (El, often appearing in compounds) and a verb meaning "to shine" or "to rise," like the sun rising. It is a theophoric name (which contains the name of God), borne by Levites and leaders in ancient Israel. The meaning of the name evokes the glory and divine splendor that manifest.
H3156H.emploi: Jizrachja appears only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 12:42. He is named among the leaders of the singers who participated in the great dedication ceremony of the walls of Jerusalem, shortly after the return from exile to Babylon (circa 445 B.C.). This event was a major celebration where the people of Israel rejoiced in the restoration of the city and the reconstruction of the temple. Jizrachja played an important role in leading the musicians and singers who proclaimed the praises of God. His presence among the key figures of this pivotal moment attests to his authority in the temple services.

sens: Fortified city of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, located in Issachar at the foot of Mount Gilboa
Royal residence and military base of the kings of Israel, notably Ahab
Place of infamy, scene of the crimes of Ahab and Jezebel
H3157H.detail:
1. Jezreel is an important city in the territory of Israel (Joshua 19:18), located in Issachar near Mount Gilboa, hence its Hebrew name meaning "God sows." It is a strategic point in the valley that dominates the trade and war routes of the Northern Kingdom.

2. Ahab made it his royal residence and operational base (1 Kings 21:1; 1 Kings 18:45), particularly to direct his campaigns against Syria. It is where he went to recover from his injuries (2 Kings 8:29), and from there Jezebel governed from the royal palace.

3. Jezreel became infamous due to the murderous intrigues of Ahab and especially his wife Jezebel: it is near the walls of Jezreel that dogs would eat the corpse of Jezebel according to the word of the prophet (1 Kings 21:23). Jehu entered there to execute divine judgment on the house of Ahab (2 Kings 9:30), marking the city as a place of divine justice against idolatry.
H3157H.origine: The Hebrew name יִזְרְעֶאל (Yizreʿel) literally means "God sows" (from זרע, to sow, and אל, God). This theophoric name reflects the fertility of the Jezreel Valley, one of the richest in Canaan. The prophet Hosea will use this same name symbolically: God will change the name "Jezreel" (which recalls the crimes of the house of Ahab) into blessing and forgiveness for his descendants (Hosea 2:24).
H3157H.emploi: Jezreel appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the accounts of the kings of Israel (1 and 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles). It is first listed as a city of Issachar (Joshua 19:18), then becomes the seat of royal power under Ahab (1 Kings 4:12). The densest usages are concentrated around the drama of the house of Ahab: the case of Naboth (1 Kings 21), the healing of Joram (2 Kings 8:29), and especially the vengeance of Jehu who executes the divine sentence on Jezebel and the descendants of Ahab (2 Kings 9-10). Hosea cites it as a symbol of judgment transformed into restoration (Hosea 2:2, 2:24), giving this name a theological dimension of justice and grace.
H3157H.portee: Jezreel reminds the reader that sin, even at the height of royal power, does not escape God's judgment. It is a place where idolatry and true worship clash, where secret crimes are illuminated by prophetic word. For the believer, the mention of Jezreel teaches that God governs history, that injustice committed by the powerful provokes a divine reaction, and that even names cursed by sin can, by God's grace, be restored into blessing.

sens: City of Issachar located northwest of Mount Gilboa
H3157I.detail: Jezreel is a city in Galilee, situated on a spur of Mount Gilboa. It occupies a strategic crossroads between the Jezreel Valley and the heights of Samaria. In the only usage we have (2 Samuel 4:4), a messenger departs from Jezreel to announce to the house of Saul the death of the king and his son Jonathan in the battle of Gilboa.
H3157I.origine: The Hebrew name Jezreel literally means "God sows" (from zara, "to sow"). It evokes the image of a fertile land, which fits well with this fertile valley of northern Galilee, one of the richest regions of Canaan.
H3157I.emploi: Jezreel appears only once in the Segond 1910, in 2 Samuel 4:4. It is mentioned as the starting point of a news that disrupts the house of Saul after the defeat at Gilboa. It is from there that the messenger runs to deliver the news of the death of the king and prince Jonathan. The city served as a forward post or information center in this region of Galilee.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, living in the time of Egypt and the desert
Son of Hur, brother of Uri, Shobal, Salma, and others
H3157J.detail:
1. Jezreel is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:3. He is presented as a descendant of the father or founder of Etham, a locality in Judah. His name appears in the midst of a genealogy that lists his family: he is the son of Hur and has brothers Uri, Shobal, Salma, Hareph, Ishma, Idbash, Penuel, and Ezer, and a sister Hatselelponi.

2. The genealogical context of the verse indicates that he lived in ancient Israel, during the time of Egypt and the desert. Although little known, Jezreel is part of the chain of ancestors of Judah and represents one of the many families that constituted this tribe.
H3157J.origine: The name Jezreel means "God sows" in Hebrew: "Jiz" comes from the verb zara ("to sow") and "reel" comes from El ("God"). This name expresses a trust in God who sows and makes grow — a profound theme in Israelite tradition. The same name appears elsewhere in the Bible to designate other people and places (notably the first son of the prophet Hosea and cities in Judah and Issachar), but here it designates this particular ancestor of Judah.
H3157J.emploi: Jezreel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:3, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented there as the son of Hur and a member of a large brotherhood. This mention is located in the genealogical section of the descendants of Judah, which traces back to the ancestors of the people. His inclusion in this list shows that he was a recognized ancestor, although few other details about his life are transmitted to us.

sens: Son of the prophet Hosea and Gomer
Symbolic name meaning "God sows"
H3157K.detail:
1. Jezreel is the firstborn son of the prophet Hosea and his wife Gomer. He appears in Hosea 1:4, where the Lord commands Hosea to give him this particular name.
2. The name "Jezreel" means "God sows." It carries a prophetic significance: God chose him to announce a judgment. In Hosea 1:4, the Lord says that the name evokes the punishment that God will bring because of the blood shed at Jezreel (the city). It is a name of rupture, marking a turning point in the history of Israel.
H3157K.origine: The name Jezreel comes from Hebrew and literally means "God sows" (from the root meaning "to sow"). Although it is an ordinary masculine name, Hosea uses it as a prophetic symbol: by giving this name to his son, the prophet embodies in his own family the message that God conveys to Israel. The name also recalls the valley of Jezreel in Israel, a place historically charged with violence and judgment.
H3157K.emploi: Jezreel is the first son of the prophet Hosea, named by divine order in Hosea 1:4. The narrative shows that Hosea receives the command to call his son by the name "Jezreel" in order to announce the impending judgment against the house of Jehu for the blood shed. This name becomes a sign for Israel: as the son bears this name laden with prophetic meaning, Israel receives a warning that the kingdom is coming to an end. The child himself is a living message of God's word.
H3157K.portee: For the reader, the story of Jezreel reveals how God uses even the children of prophets to convey His message. It also shows that even in judgment, God speaks clearly to His people. It is a call to recognize the seriousness of the Lord's words and the urgency of repentance.

sens: Fertile valley of Canaan, at the foot of Mount Gilboa, in the territory of Issachar
Fortified city located in this valley
H3157L.detail:
1. The valley of Jizreel is a wide fertile plain northwest of Mount Gilboa, a strategic passage in the land of Canaan. It is an open space where war chariots can maneuver easily, which explains why the Canaanites concentrate there with their formidable iron chariots (Joshua 17:16). Enemy armies like Midian and Amalek use it to invade Israel (Judges 6:33).
2. A city of the same name rises in this valley, inhabited by the Israelites of the territory of Issachar. It becomes the stage for God's judgments: the prophet Hosea announces that the bow of Israel will be broken there, symbolizing military defeat and divine punishment of the northern kingdom (Hosea 1:5).
H3157L.origine: The name literally means "God sows" in Hebrew: it comes from the root זרע (zara, "to sow") and the word God (El). This valley owes its name to its fertility, as it is sown with abundant crops. It is a prophetic name that recalls both the blessing of the land and, through its biblical uses, the divine judgment that "sows" misfortune.
H3157L.emploi: Jizreel appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first mentioned as a valley that the Israelites cannot fully occupy due to the military power of the Canaanites and their chariots (Joshua 17:16). During the period of the Judges, it becomes a battlefield where the enemies of God's people gather to attack them (Judges 6:33). Finally, it enters into the prophecy of judgment: Hosea uses it as a symbol of the place where God will break the strength of Israel (Hosea 1:5). At each stage, the valley embodies the military and spiritual challenges of Israel.
H3157L.portee: Jizreel reminds us that divine promises are not fulfilled without struggle or obedience. It is a place of tension between the blessing of the territory and the judgment of sin, between the abundance of the land and the fragility of the people in the face of their enemies. For the Christian reader, this valley illustrates how God governs history: it is both a place of trial and a field where God sows His sovereign purposes.

sens: City of Palestine, in the fertile valley of the same name, in Galilee
Woman from this city
Inhabitant of Jizreel
H3158G.detail: 1. Jizreel is a city in northern Palestine, located in a fertile region (the Valley of Jizreel). Its name means "God sows" or "sown by God," evoking the agricultural richness of the place. 2. The texts mention women from Jizreel, including Ahinoam, one of King David's wives. The text of 1 Samuel 27:3 designates her by this city name to identify her family origin. 3. The term can more broadly refer to an inhabitant of Jizreel, a person from this city.
H3158G.origine: The word comes directly from the name of the city Jizreel (יִזְרְעֶאל), whose root means "to sow" in Hebrew: "God sows." This name carries the image of the fertility of the land, the valley of Jizreel being one of the most productive in the Promised Land. The adjective or noun "Jizreelite" designates someone from there.
H3158G.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to refer to the woman Ahinoam, wife of King David. In 1 Samuel 27:3 and 30:5, she is presented as "Ahinoam of Jizreel" to indicate her city of origin. This same designation reappears in 2 Samuel 2:2 and 3:2, each time to identify Ahinoam in the context of her royal lineage (the birth of her sons). The use of the city name after the personal name served to distinguish individuals and express their geographical origins in the ancient world.

sens: Inhabitant of the city of Jizreel
H3158H.detail: 1. Inhabitant of the city of Jizreel, in northern Israel. The name "Jizreel" literally means "God sows" and designates an important royal city. Naboth, the owner of the vineyard coveted by King Ahab (1 Kings 21:1), is referred to as a "Jizreelite": he belongs to this city.
H3158H.origine: The Hebrew word comes directly from the name of the city Jizreel, to which the suffix -i (יִזְרְעֵאלִי) is added, meaning "of..." or "belonging to...". This is the usual way to designate someone by their city of origin. The root of Jizreel consists of three elements: "zera" (seed) and "El" (God), meaning "what God sows."
H3158H.emploi: This term appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, always to refer to Naboth in 1 Kings 21 (six occurrences in the account of the coveting of his vineyard by Ahab and Jezebel), and three other times in 2 Kings 9 and 1 Chronicles 3. Naboth becomes the biblical example of the just unjustly stripped: his quality as a Jizreelite situates him geographically and socially in the northern kingdom of Israel, where these dramatic events unfold. The term is used only as a personal designation, never as a general notion.
H3158H.portee: The case of Naboth the Jizreelite reminds believers that no one, not even an "ordinary" person lacking royal status, escapes God's interest. This peasant who refuses to sell his family inheritance becomes a martyr recognized by God Himself: his name and faithfulness are engraved in Scripture. It is a lesson in justice and the value that a humble believer possesses in the eyes of the Lord.

sens: Man from the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H3160.detail: Hubba is a man from the tribe of Asher, mentioned only once in the Bible. He was the son of Shamer and brother of Achi, Rohega, and Aram (1 Chronicles 7:34). His name, which means "hidden," is preserved in the genealogies of Asher listed during the registration of the families of Israel.
H3160.origine: The name Hubba comes from the Hebrew חֻבָּה, whose root means "hidden" or "concealed." This name belongs to the family of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel, and reflects the Hebrew onomastics of the divided monarchy period.
H3160.emploi: Hubba appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 7:34, in the context of the genealogical enumeration of the sons of Asher. This passage lists the descendants of Asher and establishes their place in the genealogy of the tribes of Israel. Although Hubba is a minor character, his mention shows that the Bible preserves the names of many historical figures of the chosen people, even the most obscure, to testify to the continuity and divine blessing on the generations of Israel.

sens: To be joined together, merged with
To put together, associate
To orient or direct towards a common goal
H3161.detail:
1. To be joined together, merged with: the word describes a fusion or union of distinct things that become one. In Genesis 49:6, Jacob asks God that his soul not be united with the assembly of violent brothers — he refuses to share their fate and guilt.
2. To put together, associate: this is the action of bringing together or gathering separate elements. The meaning extends to the idea of arranging the heart (Psalms 86:11), directing it as one would assemble the pieces of a whole towards a common goal: to fear God.
3. To be associated with, to participate in: in Isaiah 14:20, not being gathered to the grave means not sharing the common burial, being excluded from this ultimate union — a form of dishonor and definitive separation.
H3161.origine: The Hebrew word יָחַד (yachad) comes from a root meaning "together" and "unity." It is related to the idea of gathering or merging. Alongside this verb exists a noun, עַד, which denotes unity and concord. The basic image is that of things joining, tying together, like hands shaking or parts assembling to form a whole.
H3161.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 49:6, it expresses Jacob's refusal to be united with the guilt of his sons — it is a moral separation. In Psalms 86:11, the psalmist asks God to arrange (or unify) his heart to fear Him, suggesting an internal harmonization towards a goal. In Isaiah 14:20, the absence of union in the grave of other kings signifies exclusion and dishonor. The word thus oscillates between voluntary or involuntary union, and the refusal or impossibility of that union.
H3161.portee: This word reminds the believer of the importance of choosing their alliances. Jacob refuses to unite with the wrongdoings of his sons — a lesson on moral separation from sin. Conversely, the psalmist seeks the inner unity of the heart in the fear of God, an aspiration towards spiritual harmony. For the Christian reader, this evokes the call not to be bound to dark works and to seek the unity of the heart in obedience to God.

sens: In immediate proximity, in the same place or at the same time
United in a single group, forming a unity
With one heart, in the same intention or feeling
All at once, without distinction
Uniformly, in the same manner for all
H3162A.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning denotes physical or temporal proximity: people or things in the same place or at the same moment. In 1 Samuel 11:11, the Ammonite survivors do not remain "together" (they are scattered), highlighting their separation and flight.
2. The word also expresses the idea of a union or alliance between people: hearts, peoples, or groups that bind together in a common will. When David says in 1 Chronicles 12:17 that his heart will "unite" with his visitors, he expresses this fusion of intentions.
3. In particular, it refers to emotional harmony and cordial understanding among brothers or close ones: Psalm 133:1 celebrates how "pleasant" and "good" it is for brothers to dwell "together."
4. The word can also mean the totality or entirety of things considered as a whole: in Psalm 74:6, the enemies break "all" the sculptures (lit. "at once," "together").
5. Finally, it can denote equality or uniformity of treatment: in Job 34:29, God treats a "nation" and a man "equally," without preference.
H3162A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be united" or "to join." It is related to other Hebrew words expressing solidarity, agreement, and cohesion. The fundamental image is that of elements tying together into a single reality, rather than remaining dispersed or separated. This word reflects a deep concern of the Old Testament: the value of unity in the face of division.
H3162A.emploi: The word appears 43 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Job, and the prophetic books. It first describes material or temporal situations: people in proximity, simultaneous events. Gradually, its usage becomes more psychological and spiritual: the union of hearts, fraternal harmony, convergence of wills. The Psalms celebrate it as a blessing (Ps 133:1), while Job questions it in the face of suffering (Job 17:16, where even death gathers "together" the living and the dead in dust). The prophets use it to express both the gathering of the people and the alignment of forces against God (Ps 2:2).
H3162A.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the value of unity. It is not a pleasant convenience, but a precious good and a reflection of divine order: brothers who dwell "together" experience a blessing (Ps 133). Conversely, dispersion and separation mark failure or curse. For a Christian, this word illuminates the importance of unity in the body of Christ and fraternal harmony.

sens: At the same moment, in the same place, or with one another
All at once, without exception
In the same manner, jointly
Simultaneously
H3162B.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of people or things that are gathered in the same place or at the same instant. In Genesis 13:6, Abraham and Lot cannot dwell "together" because their flocks are too numerous. It conveys the idea of proximity and cohabitation.
2. The word also expresses the idea of unanimity: all the peoples will assemble "all together" in Psalms 102:23 to serve the Lord, with none missing. It indicates the absence of division.
3. The word designates an action carried out in concert, where several actors participate in the same act. In Deuteronomy 25:11, men quarrel "together," describing a conflict with multiple participants.
4. It can also mean "at the same time," marking simultaneity rather than physical gathering: to look "together" at what happens in Isaiah 41:23.
H3162B.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root יחד (yahad), which carries the fundamental idea of union and cohesion. This root is found in several Hebrew words expressing unity, communion, or junction. The adverb יָחְדָּו (yachdav) adds the relative suffix -ו, which reinforces the meaning. The basic image is that of things standing together, not being dispersed.
H3162B.emploi: This word appears 97 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in poetry (Psalms) and historical narratives. It frequently describes the assembly of the people (Exodus 19:8: "All the people answered together"), armies gathering (Judges 6:33, Joshua 9:2), or creatures living in peace (Isaiah 11:6-7: the wolf and the lamb grazing together). It also expresses a collective or unanimous action. Its meaning varies slightly depending on the context: sometimes it emphasizes common physical presence, sometimes the absence of conflict or separation.
H3162B.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the value of unity and communion. It evokes both the fraternal union that God desires for His people and the power that arises when many act with one heart. It also shows how faith sometimes requires gathering and witnessing together before God and men.

sens: Man of the tribe of Gad during the time of the divided monarchy
H3163.detail: Jachdo is a man of the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in Scripture. He is presented as the son of Buz and the father of Jeschischaï, in the genealogy of the Gadites recorded in 1 Chronicles 5:14. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel.
H3163.origine: The name Jachdo literally means "His unity" or "His cohesion" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing the idea of union or gathering. This type of theophoric name (containing a reference to God) was common among the Hebrews. The name likely reflects a trust in the divine unity or cohesion that God brings.
H3163.emploi: Jachdo is an ancestor of the Gadites whose name appears in the official genealogy of the tribe of Gad preserved in Chronicles. Although he is mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 5:14, his presence in this genealogical list indicates that he was an important figure in the history of his tribe, notable enough to be recorded among the ancestors of the leaders of Gad. This genealogy served to establish the legitimate lineages and territorial inheritance of the tribes of Israel.

sens: Leader of the tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan
Man of renown and value among the Manassites
H3164.detail: Jachdiel is a leader of a Manassite family mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:24. He appears in the list of the leaders of their fathers' houses, valiant men of renown who led the families of the tribe of Manasseh settled east of the Jordan. His name evokes trust in God: it means "my unity is God" or "God is my unity," expressing a form of solidarity or alliance with the Lord.
H3164.origine: The name Jachdiel combines two Hebrew roots: "yachad" (union, together) and "El" (God). It belongs to the family of names from ancient Israel that place divinity at the heart of personal identity. Its theophoric meaning — that is, containing the name of God — is typical of the names of leaders and important figures in Israel.
H3164.emploi: Jachdiel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:24. He is presented as one of the seven leaders of the paternal houses of eastern Manasseh during the time of the divided monarchy. The text describes him as a "valiant man" and "men of renown," indicating his importance and authority within his tribe. No other events or details of his life are reported.

sens: Levite during the time of David
Leader of a Levitical family responsible for temple service
H3165G.detail:
1. Jechdia is a Levite who lived during the time of King David, belonging to the tribe of Levi. He is the son of Shubael and is part of the leaders of the Levitical families listed in the official register of priestly divisions (1 Chronicles 24:20).
2. His name appears in the list of those responsible for the various services of the temple: Jechdia is the leader of a family of Levites, meaning he supervised a group of temple servants assigned to specific tasks of worship.
H3165G.origine: The name Jechdia means "The Lord is unity" or "unity of the Lord": it combines the divine name (Jah, a short form of the name Lord) and a root evoking unity or agreement. It is a theophoric name typical of the monarchical period, expressing the confession of faith in the oneness of God. The name reflects the piety of the Levitical families during the time of David.
H3165G.emploi: Jechdia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:20, in the context of the official classification of Levitical families established by David. This list enumerates the leaders of the priestly and Levitical divisions, organized according to their lineages. Jechdia is mentioned as a direct descendant of Shubael and as the head of his family, responsible for a portion of the temple service. His unique mention indicates his administrative and spiritual role in the organization of Israelite worship.
H3165G.portee: The name of Jechdia, inscribed in the list of official temple servants, reminds us that true worship relied on precise organization and families devoted to God. His name, proclaiming the unity of the Lord, expresses the fundamental conviction of Israel: all temple services, all organization of the people, converged towards the worship of the one God. It is a lesson on order and faithfulness in the service of God.

sens: Levite under the reign of King David
H3165H.detail: Jechdia was a Levite who lived during the time of King David and served in his administration. He was from Meronoth and was in charge of the royal donkeys, meaning he supervised the donkeys belonging to the king's court (1 Chronicles 27:30).
H3165H.origine: The name Jechdia means "Jehovah is unity" in Hebrew, composed of the divine name Jehovah and an element evoking unity or cohesion. It was a name borne by Levites, this group of Israelites dedicated to the service of worship and the administration of the people.
H3165H.emploi: Jechdia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:30. This passage lists the overseers of the flocks and goods of King David. Jechdia is among these royal officers with the specific responsibility of overseeing the donkeys, while others took care of camels, horses, or other animals of the crown. He represents the trustworthy men that David placed at the head of the various royal institutions.

sens: Benjaminite warrior who joined David at Ziklag
H3166G.detail: Jachaziel is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:4. He is presented as a valiant warrior who joined David at Ziklag, the city where David had taken refuge before becoming king. His name literally means "the one whom God has looked upon" or "sighted by God," expressing the idea that God has cast His protective gaze upon this man.
H3166G.origine: The name Jachaziel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "jaha" (looks, sees) and "el" (God). It belongs to the family of theophoric names, that is, names containing the name of God, which was common in Israel to express the relationship between a person and the Lord. This type of name reflects the conviction that God watches over those who bear His name.
H3166G.emploi: Jachaziel is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 12:4, in a list of valiant warriors who joined David at Ziklag. This passage enumerates the men of Benjamin, relatives of Saul, who chose to leave Saul's house to side with David while he was fleeing. Jachaziel is among these faithful companions-in-arms, highlighting his commitment to David and his recognition of God's plan for the future king of Israel.
H3166G.portee: The mention of Jachaziel reminds us that the progress of God's kingdom comes through ordinary men and women, many of whom remain in the shadows of history. Although we know of him only from a brief reference, this Benjaminite warrior chose to stand by the one whom God had chosen, showing how faithfulness to God can be expressed through support for His servants in difficult times.

sens: Priest during the reign of King David who sounded the trumpet before the ark of the covenant
H3166H.detail: 1. Jachaziel is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when King David brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. Along with Benajah, he was tasked with continually sounding the trumpet before this holy ark (1 Chronicles 16:6), making him an important figure in the public worship of Israel at that time.
H3166H.origine: The name Jachaziel means "the one whom God has looked upon" or "God sees": it is composed of two Hebrew elements that express that God sees and cares for the one who bears this name. It is a typical name of the Levites and priests of the people of Israel, reminding of divine protection.
H3166H.emploi: Jachaziel appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 16:6. He is presented as one of the two priests (along with Benajah) that King David appointed to sound the trumpet permanently before the ark of the covenant of God. This role was prestigious and important: the trumpet marked solemn religious moments and reminded of God's presence at the heart of Israel's worship.

sens: Levite, son of Hebron
Priest during the time of King David
Member of the tribe of Levi assigned to the service of the Temple
