H3166I.detail: Jachaziel is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi responsible for religious service in the Temple of Israel. He is the third son of Hebron (1 Chronicles 23:19), who was himself a chief of the Levitical family. Along with his brothers Jeriah, Amariah, and Jekameam, Jachaziel is part of the descendants of Levi that King David organized for the worship of the Temple. His name literally means "God has looked" or "looked upon by God," expressing that the Lord has set His gaze upon this child. His two consecutive mentions in the lists of Levitical families (1 Chronicles 23:19 and 24:23) show the importance of his role in the organization of worship at the Temple.
H3166I.origine: The name Jachaziel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "ḥazah" (to see, to look, to behold) and "El" (God). Its literal meaning is therefore "the one whom God has looked upon" or "looked upon by God." This construction is common in Hebrew names: it expresses the belief that the Lord has paid attention to the birth or destiny of the person. The root "ḥazah" is also the root of the word "prophet" in Hebrew, as prophecy is a form of vision granted by God.
H3166I.emploi: Jachaziel appears twice in the Bible, always in genealogical lists of the Levites during the time of King David (1 Chronicles 23 and 24). Son of Hebron, he is the third of a sibling group of four: Jeriah the eldest, Amariah the second, Jachaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth. These two identical passages provide the composition of Hebron's Levitical family, charged with specific responsibilities in the service of the Temple. Unlike other Levites mentioned in the Bible, no specific act or event of his life is known: only his place in the genealogy and his holy function speak to us.

sens: Levite son of Zechariah, of the lineage of Asaph, during the time of King Jehoshaphat
H3166J.detail: Jachaziel is a Levite (a member of the priestly tribe of Levi) who appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 20:14, presented as the son of Zechariah and belonging to the family of the sons of Asaph. He played a role in the liturgical service of the temple during the time of King Jehoshaphat of Judah.
H3166J.origine: The name Jachaziel means "God has seen" or "contemplated by God" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: the root that expresses the action of seeing or contemplating, and "El," which denotes God. It is a typical theophoric name in Israelite tradition, expressing the belief that God sees and knows His people.
H3166J.emploi: Jachaziel appears only once in the provided biblical texts, in 2 Chronicles 20:14. He is mentioned as a Levite from the family of Asaph (one of the great families of musicians and singers of the temple), son of Zechariah. The context indicates that he received the Spirit of the Lord in the midst of the assembly to deliver a divine message, suggesting that he exercised a prophetic function or served as a spokesperson for the Lord in worship.
H3166J.portee: The mention of Jachaziel reminds us that the Spirit of God was active in the worship of Israel, speaking through chosen men to encourage and guide the people. His intervention on behalf of King Jehoshaphat shows how God made Himself accessible to His servants, even the lesser-known ones, to accomplish His purposes.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin who joined David at Ziklag
Priest during the time of King David who assisted in transporting the ark
Levite from the family of Hebron, son of Kohath
Levite son of Zechariah, descendant of Asaph, during the time of King Jehoshaphat
Ancestor of a family that returned from exile with Ezra
H3166K.detail: 1. Jachaziel was a warrior from Benjamin who joined David when he was hiding at Ziklag, fleeing from King Saul. 2. A priest of the same name served under King David and participated in the solemn transport of the ark of the covenant. 3. A Levite named Jachaziel, from the family of Hebron and son of Kohath, held a position in the worship at the temple. 4. Under the reign of King Jehoshaphat, another Levite named Jachaziel, son of Zechariah and from the lineage of the musician Asaph, served the Lord. 5. Jachaziel was also the ancestor of a family of Levites who returned from captivity in Babylon with the scribe Ezra, as shown in Ezra 8:5 where his son Shecaniah is mentioned.
H3166K.origine: The name Jachaziel means "the one whom God has looked upon" or "contemplated by God." It combines two Hebrew elements: "yaha" (he has seen, he has looked) and "el" (God). This name expresses the relationship of divine favor towards the person who bears it, suggesting that they are under the protective gaze of the Lord.
H3166K.emploi: The name Jachaziel appears in the Old Testament to designate several different characters, all linked to religious or military service within Israel. These men lived at different times: during the reign of King David, during the reign of Jehoshaphat, and at the time of the return from Babylonian exile. The mention in Ezra 8:5 situates one of them among the Levites who accompanied Ezra in the repatriation of the exiles to Jerusalem, highlighting the importance of this family in the restoration of worship after captivity.

sens: Man of the time of the Exile and the Return
Leader of Israel at the time of Ezra
H3167.detail: Jachzia is a man who appears only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile under the leadership of Ezra. He is the son of Tikvah. He is an important figure in the context of the reconstitution of the people, as he stands alongside Jonathan and Meshullam to oppose the decision of an assembly (Ezra 10:15). His role suggests that he was a respected leader or authority among those returning from exile.
H3167.origine: The name Jachzia means "Jehovah sees" or "Jehovah looks." It is composed of the divine name and a root evoking sight, vision. This name expresses a statement of faith: that God sees what is happening, that He observes the actions of His people. Tikvah, the name of the father, means "hope" — a beautiful spiritual paternity for one who bears the name of Jachzia.
H3167.emploi: Jachzia appears only once in the Holy Scriptures, in Ezra 10:15. He lived at the time of the Exile and the Return, after Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed Jerusalem and the Jews had been taken captive to Babylon. When Ezra returns to Jerusalem to restore worship and the law of God, a situation arises: some Israelites had taken foreign wives. An assembly of the people gathers to address this matter. Jachzia, son of Tikvah, is one of the few who rises against the resulting decision, alongside Jonathan and Meshullam, with the support of the Levite Shabbethai. His intervention shows that he had sufficient authority and credibility to contest a majority.
H3167.portee: The mention of Jachzia reminds us that, even in times of crisis and reform, there are men of character who dare to take a stand against the prevailing current, guided by their conscience. His brief but significant appearance illustrates that the Lord knows those who rise for justice, even if the Bible only retains a moment of their life.

sens: Priest responsible for the twentieth group of service at the Temple during the time of David
H3168G.detail: 1. Ezekiel is a priest who, during the time of King David, directed the twentieth course (or group of service) of the Temple — an organizational system where priests took turns to ensure worship (1 Chronicles 24:16).
H3168G.origine: The name Ezekiel means "God strengthens" or "God fortifies": it expresses the confidence that God provides strength and courage. This name was borne by several important figures in Israel, the most famous being the prophet Ezekiel, son of Buzi, who was exiled to Babylon and received spectacular visions from God.
H3168G.emploi: This Ezekiel mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 24:16 is a priest of the lineage of Aaron living under the reign of King David. He is part of the list of heads of priestly houses who organized the service of the Temple in successive courses, each ensuring worship for a week. He should not be confused with the great prophet Ezekiel of the 6th century BC.

sens: Prophet and priest during the exile in Babylon
Son of Buzi
Author of the book that bears his name
H3168H.detail: Ezekiel is a prophet and a priest who lived during the exile of the people of Judah in Babylon in the 6th century BC. Son of Buzi, he receives God's call and prophesies for about 22 years in the land of exile, bringing messages of judgment and hope to Israel. The book of Ezekiel, which he wrote, is one of the great prophecies of the Old Testament, filled with spectacular symbolic visions such as the chariot-throne of God and the dry bones.
H3168H.origine: The name Ezekiel comes from Hebrew and literally means "God strengthens" or "God fortifies." It is composed of two elements: "El" which refers to God, and "chazak" which means to strengthen or fortify. This name evokes the idea that God gives strength to His servant to accomplish his prophetic mission, even in times of exile and distress.
H3168H.emploi: Ezekiel primarily appears in the book that bears his name. The first occurrence is found in Ezekiel 1:3, where God directly addresses His word to Ezekiel near the Kebar River in Chaldea, and where the hand of the Lord rests upon him to set him apart as a prophet. Ezekiel is also mentioned in Ezekiel 24:24, where he is designated as a sign for the house of Israel. Although few in number, these passages show that Ezekiel is recognized by God Himself as His instrument to convey a crucial message to the exiled people.
H3168H.portee: Ezekiel reminds believers that God does not abandon His people even when they are far from their land and deprived of freedom. His ministry in exile shows that God can speak and act anywhere, and that prophetic faith remains possible even in the most difficult circumstances. Ezekiel's extraordinary visions invite the reader to see beyond appearances and recognize the holiness and sovereignty of God.

sens: An Ephraimite leader during the reign of King Ahaz
H3169G.detail: 1. Hezekiah is a leader of the tribe of Ephraim mentioned only once in the Bible, at a time when the kingdom of Israel was divided. He appears in 2 Chronicles 28:12, alongside other leaders who rise up against the soldiers returning from a military campaign, to prevent the prisoners of Judah from being enslaved.
H3169G.origine: The name Hezekiah means "the Lord has strengthened" or "the Lord has fortified." It comes from the Hebrew root that evokes strength and solidity. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name, which was common in Israel to express the relationship between a person and God. The same name has been borne by other important figures in the history of Israel.
H3169G.emploi: Hezekiah is a minor character mentioned only once in Scripture, in 2 Chronicles 28:12. He is among the leaders of Ephraim who, during the reign of King Ahaz of Judah, protest against the treatment of the Judean prisoners. He represents a moment when some leaders of the Northern tribe chose to oppose violence and slavery, showing a moral conscience even in a time of conflict between the divided kingdoms.
H3169G.portee: This account shows us that through political divisions and conflicts, there were men who listened to the voice of their conscience and that of prophets to defend the weak and the captives. Hezekiah embodies the possibility of justice and compassion, even in times of war.

sens: King of Judah at the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel
Son of King Ahaz and Abi
Father of Manasseh
H3169H.detail:
1. Hezekiah is a king of Judah who reigned during the period of the division of the kingdom into Israel (north) and Judah (south). He is among the important kings mentioned during the ministry of the prophets Hosea and Micah (Hosea 1:1, Micah 1:1), which places his time around the 8th century BC.

2. He is the son of King Ahaz and Queen Abi (or Abijah), making him an heir of the royal house of Judah established since the time of David.

3. His son Manasseh succeeded him on the throne of Judah, continuing the lineage of the kings of the tribe of Judah.
H3169H.origine: The name Hezekiah (in Hebrew יְחִזְקִיָּה, Yehizqiyyah) literally means "The Lord has strengthened" or "God strengthens" (from Yahweh "the Lord" and hizqaq "to be strong"). This theophoric name, meaning containing the divine name, was common among the kings of Judah and expressed confidence in divine protection over the reign.
H3169H.emploi: Hezekiah appears twice in the Segond 1910, only in the prophetic titles of Hosea and Micah, both contemporaries of his reign (Hosea 1:1, Micah 1:1). These two mentions place him as a major king of Judah, alongside other important rulers like Jotham and Ahaz. His presence in these prophetic introductions indicates that he marked the era from a political and religious perspective.

sens: Head of a family returning from exile at the time of Nehemiah
H3169I.detail: 1. Hezekiah is the name of a man who led a family among the Jews who returned from Babylonian captivity. He is mentioned in Ezra 2:16 as the ancestor of a family whose ninety-eight members returned to Jerusalem to rebuild the Temple.
H3169I.origine: The name means "Jehovah has strengthened" or "The Lord has made strong." It comes from two elements: the divine name Jehovah and a root that expresses strength and solidity. This name has been borne by several important men in the history of Israel, notably King Hezekiah of Judah, known for his piety and religious reforms.
H3169I.emploi: This Hezekiah appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 2:16. He is named among the heads of families whose descendants participated in the return from exile under the governance of Zerubbabel, after the Babylonian captivity. He is a man known for leading a large family (ninety-eight people), indicating his importance and prestige within the reconstructing community.
H3169I.portee: This character represents the work of restoration of the Jewish people after the exile. His existence and that of his family remind us that, despite destruction and deportation, God had not abandoned His people: large families were returning to rebuild the Temple and religious life in Jerusalem.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi living during the Exile and Return
Priest of the house of Immer
Ancestor of Adiel and son of Meshullam
H3170.detail: Jahziah is a Levitical priest mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of priests who returned from the Exile to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 9:12). His name appears in the genealogy of Adiel, showing his role in the continuity of the priestly service. He belongs to the house of Immer, one of the important priestly families of the temple, and his son Adiel continued the religious service after the return of the Exiles.
H3170.origine: The name Jahziah means "the one whom God brings back" or "whom God causes to return" (from the Hebrew verb חזר, hazâr, "to return"). This name was particularly appropriate for a priest living at the time of the Return from Exile, a moment when God brought His people back to the Promised Land after the Babylonian captivity. The mention of this character emphasizes the restoration of worship and the priesthood after the Exile.
H3170.emploi: Jahziah is mentioned only once in the French New Testament, in 1 Chronicles 9:12, in a genealogy of priests who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem during the reconstruction. There is no other information about his personal life or actions. His appearance in this context shows the importance the Bible places on the continuity of priestly lineages and the restoration of worship after the Exile. His name appears between that of his father Meshullam and that of his son Adiel, establishing a link in the chain of temple service.

sens: Levite musician in the service of King David
H3171G.detail: Jehiel is a Levite who belongs to the priestly tribe of Israel. He is mentioned as one of the chief musicians during the time of King David, tasked with playing instruments in religious processions and celebrations. The three biblical mentions always show him associated with other Levite musicians (such as Asaph, Zechariah, and Shemiramoth) and equipped with string instruments — lutes and harps — to accompany the worship service (1 Chronicles 15:18, 15:20, 16:5). His role was to contribute to sacred music during these important moments in the life of the kingdom.
H3171G.origine: The name Jehiel means "God sees" in Hebrew, composed of "Yah" (God) and "chay" (living). It is a theophoric name characteristic of ancient Israel, expressing the belief that God is alive and active. Several people have borne this name at different periods in Israel's history, from the time of David to the period of the Temple's restoration after the exile.
H3171G.emploi: Jehiel appears three times in the First Book of Chronicles, exclusively in chapters 15-16, during the description of the preparations to transport the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem under David. He is listed each time among the Levite musicians chosen for this grand religious ceremony. His successive appearances show the importance given to musicians in Davidic worship and his stable role as one of the recognized instrumentalists of that time.
H3171G.portee: This character embodies the role of the Levite in Israelite worship: serving God through musical talent dedicated to the community. His example shows how artistic and musical gifts had a sacred place in the worship of the true God, not as entertainment, but as an expression of praise and reverence.

sens: Chief Levite during the time of David, son of Laadan
H3171H.detail: Jehiel is a Levite who appears in the account of the preparations for the temple under the reign of King David. In 1 Chronicles 23:8, he is presented as the chief (the first named) among the three sons of Laadan: Jehiel, Zetham, and Joel. In 1 Chronicles 29:8, this same Jehiel, described as a Gershonite (that is, belonging to the clan of Gershon, one of the three branches of the Levites), is responsible for keeping the treasure of the house of the Lord — the precious stones offered for the construction of the temple. Jehiel is therefore a trusted Levite, entrusted with important functions in the organization of worship and the resources of the sanctuary.
H3171H.origine: The name Jehiel means "God sees" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: the divine name (Yah or God) and a verb meaning "to live." It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing the confession that God is alive and active. Several characters bear this name at different periods in Israel's history.
H3171H.emploi: Jehiel is mentioned twice in Chronicles, both times in connection with the time of David and the organization of the temple. He is listed among the Levite leaders during the structuring of the clergy and worship (1 Chronicles 23), and he is later tasked with managing the precious gifts intended for the construction of the temple (1 Chronicles 29). These mentions make Jehiel one of the administrative and religious figures of the sanctuary service at the time of its preparation.

sens: Man from the time of the divided monarchy, son of Hacmoni
H3171I.detail: Jehiel is a character mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 27:32. He is a man who lived during the time of King David and served among the king's sons as a tutor or advisor. Son of Hacmoni, he was responsible for the education and guidance of the royal children, alongside other important officials like Jonathan, David's uncle, who was himself an advisor to the king.
H3171I.origine: The name Jehiel means "God sees" in Hebrew, composed of two elements: the divine name Yah (abbreviated from the name of God) and the verb "to live." It is a common theophoric name in ancient Israel, expressing a confession of faith: God is alive and present.
H3171I.emploi: Jehiel appears only once in the provided references, in 1 Chronicles 27:32, where he is presented as "son of Hacmoni" and as a man responsible for the education of King David's sons. His role as a royal tutor shows that he was a trusted person of some authority at the royal court during David's reign.

sens: Son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, during the time of the divided monarchy
H3171J.detail: Jehiel is a prince of Judah, son of King Jehoshaphat. He is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 21:2 as one of the brothers of Joram, the king who succeeded Jehoshaphat. He belonged to a brotherhood of seven royal sons. His name literally means "God sees" or "God is alive," expressing confidence in the divine presence. Joram, having become king, killed all his brothers to consolidate his power, which likely included Jehiel.
H3171J.origine: The name Jehiel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "yah" (a contraction of the divine name Yahweh, meaning "God") and "chai" (meaning "living"). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, proclaiming that God is alive. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, including Levites and temple musicians.
H3171J.emploi: Jehiel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 21:2. He is part of the sons of Jehoshaphat listed in this verse, identified as one of Joram's brothers. His brief appearance in biblical history illustrates how some members of the royal family of Judah have remained forgotten in history, even though their existence is documented by the Word of God.
H3171J.portee: This brief account reminds us that even the most powerful royal figures cannot escape God's judgment. The death of Jehiel and his brothers at the hands of Joram illustrates the consequences of sin and unrestrained ambition. For the believer, this passage shows that true life does not come from human position or earthly power, but solely from God, as his name proclaims.

sens: Levite from the tribe of Heman who participated in the restoration of worship under King Hezekiah
H3171K.detail: 1. Jehiel is a musician from the house of Heman, one of the chief singers of the Lord in the temple. During the time of King Hezekiah, he was called to take part in the solemn restoration of worship after years of neglect and defilement (2 Chronicles 29:14). His name appears alongside other Levites carrying out this work of spiritual renewal of the sanctuary.
H3171K.origine: The name Jehiel means "God sees" or "living God," composed of two Hebrew elements: Jah (the Lord) and the verb meaning to live. It is a theophoric name, meaning it bears the name of God and affirms divine life. Several characters bear this name in the Bible, all linked to temple service or royal and priestly functions.
H3171K.emploi: Jehiel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 29:14. He appears in the account of the religious reforms of King Hezekiah of Judah in the 7th century BC. At that time, the temple in Jerusalem had been closed and profaned, and Hezekiah ordered its purification and the restoration of worship. Jehiel, as a son or descendant of Heman (one of the great musicians appointed by King David), was among the Levites mobilized to lead the songs and sacrifices during this solemn restoration.

sens: Levite employed in the administration of the temple under King Hezekiah
H3171L.detail: 1. Jehiel is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi dedicated to the service of the temple. In 2 Chronicles 31:13, he appears among the officials who managed the affairs of the temple under the direction of Conaniah and Shimei, following the orders of King Hezekiah and Azariah, chief of the house of God. His role was therefore to administer the goods and organization of the temple.
H3171L.origine: The name Jehiel means "God sees" in Hebrew: composed of "God" (El) and the verb "to live" (chayah). It was a name borne by several Levites throughout the centuries of Israel, expressing the belief that God is the eternal Living One.
H3171L.emploi: Jehiel appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 31:13, where he is mentioned as one of the ten Levites responsible for the temple under King Hezekiah (around 700 B.C.). This enumeration occurs during the king's religious reforms, when he restored the worship of the Lord after the impiety of his predecessor Ahaz. Jehiel was part of the high-level administrative and religious team that ensured the proper functioning of the temple and the management of its treasures.

sens: Prince of the temple during the time of King Josiah
Responsible for the finances and treasures of the sanctuary
H3171M.detail:
1. Jehiel is a prince or chief of the temple during the religious reform of King Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:8). He is a man of responsibility who administers the house of God.
2. As a prince of the temple, he has authority over the sacred finances: he oversees the gifts and offerings intended for the priests and Levites. During Passover, he generously contributes by providing animals for the sacrifices (2 Chronicles 35:8).
H3171M.origine: The name Jehiel means "God sees" or "May God live." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name) and "chiel" (to live). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God, which was common among priestly and Levite families in Israel.
H3171M.emploi: Jehiel appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 35:8. He is mentioned among the chief leaders of the temple (with Hilkiah and Zechariah) during the great celebration of Passover under Josiah. He is referred to as a prince (or chief) of the house of God, indicating a high-level administrative and religious role. His act of generosity (giving livestock for the sacrifices) shows his commitment to the religious life of the people.
H3171M.portee: The brief mention of Jehiel reminds us that worship of God requires faithful, skilled, and generous leaders. His example of active participation in the religious reforms under Josiah encourages believers to support, in their own church, those who serve God with integrity and liberality.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi at the time of the return from exile
Father of Obadiah among the sons of Joab
H3171N.detail:
1. Jehiel is a Levite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the Jews return from captivity in Babylon. He appears in Ezra 8:9 as the father of Obadiah, who is among the descendants of Joab returning with Ezra to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple.
2. His name means "God sees," expressing the confidence that God continues to live and govern, even during exile and return. It is a name borne by several important Levites in the history of Israel, including musicians and temple guardians during the times of David and Hezekiah.
H3171N.origine: The name Jehiel comes from two Hebrew elements: "Je" (God) and "hiel" (lives, life). It expresses faith in the permanence and survival of God, particularly significant for a people returning from exile. This name has been borne by several key figures in temple service throughout the history of Israel.
H3171N.emploi: Jehiel is mentioned in Ezra 8:9 as the father of Obadiah (or Abdiah in French), among the sons of Joab returning from exile with Ezra. This is the only occurrence of this particular name in the cited passage. The context shows a Levite family participating in the return from exile and the restoration of temple worship in Jerusalem.

sens: man of Israel during the time of exile and return
H3171O.detail: Jéhiel is a name borne by several men throughout the history of Israel. The most well-known in this passage is the father of Shecaniah, mentioned in Ezra 10:2, where Shecaniah acknowledges before Ezra that the people have sinned by marrying foreign women.
H3171O.origine: The name Jéhiel means "God sees" in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: the divine name (God) and a verb meaning "to live." It is a theophoric name, meaning it includes the name of God, which was common among the Israelites.
H3171O.emploi: Jéhiel appears only once in the Segond in Ezra 10:2, where he is presented as the father of Shecaniah, a man of the sons of Elam who spoke out during the crisis of remarrying foreign women at the time of the return from exile.

sens: Character from the time of the Exile and Return
Priest from the family of Harim
H3171P.detail: Jehiel is a man living during the time of the Exile and Return. In the only passage where he is mentioned by name (Ezra 10:21), he appears as a priest belonging to the family of Harim who, like many other Israelites returning from Babylonian captivity, had to separate from his foreign wife during the reforms led by Ezra to purify the people.
H3171P.origine: The name Jehiel means "God sees" (from two elements: "God" and "sees"). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that includes the name of God to express a religious trust or affirmation. In the Hebrew Bible, several characters have borne this name at different periods (during the time of David, Hezekiah, Josiah, and at the time of the Return), but they are not all the same person.
H3171P.emploi: Jehiel is a name borne by at least eleven distinct characters in biblical history. The one in question here is specifically the Jehiel mentioned in Ezra 10:21, a priest of the sons of Harim living at the time of the Return from Exile (around the 5th century B.C.). He is among those who accepted Ezra's directive to separate from their foreign wives, in order to maintain the religious and ethnic purity of the freshly returned people of Israel.

sens: Man of the time of exile and return
Name attested among several Levites and important men
Means "God sees"
H3171Q.detail: 1. Jehiel is a Hebrew name borne by several important men in the history of Israel, from the time of King David to the return from exile in Babylon. The only Jehiel mentioned in the Segond 1910 is that of Ezra 10:26, a man of the tribe of Elam who had to repudiate his foreign wife after the return from exile, thus obeying the decree of the governor Ezra against mixed marriages. 2. The name Jehiel literally means "God sees," composed of two Hebrew elements: "Yah" (God) and "chai" (living). This name expressed the faith of the parents in the living presence of God and His protection over their child.
H3171Q.origine: The name Jehiel comes from the Hebrew root חיה (chayah), which means "to live." It belongs to the family of theophoric names, that is, names containing the name of God (Yah). The structure "Yah + adjective or verb" was common in Israel to express a profession of faith or trust in God. Variants or similar names include Jéhiel or Jéhiël according to transliterations.
H3171Q.emploi: Jehiel is a name borne by at least eleven different people in the Old Testament, according to ancient sources, but only one of them appears in the Segond 1910 translation: that of Ezra 10:26. This Jehiel was one of the sons of Elam who, at the time of the return from Babylon in the fifth century B.C., accepted to repudiate his foreign wife. This action was part of the religious reforms led by Ezra to maintain the purity and identity of the Jewish people. His name, though common, underscores how ordinary men participated in the significant turning points of salvation history.
H3171Q.portee: This Jehiel reminds us that faithfulness to God may require difficult personal sacrifices. Although his act may seem harsh by modern values, it reflects a generation that took the covenant with the Lord seriously and was willing to obey even at the cost of a painful decision. His discreet existence in the biblical narrative also shows that God notices and counts the obedience of those who are neither kings nor prophets, but simply faithful believers.

sens: Levite of the tribe of Levi, responsible for the treasures of the Temple
H3172.detail: 1. Jehiéli is a Levite from the family of the Gershonites, descendants of Laadan. He is mentioned as the chief of a paternal house among the Levites assigned to the service of the Temple (1 Chronicles 26:21). With his sons Zetham and Joel, he guarded the treasures of the house of the Lord, that is, the sacred goods and offerings of the Temple (1 Chronicles 26:22).
H3172.origine: The name Jehiéli means "God will save alive" or "swept by God." It is a variant or another name used by Jehiel (יְחִיאֵל), one of the Levites during the time of the Divided Monarchy. The name belongs to the family of the Gershonites, one of the three major branches of the Levites according to the priestly genealogy.
H3172.emploi: Jehiéli appears twice in the biblical text, both in 1 Chronicles 26, during the counting of the Levites conducted by King David. He is presented as an ancestor or a representative of the Levitical lineage responsible for guarding the sacred treasures of the Temple. His sons Zetham and Joel are specifically mentioned to highlight the importance of their role concerning the goods consecrated to the Lord.

sens: Who is alone of its kind, without equal
Who is one of its kind, particular
Only child, child without siblings
Life, considered as what one has most precious
H3173.detail:
1. The word describes what is alone, incomparable, without equivalent. In Genesis 22:2, God calls Isaac "your only one": he is indeed the special child, the promised child, the one who has no brother to replace him.
2. It can simply mark singularity: what is set apart, distinct. The context determines whether it is total absence (only one) or preciousness (the most remarkable).
3. Applied to a child, it emphasizes not only the absence of siblings but the tenderness of the unique bond: in Proverbs 4:3, the "only" son with his mother is cherished, vulnerable, precious. In Amos 8:10, the mourning for an "only son" symbolizes the most heartbreaking loss.
4. In the psalms of supplication (Psalms 22:21 and 35:17), "my life" is life itself—what one cherishes above all, what one prays God to protect as one would protect an only child.
H3173.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of singularity, isolation, or separation. It carries the image of one who stands alone. That is why it can designate both the only son (the child without siblings) and, by metaphorical extension, life itself—what each person possesses in a unique and irreplaceable way, which cannot be duplicated or replaced.
H3173.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Bible, concentrated mainly in the psalms and the prophets. Its primary usage is the only child: Genesis 22:2, 22:12, 22:16 (Isaac), Judges 11:34 (the daughter of Jephthah), Proverbs 4:3 (the son of the wise). These passages emphasize tenderness and vulnerability. In the psalms (22:21, 25:16, 35:17, 68:7), it takes on a metaphorical meaning: "my life" refers to what one holds most dear, what one asks God to keep safe. Finally, Amos 8:10 and Zechariah 12:10 use it to intensify mourning—crying for one's "only son" means experiencing the deepest sorrow. The word thus shifts from the concrete (child without siblings) to the precious (cherished life).
H3173.portee: The word "unique" reveals how the Bible speaks of what truly matters. God values singular bonds: the only child is loved and entrusted to God (Isaac). But the word also reminds us of our own preciousness: each person has a unique life, and it is before God that it reveals itself as what we protect jealously. For the Christian, this resonates with Jesus being called the "only Son" of God—the unique bond between God and humanity.

sens: Levitical musician and porter of the ark during the time of David
H3174.detail: Jechija is a Levite from the time of King David, specifically mentioned during the transfer of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. He serves as a porter (or guardian) of the ark, alongside Obed-Edom. His name appears in the list of Levites who accompany this solemn procession, where other Levites sound trumpets and perform sacrifices.
H3174.origine: The name Jechija (יְחִיָּה) means "Jehovah lives" or "the Lord lives," composed of two Hebrew elements: Yah (יָה), the abbreviated divine name, and a form of the verb "to live." This name expresses faith in the eternal life of God and His permanence. Jechija is also known by the name Jeiel (יְעִיאֵל), indicating that he bore two names or that these two names refer to the same person.
H3174.emploi: Jechija is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 15:24. He is among the Levites responsible for transporting the ark of the covenant during its installation in Jerusalem under King David's reign. His role as a porter shows that he was a trustworthy man, designated to guard a sacred object above all. His association with Obed-Edom and his place in this prestigious procession highlight his importance within the worship of the people of Israel.
H3174.portee: The character of Jechija reminds us that the worship of the Lord in Israel relied on the dedication of many anonymous servants. His name, "the Lord lives," proclaims a fundamental trust in the permanence and faithfulness of God. For the believer, this example invites faithfulness in the tasks entrusted, even the most discreet, in the service of God.

sens: to wait for something with patience and confidence
to hope in silence
to remain in waiting without agitation
H3175.detail:
1. To wait for something with patience and confidence: this is the basic meaning of the word, which describes the action of remaining in a posture of waiting. In Lamentations 3:26, the one who suffers is invited to "wait" for the help of the Lord, which means to remain present and available, without seeking hasty solutions.
2. To hope in silence: the word carries a nuance of inner hope; it is not a mere passive waiting, but a trust in the one being awaited. The waiting described in Lamentations is "good" because it rests on the certainty that God will come.
3. To remain in waiting without agitation: the verb suggests a voluntary stillness, a restraint of the heart in the face of the urge to act hastily. It is an invitation to peace in adversity.
H3175.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of remaining in place, of holding back. It is related to words that evoke patience and rest. The context of the book of Lamentations, which speaks of the destruction of Jerusalem, shows that this waiting is not passive but active: it requires moral strength to remain confident despite evil.
H3175.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 3:26. It is part of a passage from the prophet Jeremiah who comforts the exiles by urging them not to lose hope despite the catastrophe. The context is one of collective suffering and the need to turn to God. This unique occurrence shows the importance of this word: it is a central message addressed to the afflicted people.
H3175.portee: This word teaches the believer that waiting on God is not passivity, but a form of strength and faith. It invites one to abandon impatience and haste to stand confidently before God, even in the darkest trials. It is a word of comfort for anyone going through difficult times and doubting God's presence.

sens: To remain still in one place for a certain time, waiting for something or someone to arrive.
To rely on an upcoming event; to trust that it will happen.
To hope in God, to trust Him for the future.
H3176G.detail:
1. To wait means to stay in place for a period, anticipating what is to come. Noah "waited" seven days before releasing the dove (Genesis 8:12), and Saul "waited" for the time set by Samuel, remaining still while the people dispersed (1 Samuel 13:8). It is simply the passage of time in expectation.
2. To wait also means to count on something, to have the certainty that it will happen. Job "waited" for the end of his friends' speeches while listening to their reasoning (Job 32:11) — he knew they would finish. In the Psalms, one "waits" in silence, keeping hope that God will act (Job 29:21).
3. When the term is directed towards God, "to wait" or "to hope" means to place one's trust in Him, to acknowledge His power to fulfill what He has promised. The psalmist says: "It is in You that I hope; You will answer, Lord, my God!" (Psalms 38:16). It is an active rest of faith: one does nothing by oneself, but relies on God.
H3176G.origine: The verb יָחַל (ya.chal) comes from a root that evokes the idea of fixing, of firmly placing — the image is of someone who "stops" or "stands" in one place, waiting. In Hebrew, the word also carries the notion of hope and assurance: one does not move because one knows that what is awaited will come. This root expresses an immobile, patient trust.
H3176G.emploi: The verb appears about fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and the Psalms. In history, "to wait" is often a material action: Noah waits before releasing the dove, Saul waits for the appointed time. In the Psalms and Job, the word takes on a spiritual hue: one waits for God, one hopes in Him. The context shows a nuance: waiting can be passive (staying in place) or active (counting on, trusting). In Job particularly, "to wait" becomes synonymous with enduring with confidence, as in Job 14:14 where the question "Will man live again after he dies?" engages the idea of waiting in trial.
H3176G.portee: For the believer, this word invites a confident waiting on God. To wait is not passive inactivity, but a posture of faith: to recognize that one does not control events, to accept the delay, and to stand firm in the conviction that God will act. This is particularly powerful in prayer and suffering: rather than becoming agitated or doubtful, one "waits" for God, one "hopes" in Him. This transforms the waiting time into an opportunity for trust and intimacy with God.

sens: To wait confidently for the fulfillment of what one desires
To rely on someone or something with assurance
To direct one's heart towards God in expectation of His help
To maintain hope despite difficulties
H3176H.detail:
1. To hope means to wait for something with confidence, not passively but with one's eyes turned towards the one in whom trust is placed. When the psalmist says, "I hope in the Lord; my soul hopes, and I wait for His promise" (Psalms 130:5), he describes a state where his whole being turns towards God, ready to receive what He has promised.

2. It is also to firmly rely on the word or goodness of someone. The Psalms often express this trust: "The eye of the Lord is on those who fear Him, on those who hope in His goodness" (Psalms 33:18), where hoping means leaning on God's known faithfulness.

3. Biblical hope directs the heart towards God Himself, not just towards a future outcome. When the believer says, "Hope in God" (Psalms 43:5), he encourages himself to place all his expectation in Him, knowing that He is the source of salvation.

4. It is also the ability to maintain hope in the face of trials. Job asks, "Why hope when I have no strength left?" (Job 6:11): even in suffering, hope remains a choice, an act of trust towards God despite everything.
H3176H.origine: The Hebrew verb יָחַל (yachal) expresses the idea of "turning towards" or "waiting." Its root suggests a vigilant, active waiting, not mere passivity. It is linked to the notion of waiting for someone or something with a positive tension, the heart turned towards the object of hope. In the Hebrew Bible, it is the key word to describe the believer's attitude towards God: a trust that lasts, perseveres, and awaits the fulfillment of His promises.
H3176H.emploi: This verb appears 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the Psalms (17 occurrences) and in the wisdom and prophetic books. It paints the portrait of the believer in waiting: one who hopes in God when all seems lost (Job), one who encourages his soul to persevere (Psalms 42 and 43), one who bases his existence on the divine promise (Psalms 119 and 130). Hope is never vague: it relies on the "promises" (Psalms 119:74), the "goodness" (Psalms 33:18), the "law" of God (Isaiah 42:4). Even in Lamentations, in the midst of desolation, hope remains the heart's impulse towards God: "This I recall to my mind, and therefore I have hope" (Lamentations 3:21).
H3176H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites transforming worry into confident waiting. Biblical hope is neither naive optimism nor daydreaming: it is an anchor in God's faithfulness even when circumstances seem impossible. It transforms the one who hopes, restoring strength and joy (Psalms 31:25, Psalms 130:7). It is a school of perseverance and true faith.

sens: Son of Zebulun mentioned during the descent into Egypt
Founding ancestor of the Jahleelites clan
H3177.detail:
1. Jahleel is one of the three sons of Zebulun, listed with his brothers Sered and Elon during the enumeration of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:14). He is a figure from the time of slavery in Egypt and the Exodus.
2. He became the founder of a family or clan, the Jahleelites, whose descendants are counted during the census of the people in the wilderness (Numbers 26:26). Like his brothers, his lineage constitutes a branch of the tribe of Zebulun.
H3177.origine: The name Jahleel means "God waits": it associates the name of God (El) with the idea of waiting. It is a typical theophoric name in the Bible, constructed with the divine name. Jahleel is a direct descendant of Jacob through Zebulun, one of the twelve sons of Israel.
H3177.emploi: Jahleel appears only twice in the Bible. He is first mentioned in Genesis 46:14 among the sons of Zebulun who accompany Jacob into Egypt. He is then mentioned in Numbers 26:26 during the second census of the people in the wilderness, not as a living person, but as the ancestor of the Jahleelites clan. He thus represents an important genealogical line of the tribe of Zebulun through the generations.

sens: Descendants de Jahleel, homme de la tribu de Zabulon
Famille issues de Jahleel lors du dénombrement d'Israël
H3178.detail:
1. The Jahleélites are the descendants of Jahleel, a man from the tribe of Zebulun. Jahleel first appears in Genesis 46:14 as the son of Zebulun during Jacob's descent into Egypt. His name means "the hope of God" and marks his place in the genealogy of the chosen people.

2. During the census of the Israelites in the desert, forty years after the exodus from Egypt, the family of Jahleel is designated as one of the families of Zebulun, alongside that of the Sardites (descendants of Sered) and the Elonites (descendants of Elon). It is at this time that the family name "Jahleélites" clearly appears (Numbers 26:26).
H3178.origine: The name comes from Jahleel (יַחְלְאֵל), which means "the hope of God" or "God gives hope." The form "Jahleélites" follows the Hebrew method of deriving family names from an ancestor: adding a suffix to designate all descendants of the same lineage. Jahleel himself was the son of Zebulun, one of the twelve tribes of Israel.
H3178.emploi: The word "Jahleélites" appears only once in Scripture, in Numbers 26:26, during the second census of the Israelite people in the desert of Paran. This census, conducted forty years after the exodus from Egypt, lists all the families of each tribe to prepare for entry into Canaan and the division of the land. The Jahleélites are enumerated as one of the three families of the tribe of Zebulun, confirming the continuous descent of Jahleel into the second generation of the desert.

sens: Fils de Tola, chef de famille de la tribu d'Issacar
H3181.detail: Jachmaï is a family chief from the tribe of Issachar, the son of Tola. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:2 among the heads of paternal houses of Tola, recognized as valiant men of their generations. In the time of King David, the lineage from which he comes counted twenty-two thousand six hundred warriors.
H3181.origine: The name Jachmaï means "the one whom Jehovah keeps" or "whom Jehovah protects." It is formed from the Hebrew root חמה which refers to the idea of protection or guarding, and the divine name YHWH (Jehovah). This name expresses trust in divine protection, a common conviction among ancient Israelites who gave their children names evoking God's saving action.
H3181.emploi: Jachmaï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:2. He is listed among the six sons of Tola, all important family heads of Issachar during David's time. This genealogical passage highlights the significance of his lineage: his descendants, although Jachmaï himself is not further detailed, formed a considerable military branch, which attests to the prosperity and power of his family within the tribe.

sens: To have bare feet, without shoes or sandals
The state of one who has removed their shoes, walking with uncovered feet
A figure of poverty, destitution, or captivity
A prophetic sign or sign of humiliation
H3182.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to have bare feet, without the protection of shoes. It is the physical state of one who walks with uncovered feet: Isaiah removes his shoes and walks "bare and barefoot" to symbolize what will happen (Isaiah 20:2).

2. The state of bare feet can signify a stripping away, a state of destitution. The captives taken by the king of Assyria walk "bare and barefoot," without possessions or dignity (Isaiah 20:4).

3. Bare feet can express mourning and humiliation. David ascends the Mount of Olives "barefoot," weeping, a sign of his great affliction (2 Samuel 15:30).

4. Walking barefoot can be a prophetic act that announces or symbolizes a threat. Isaiah's gesture "will be for three years a sign and a portent for Egypt and for Ethiopia" (Isaiah 20:3), predicting their coming captivity.
H3182.origine: The Hebrew word יָחֵף (yacheph) is related to roots that express the idea of being deprived, lacking, exposed. In Hebrew, the nakedness of the feet is linked to absence or lack: it is the image of a person without protection. The word also appears in contexts of servitude or shame, where physical destitution accompanies the reduction of man.
H3182.emploi: The word appears five times in the biblical text, mostly among the prophets and in royal history. In 2 Samuel 15:30, David uncovers his feet in flight, a gesture of humiliation in the face of Absalom's revolt. In Isaiah (20:2, 20:3, 20:4), the prophet walks barefoot for three years to announce the capture and captivity of Egypt and Ethiopia by Assyria: it is a symbolic act, a living sign of the divine word. In Jeremiah 2:25, the image of bare feet signifies the exhaustion and shame of one who pursues idols. The word always designates a situation of deprivation, mourning, or prophetic significance.
H3182.portee: This word reminds the Israelite that nakedness and destitution are visible signs of judgment or mourning. For the Christian, it shows how God uses bodily signs to manifest His word and call His people. David barefoot fleeing his palace, Isaiah walking barefoot: these images teach that obedience to the prophets can involve humiliation, and that God always announces before judging.

sens: A man from the tribe of Naphtali
The founder of the family of the Jahtseelites
H3183.detail:
1. Jahtseel is a man from the tribe of Naphtali, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. He lived during the time of Egypt and the wilderness, and is first mentioned in Genesis 46:24 as one of the sons of Naphtali, alongside his brothers Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
2. Jahtseel is the founder of a family bearing his name, the Jahtseelites. During the census in the wilderness reported in Numbers 26:48, his descendants are counted as a distinct family within the tribe of Naphtali, showing his genealogical importance in the history of Israel.
H3183.origine: The name Jahtseel means "God divides." It is composed of two Hebrew elements: the divine "Yah" (an abbreviation of Yahweh, the name of God) and a verb meaning "to divide" or "to share." This name reflects the faith of the ancient Israelites in divine providence, expressing the idea that God distributes or allocates portions according to His wisdom.
H3183.emploi: Jahtseel appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in official genealogical lists. In Genesis 46:24, he is presented as one of the sons that Naphtali brings to Egypt during Jacob's descent. In Numbers 26:48, during the census of the tribes after the wilderness period, the "family of the Jahtseelites," descendants of Jahtseel, is counted. The Book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 7:13) also mentions this ancestor under a variant of his name (Jahziel), confirming his foundational role in the genealogy of Naphtali. His importance primarily lies in his place in the genealogical structure of Israel.

sens: group of descendants of Jahzeel, son of Naphtali
H3184.detail: 1. The Jahtseelites are the members of the family clan that descended from Jahzeel, son of Naphtali (Numbers 26:48). Jahzeel lived during the time of Egypt and the wilderness, and his name means "God divides." His descendants formed a recognized family among the tribes of Israel.
H3184.origine: The word comes from Jahzeel (יַחְצְאֵל), whose name means "God divides" — the image of a division or partition that God operates. The suffix "-ite" (in Hebrew, the end of the word) indicates belonging to a family or clan group. Jahzeel is also referred to as Jahziel in 1 Chronicles 7:13. Jahzeel was the son of Naphtali and brother of Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
H3184.emploi: The Jahtseelites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in the wilderness census in Numbers 26:48, where Moses enumerates the families of the tribe of Naphtali. They appear alongside other clans born of Naphtali, such as the Gunites and the Jezerites. This census aimed to organize Israel in view of the conquest of Canaan.

sens: son of Naphtali
ancestor of a family of Israel
H3185.detail:
1. Jahtsiel is one of the four sons of Naphtali, himself a son of Jacob. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 7:13 as the first son of Naphtali, indicating his importance in the genealogy of the tribe.
2. As a son of Naphtali, Jahtsiel is the founding ancestor of a family lineage within the tribe of Naphtali. These genealogical lineages marked the identity and place of each family within the people of Israel.
H3185.origine: The name Jahtsiel means "God divides" in Hebrew. It reflects a theology where God is the one who distributes and shares blessings. This name belongs to the generation of the twelve sons of Jacob and carries the imprint of the patriarchs' faith in divine providence.
H3185.emploi: Jahtsiel is mentioned only once in the Bible in 1 Chronicles 7:13, in the genealogical list of the sons of Naphtali. He is presented as the first of Naphtali's four sons, born of Bilhah (Rachel's maid). This genealogical mention places Jahtsiel in the history of the people of Israel as the founder of a family that will bear his name, the Jahtzeelites.

sens: To inscribe a person on a genealogical list or family register
To establish or recognize someone's ancestry and descendants
To count someone as belonging to a recognized group or lineage
H3187.detail:
1. Genealogically register means to inscribe a person's name in a genealogical register, that is, in a list that traces their lineage and belonging to a family. In 1 Chronicles 9:22, porters were "registered in genealogies according to their villages," meaning their names appeared in official lists that identified each family and clan.
2. It also means to publicly establish or recognize someone's lineage — who their ancestors are, their father, their mother, their tribe. In 1 Chronicles 5:17, people "were all registered in genealogies during the time of Jotham and Jeroboam," meaning their genealogies were officially documented and recognized.
3. By extension, it is to count someone as part of a recognized community: in Ezra 2:62, individuals could not be recognized as priests because their genealogy was not recorded, thus they were excluded from temple service.
H3187.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root meaning "to calculate" or "to count." It depicts the action of marking, noting, keeping a record — in this case, keeping the register of families and their descendants. The form used in the Bible (the Hithpael) adds the sense of a reflexive action: "to be registered," "to be counted in a genealogical list." This vocabulary was central to the life of the people of Israel, where lineage and tribal belonging determined religious and social rights.
H3187.emploi: This verb appears eighteen times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah — the historical books that reconstruct Israel after the exile. Chronicles uses it to describe how the Levites, priests, and warriors were inscribed in official records (1 Chronicles 5:17, 7:9, 9:22). Ezra and Nehemiah use it when they report the return from exile and the establishment of genealogies of the families of Israel (Ezra 8:3, Nehemiah 7:5). In all these contexts, being "genealogically registered" means being officially recognized as belonging to the people of God, which was crucial for participating in worship or accessing priestly duties.
H3187.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the importance of identity and belonging. Israel carefully preserved its genealogies because they proved who one was, where one came from, and what one's right to worship God was. Spiritually, being "registered" among the people of God — known by God, recognized as His — remains a precious reality: Luke 10:20 speaks of names written in heaven. This word invites the reader to meditate on the security of their status in Christ and the value of true identity in God.

sens: Official list of names and generations of a family or group
Written document that records and preserves origins and descendants
State of one who is inscribed or registered in a genealogy
H3188.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a list, a register that records the names of the generations of a family. In 2 Chronicles 31:17, the priests are "registered" according to their paternal houses: an official document was drawn up bearing their name and their connection to their clan, to organize the service of the sanctuary according to these family divisions.
2. More broadly, it is the written document itself that preserves and organizes these genealogies. In Nehemiah 7:5, Nehemiah discovers a "genealogical register" of the first exiles who returned to Jerusalem: it is a scroll or document where the names of ancestors and their descendants are noted, allowing knowledge of the origins of the inhabitants.
3. The word can also describe the act of being registered, inscribed in this register (2 Chronicles 31:18): those of the assembly who are "registered" with their families are recognized as officially belonging to the people dedicated to the service of God.
H3188.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to count," "to enumerate," or "to recount a genealogy." It is related to the verb "to count" and the noun "genealogy" (ḥasab). The image is that of tracing a continuous line of names, from generation to generation, as one enumerates or counts the steps of a lineage. In biblical Hebrew, genealogies are essential for establishing identity, heritage, and legal status of a person or family within the community of Israel.
H3188.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always in the context of the administrative and religious organization of Israel. In 2 Chronicles 31:17-18, in the context of King Hezekiah's reforms, the genealogical register serves to organize the priests and Levites according to their families and to officially recognize those who dedicate themselves to the worship of the sanctuary. In Nehemiah 7:5, after the return from exile, a genealogical register allows Nehemiah to know who has returned and to establish their legitimate status in the restored community. Each time, the genealogical register is a tool of legitimacy and organization: it establishes who truly belongs to the people of Israel and how families are connected to God's covenant.
H3188.portee: This word reminds us that God knows each person's name, lineage, and history. The genealogical registers in the Bible express the importance of identity: God does not forget His children, He counts them, He knows them. For us, this means that our life and our place in the people of God are not the result of chance, but are rooted in a history and a name recognized by the Lord.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah
Son of Reaiah
Father of Achumai and Lahad
H3189G.detail: Jachath is a man of the tribe of Judah, mentioned in the genealogies of the book of Chronicles. He is the son of Reaiah and the grandson of Shobal (1 Chronicles 4:2). He appears as the father of Achumai and Lahad, which shows his role in the genealogical continuity of Judah. His name means "He will seize" or "He will take away," evoking the divine action of taking or removing.
H3189G.origine: The name Jachath comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of seizing or taking away. This name belongs to the onomastic tradition of Israel, where names often express an action or quality attributed by the parent to their child, like a prayer or a vow. In the context of the genealogies of Judah, this name fits into the series of family names that mark the transmission of promise and heritage.
H3189G.emploi: Jachath is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 4:2, where he appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Judah. He is presented as an important link in the genealogical chain: son of Reaiah, grandson of Shobal, and father of Achumai and Lahad. This appearance in Chronicles reflects the importance that the sacred writers placed on genealogical transmission in the tribe of Judah, as these lists guaranteed the heritage and identity of the people.

sens: Son of Shimei, a Levite of the lineage of Gershom
H3189H.detail: Jachath is a Levite belonging to the tribe of Levi, a descendant of Gershom (who himself was a son of Levi). He is the eldest son of Shimei and the brother of Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. According to 1 Chronicles 23:10-11, Jachath was the head of the paternal house of Shimei during the census of the Levites at the time of King David.
H3189H.origine: The name Jachath means "He will take away" or "He will remove," formed from a Hebrew root expressing the action of seizing or taking away. This theophoric name reflects the parents' hope in God's action.
H3189H.emploi: Jachath appears twice in 1 Chronicles, in chapter 23. He is mentioned as the son of Shimei, a Levite of the lineage of Gershom. During the census of the Levites under the reign of David, Jachath is designated as the chief (the principal) of the paternal house of Shimei, while his brother Zina held the second rank. His two other brothers, Jeush and Beriah, had few sons and formed one paternal house with the others.

sens: A Levite, son of Libni and grandson of Gershom
H3189I.detail: Jachath is a member of the tribe of Levi, descended from Gershom, son of Levi. He is the son of Libni and the father of Zimma (1 Chronicles 6:20). He appears in the genealogy of the Levites, the priestly lineage of Israel responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple.
H3189I.origine: The name Jachath means "He will seize" or "He will take away," formed from a Hebrew root expressing the action of seizing or taking. This name reflects an attitude of power or taking control. Several men bore this name in the history of Israel, but the provided usages specifically concern a Levite from the lineage of Gershom.
H3189I.emploi: Jachath appears twice in the text of 1 Chronicles, in verses 6:20 and 6:43, both in the genealogy of the Levites. Verse 6:20 mentions him as the son of Libni and father of Zimma, in the direct succession. Verse 6:43 confirms this by placing him in the complete lineage: son of Jachath, son of Gershom, son of Levi. These two mentions establish his fixed place in the genealogical record of God's people.

sens: Levite of the clan of Shelomoth
member of the priestly family assigned to the temple
H3189J.detail: Jachath is a man of the tribe of Levi mentioned only once in Scripture, at the time of the organization of the priestly families during the divided kingdom. He belongs to the lineage of Shelomoth and is one of the family heads of the Levites assigned to the service of the temple.
H3189J.origine: The name Jachath means in Hebrew "he will take away" or "he will snatch away," evoking an action of seizing or snatching. It comes from a Hebrew root expressing this idea of rapid or violent taking. It is a name typically given to descendants of Levi, whose descendants were dedicated to the cultic service of the God of Israel.
H3189J.emploi: Jachath appears only once in Scripture: 1 Chronicles 24:22, a passage that enumerates the organization of the Levitical families during the divided kingdom. He is cited there as the son of Shelomoth, one of the heads of Levitical houses whose descendants had specific responsibilities in the temple worship. This passage shows that even lesser-known or lower-ranking Levites were counted and recognized in the official structure of Israelite ministry.

sens: Levite during the reign of King Josiah
son of Shelomoth
Merrarite Levite
H3189K.detail: Jachath is a Levite who lived during the reform of King Josiah in the 7th century BC. He appears in 2 Chronicles 34:12, where he is mentioned as one of the overseers of the temple repairs: he is a Levite "of the sons of Merari," meaning belonging to the Levitical branch of the Merarites. His role was to supervise the work with integrity (honesty and uprightness), alongside other Levitical leaders like Abijah. He embodied the trust placed in him to manage the sacred work.
H3189K.origine: The name Jachath means in Hebrew "He will tear away" or "He will seize" (from the root חתת, "to seize"). This name reflects the strength and authority expected of a leader. Several men bore this name in the history of Israel: descendants of Levi across different generations, which shows its importance in Levitical families.
H3189K.emploi: Jachath appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 34:12, in the account of the temple restoration under King Josiah in the 7th century BC. On this occasion, the chronicler designates him as one of the Levitical leaders responsible for overseeing the repairs of the sanctuary. He is presented as a man "who acted with integrity," highlighting his moral integrity and administrative competence. His mention alongside other renowned Levites indicates that he was a respected and trusted figure in the temple service.
H3189K.portee: The mention of Jachath reminds us that God's work requires faithful and upright men and women to be accomplished. Although he is named only once, Jachath represents those loyal servants whose honesty and diligence contribute to the spiritual renewal of a community. His example encourages the reader to seek integrity in their responsibilities, whether small or great.

sens: To be in good condition, to be suitable, to go well
To please, to be agreeable
To rejoice, to be content
To do good, to treat favorably
To do well, to act correctly
To beautify, to make beautiful
H3190.detail:
1. The word first describes a situation that is going well, that is suitable. Cain should lift his face "if you do well" (Genesis 4:7): it is an action that produces a good result, that arranges things. Moses tells Israel: "all that they have said is good" (Deuteronomy 5:28), meaning that their words correspond to what is right and appropriate.
2. The word also means to please, to be agreeable to the eyes or ears. In Proverbs 15:2, "the tongue of the wise makes knowledge pleasant": it makes it pleasant to hear, it pleases. It is an action that makes an impression, that captivates.
3. It expresses joy and satisfaction: "let your heart rejoice" (1 Kings 21:7) speaks of a feeling of well-being, of inner joy. The soul flourishes, it tastes what is good.
4. To be good to someone means to act with kindness, to do good to them. "The Lord will do good to me" (Judges 17:13) expresses trust in a favorable intervention from God. It is to treat someone with generosity and care.
5. The verb also denotes the action of doing well, of acting correctly according to God's will. "Do well what is before your eyes" is the call to accomplish one's task with care and faithfulness.
6. Finally, it can mean to beautify or perfect: to make something beautiful, complete, reformed. It is to restore what was lacking.
H3190.origine: The verb יָטַב comes from a root that expresses the idea of suitability and rectitude. In Hebrew, the family of this word includes טוֹב "good," which is one of the greatest biblical concepts: what is suitable, just, pleasant, capable of nourishing and satisfying. The noun טוּב "goodness" also derives from it. This root expresses harmony, a natural order: when something "is good," it fulfills its function, it pleases, it builds up.
H3190.emploi: This verb appears about 110 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives, the Law, and biblical wisdom. In the commandments (Deuteronomy 5:16, 6:3, 12:25), it often carries the idea of acting well so that it goes well with you. In the Psalms and Proverbs, it expresses spiritual and moral well-being: rejoicing before God, or making something pleasant. With God as the subject, it signifies divine kindness: "the Lord will do good to me" (Judges 17:13). With a human being, it can describe a concrete action (treating someone well, acting justly) or a disposition (rejoicing, finding something good). The context determines whether the emphasis is on the action, the feeling, or the result.
H3190.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian life has a dual dimension: doing good (obeying, acting justly) and receiving good (enjoying God's kindness). It states a fundamental biblical principle: whoever acts well finds that it goes well for them, and whoever receives good from God rejoices in it. This verb invites us to seek what is truly good, not according to our desires, but according to the will of the Lord.

sens: To have a good nature, a positive quality
To do good, to act positively
To seem appropriate, to suit, to please
H3191.detail:
1. The word describes what is good in itself, possessing a positive quality. It is the state or nature of what opposes evil or deficiency. In Ezra 7:18, King Artaxerxes grants Ezra and his brothers the right to do with the silver and gold "what you deem good" — that is, what seems just and beneficial to them.
2. To be good also means to accomplish what is benevolent, useful, advantageous. It is to act positively towards others.
3. The verb can designate what seems suitable, appropriate, or pleasing to someone — what pleases them or aligns with their will.
H3191.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew יָטַב (ya.tav), which means "to be good" or "to go well." The root fundamentally expresses the idea of goodness, benevolence, and usefulness. It belongs to the same group of words as "good" (טוֹב, tov) in Hebrew, which describes what has a positive or benevolent quality.
H3191.emploi: This Aramaic verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 7:18. It is found in the decree of King Artaxerxes I to Ezra: the king acknowledges the high priest and his companions the power to freely decide the use of gold and silver, "according to what seems good to you." The context shows that the word here means "to judge appropriate" or "to find good," that is, to exercise benevolent discernment. The Aramaic usage remains very close to classical Hebrew.
H3191.portee: This word reminds us that goodness is not merely a subjective impression: it is a real quality, a good to be accomplished, and also a wise judgment that discerns what is fitting. For the believer, doing what is "good" means aligning one's actions with God's will and seeking the benefit of others.

sens: City of Judah, homeland of Meshullameth
H3192.detail: Jotba is a small city in the kingdom of Judah, known in Scripture as the birthplace of Meshullameth, mother of King Amon (2 Kings 21:19). Its name means "pleasant" or "agreeable," perhaps evoking a fertile or appreciated place. Although it is mentioned only once in the Bible, this reference allows us to know the geographical origins of the mother of a king of Judah.
H3192.origine: The name Jotba comes from Hebrew and literally means "pleasant" or "agreeable." It is a toponym, that is, a place name, which likely reflects the characteristics or reputation of the site at the time it received this name.
H3192.emploi: Jotba appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 21:19, where it is designated as the city of origin of Meshullameth. She was the daughter of Haruz and became the wife of King Manasseh of Judah, then the mother of King Amon. This unique mention places Jotba in the dynastic history of the kingdom of Judah, even though we have no other biblical information about the city itself.

sens: Stage in the desert where the Israelites camped during the Exodus
Place characterized by the presence of water and waterways
H3193.detail: 1. Jothbatha is a stop in the long journey of the Israelites through the desert after their departure from Egypt. It is mentioned in the itineraries of successive stops: after leaving Hor-Haggidgad, the people camped there before departing for Abronah (Numbers 33:33-34). 2. What distinguishes Jothbatha is its geographical particularity: unlike many other stops in the arid desert, it is a "land where there are streams of water" (Deuteronomy 10:7). In the midst of the desert, the presence of water was precious and marked a place of welcome for the weary people.
H3193.origine: The Hebrew name means "pleasant" or "joke," evoking a pleasant place. Its spelling varies slightly between Numbers (Jothbatha) and Deuteronomy (Jothbatha), but it designates the same location. The name likely reflects the positive impression this verdant site left on desert travelers.
H3193.emploi: Jothbatha is mentioned three times in the Bible, exclusively to mark the stops of the Exodus. It appears in the detailed list of the forty-two encampments in the desert (Numbers 33:33-34) and is recalled in the account of Deuteronomy 10:7 when Moses enumerates the journey taken. These references show that it was an established and memorable stop on the Israelites' journey to the Promised Land.

sens: Fortified city in the mountains of Judah, between Maon and Carmel
H3194.detail: 1. Jutta is a mountain city located in the territory of Judah, near Maon and Carmel (Joshua 15:55). It is one of the cities assigned to the Levites for them to dwell in with their flocks (Joshua 21:16), making it an important religious and administrative center in this mountainous region.
H3194.origine: The name Jutta literally means "expanse" or "stretched out," likely referring to the shape of the site or its territorial extent. Modern archaeology has identified this ancient city with the current site of Yutta in the West Bank, confirming the continuity of the name through the centuries.
H3194.emploi: Jutta is mentioned three times in the Old Testament, all in contexts of territorial divisions. It first appears in the list of cities of Judah (Joshua 15:55), then in the list of Levitical cities assigned to the children of Kohath (Joshua 21:16 and 1 Chronicles 6:59). Its inclusion among the cities of the Levites shows that it had a religious function and served as a refuge for these descendants of Aaron who had no land of their own.

sens: Son of Ishmael and ancestor of an Arab people
H3195G.detail: Jethur is one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, mentioned in the genealogies of the Old Testament. His descendants formed an Arab tribe that lived east of the Jordan and, according to biblical history, had hostile relations with Israel. The name evokes the idea of enclosure or fencing, perhaps alluding to defined lands or a group with set borders.
H3195G.origine: The name Jethur (יְטוּר) comes from Hebrew and means "he who is enclosed" or "fenced in," derived from a root that evokes the enclosing or delimiting of territory. It is a typical Semitic name from the patriarchal tradition, reflecting both a genealogical identity and possibly a geographical or territorial characteristic of the people of whom he is an ancestor.
H3195G.emploi: Jethur appears only twice in the Bible, both in the genealogies of Ishmael. In Genesis 25:15, he is listed among the twelve sons of Ishmael along with his brothers Hadad, Tema, Naphish, and Kedmah. This list is found almost identically in 1 Chronicles 1:31. These genealogies establish the origin of the Arab peoples contemporary to the patriarchal times and remind us of the common roots between Israel and these desert peoples, all descended from Abraham according to the biblical account. Jethur represents one of these eponymous ancestors whose descendants occupied the desert regions east of the Jordan.

sens: Son of Ishmael
People living east of the Jordan
H3195H.detail: Jethur is one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, himself the son of Abraham. The name literally means "enclosed" or "surrounded." The descendants of Jethur formed a nomadic people or tribe that settled east of the Jordan, in the territory of Transjordan. This people is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 5:19 as having fought against the Israelite tribes of the Reubenites, Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, alongside other peoples: the Hagarites, Naphish, and Nodab. Later, the region they occupied became known as Iturea, a territory recognizable in New Testament times.
H3195H.origine: The name Jethur comes from the Hebrew root that evokes the idea of being "surrounded" or "closed in." He is a direct descendant of Ishmael, whose name means "God has heard." Ishmael's family had twelve sons who became the ancestors of nomadic desert peoples of Arabia and Transjordan.
H3195H.emploi: Jethur appears only once in the Bible: in 1 Chronicles 5:19. He is cited as one of the tribes against which the Israelites fought during territorial conflicts east of the Jordan. This passage shows that the descendants of Jethur formed a military power significant enough to pose a threat to the established Israelite tribes in Transjordan. The biblical text places them among other nomadic and warrior peoples of the eastern desert.

sens: Fermented drink made from grape juice
Consumer product and commercial exchange
Cause of drunkenness and intoxication
Symbol of divine anger and judgment
Element of worship and religious offering
Poetic image of love and sweetness
H3196.detail:
1. Wine is the fermented drink made from grapes, very common in the diet of the Hebrews. Noah drank it and became drunk (Genesis 9:21). It is a regular part of meals, served at royal banquets (Esther 7:2) and ceremonies.
2. It is a precious commodity that is produced, preserved, bought, and sold. Damascus provides high-quality wine (Ezekiel 27:18), and King David receives it as a gift (2 Samuel 16:2). Wine reserves protect a city in case of siege (2 Chronicles 11:11).
3. Drinking too much wine leads to drunkenness and loss of self-control. Genesis 9:21 clearly shows this: Noah "became drunk" and uncovered himself. Proverbs 20:1 warns: "Wine is a mocker."
4. In prophetic language, wine becomes an image of divine anger poured out on enemies. The cup of wine (or judgment) symbolizes the punishments that God inflicts (Psalms 75:9).
5. Wine is included in offerings at the sanctuary: it is a libation poured on the altar to honor God (Exodus 29:40, Numbers 15:5).
6. In poetry and love, wine evokes sweetness, the intoxication of feeling. The Song of Solomon mentions it as a symbol of savoring love (Song of Solomon 1:4).
H3196.origine: The Hebrew word יַיִן (yaïn) is an ancient root found in other Semitic languages. It simply refers to fermented grape juice.
