The starting image is that of pressed grapes fermenting and transforming: a natural, slow, and chemical process that fascinates the ancient world. This is why wine often represents change, transformation, the intoxication of the heart or spirit.
H3196.emploi: The word wine appears 134 times in the Hebrew Bible, highlighting its crucial importance. It is mentioned in almost every book, from the early narratives (Genesis 9 and 14) to the wisdom literature (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes) and the prophecies (Isaiah, Ezekiel). In its primary sense, it is an ordinary drink at meals and celebrations, a symbol of prosperity (Deuteronomy 14:26). However, gradually, the intoxication of wine becomes a metaphor for the effects of divine judgment, particularly among the prophets. The prohibitions against wine (Numbers 6:3 for the Nazarite, Leviticus 10:9 for priests on duty) also show that it symbolizes consecrated separation or holiness. Its absence marks times of wilderness (Deuteronomy 29:6) where God acts independently of the land.
H3196.portee: Wine reminds us that all joy and pleasure come from God, but that abuse corrupts the heart and disturbs judgment. Drinking wine without wisdom is to abandon self-control. Conversely, receiving wine from God's hands is to enjoy His blessings with gratitude. In the prophetic vision, the cup of wine of divine anger teaches that judgment is certain and extends to all peoples: none escape it. It is a call to repentance and obedience.

sens: Prove something, establish that one is right
Judge between people, arbitrate a dispute
Address reproaches, reprimand
Correct, punish to amend
H3198.detail:
1. Prove or establish something: show that one is right in a matter, demonstrate the justice of a position. In Genesis 31:37, Jacob asks Laban: "Let them search for themselves if there is anything of yours with me," seeking to prove his innocence.
2. Judge or arbitrate between people: serve as a judge to resolve a dispute, decide between two parties. In Isaiah 2:4, it is said of the Messiah: "He will judge the nations, arbitrate for many peoples."
3. Address reproaches, reprimand someone: point out their faults, express disapproval with the intention of amending. In Proverbs 9:8, it is written: "Reprove a wise man, and he will love you," showing that reproof can be received with gratitude.
4. Correct or punish: chastise someone for their errors in order to correct them. In Psalms 38:2, the psalmist implores: "O Lord! Do not rebuke me in Your anger," showing that God reproves His children to correct them.
H3198.origine: The Hebrew verb יָכַח comes from a root that evokes the idea of separating, distinguishing, thus highlighting what is right or wrong. The word family includes יַכְחַ (argument, reproach) and is used with nuances depending on the context: deciding in a judgment, proving a point, or correcting someone. The word always carries the idea of a demonstration of truth, whether legal, logical, or moral.
H3198.emploi: This verb appears 55 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and the prophetic books. As judgment or arbitration, it denotes the action of a judge who decides, notably the Messiah (Isaiah 2:4, 11:3-4). As reproof or correction, it is often used to describe divine discipline towards His people or His relationship with the righteous (Proverbs 3:12: "For the Lord reproves him whom He loves"), but also among humans (Leviticus 19:17: "You shall not hate your brother"). Job frequently uses this verb to express his desire to plead his case before God (Job 13:3, 13:15). The meaning extends from legal to moral: to correct for improvement, not for destruction.
H3198.portee: This word shows that reproof and correction, far from being simply negative, can be forms of divine love and attention. For the believer, accepting a just reproof from God or a wise person is to receive a blessing. It also reveals that God does not ignore injustices: He will judge, plead the cause of His elect, and establish justice. Finally, it invites discernment between a reproof received with humility, which builds, and a refusal to listen, which hardens.

sens: Son of Simeon, one of the twelve patriarchs of Israel
Head of a family and founder of the clan of the Jakinites
H3199G.detail:
1. Jakin is one of the sons of Simeon, listed among the children of the patriarch during the descent into Egypt. He appears in the genealogical list alongside his brothers Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Tsochar, and Saul (Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15).
2. In the next generation, Jakin is recognized as the head of a household: his descendants bear the family name "Jakinites" (Numbers 26:12), making him an ancestral founder of a branch of the people of Israel.
H3199G.origine: The name means "He will establish" or "He will strengthen." It derives from a root expressing the idea of founding, consolidating, establishing firmly. In the Old Testament, this name carries the hope of stability and assured posterity by God, which perfectly corresponds to Jakin's genealogical role: ancestor of a lasting tribal lineage in Israel.
H3199G.emploi: Jakin is mentioned only three times in the Bible, all in genealogical and census passages. He first appears in the list of the sons of Simeon who descend into Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:10), then repeated in the account of the Exodus (Exodus 6:15) when Moses and Aaron are presented. Finally, during the census in the wilderness, his descendants are counted as a full family among the tribes of Israel (Numbers 26:12). These three mentions show the importance of genealogy among the chosen people: Jakin, though little known, constitutes an essential link in the continuity of Israel.

sens: Right column of Solomon's temple
H3199H.detail: 1. Jakin is the name of the right column that stood at the entrance of the temple in Jerusalem, built by King Solomon. This monumental bronze column, eighteen cubits high according to 1 Kings 7, was a major architectural structure of the sanctuary. Together with its twin Boaz, placed on the left, it formed an imposing entrance portico symbolizing the power and stability of the temple of the living God (1 Kings 7:21 and 2 Chronicles 3:17).
H3199H.origine: The name Jakin literally means "He will establish" or "He will make firm" in Hebrew, derived from the root "kun" which means "to establish, to found, to make firm." This prophetic name expresses the idea that God establishes and strengthens His temple and His presence among His people. The right column (Jakin) and the left column (Boaz, "In Him is strength") together form a confession of faith: the Lord establishes and fortifies His house.
H3199H.emploi: Jakin appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the description of Solomon's temple: in 1 Kings 7:21 and in 2 Chronicles 3:17. These two identical passages report how King Solomon, through his craftsman Hiram, named the two bronze columns of the temple portico. Jakin, placed on the right, was associated with the theme of divine establishment, while Boaz on the left emphasized the strength of the Lord. These monumental columns did not have a major structural function; they were primarily symbolic, proclaiming the nature of the God whose temple had just been built.
H3199H.portee: These two column names reveal the theology of the temple: God establishes His dwelling in the midst of His people and manifests His unshakeable strength there. For the Christian, the physical temple of Jerusalem foreshadows the Church, the body of Christ, where God establishes and fortifies the foundations of His presence and salvation.

sens: Levitical priest during the exile and return
H3199I.detail: Jakin is a priest of the tribe of Levi mentioned twice in the Bible, at key moments in Israel's history. His name means "He will establish" or "He will make firm," expressing a trust in the stability that God brings. He first appears in 1 Chronicles 9:10, among the priests who returned from exile in Babylon and were restored to temple service. He is then found in Nehemiah 11:10, where he is mentioned as a priest at the time of Nehemiah, when Jerusalem is rebuilt and reorganized after the exile. These two mentions show that Jakin played a role in the restoration of worship and the Jewish community after captivity.
H3199I.origine: The name Jakin comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to establish," "to make firm," or "to prepare." This name expresses the idea of stability and foundation—a trust that God will establish or make firm something. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries a word about God and His action.
H3199I.emploi: Jakin appears twice in the provided biblical usages, always designated as a priest (sacrificer). In 1 Chronicles 9:10, he is listed among the priests who returned from exile and were reestablished in Jerusalem for temple service. In Nehemiah 11:10, he is named among the priests established in the rebuilt city at the time of Nehemiah. These two passages place Jakin in the post-exilic restoration period when Israel reorganizes its worship and community life after Babylonian captivity.
H3199I.portee: The name Jakin, "He will establish," resonates with his function as a priest at the time when the people return from exile. As a servant of worship, he represents the faithfulness and continuity of the relationship between God and His people, even after the judgment of captivity. His role in the restoration of the temple invites the reader to see how God remains present and firm with His people, even in moments of fragility.

sens: Priest during the time of David
Chief of the twenty-first order of service in the temple
H3199J.detail: Jakin is a priest who lived during the reign of David. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:17, where he is designated as the head of the twenty-first order or division of priests. David organized the priesthood into twenty-four courses (or groups), each responsible for serving in the temple for a defined period. Jakin led one of these priestly courses, indicating that he was a man of rank and religious authority in the temple worship.
H3199J.origine: The name Jakin means "he will establish" or "he will make stable," coming from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of fixing, consolidating, or erecting. This name reflects the Israelite theological conviction that God establishes and strengthens what is enduring. Several priests and Levites bore this name in sacred history, highlighting its prestige in the context of the priesthood.
H3199J.emploi: Jakin is mentioned exclusively in 1 Chronicles 24:17. According to this passage, David had reorganized the priests into twenty-four courses to ensure continuous service in the temple. Jakin was responsible for the twenty-first of these divisions. This organization aimed to guarantee that worship would be conducted without interruption throughout the year. The text places him among other priestly leaders, showing that temple service was structured and hierarchical.
H3199J.portee: This passage reminds the believer that sincere worship requires order, regularity, and responsibility. The presence of Jakin among David's priests illustrates how God organizes His people to serve Him with respect and faithfulness. It invites us to reflect on the place of service and regular commitment in the Christian life.
